content: It may not be long before the whole US stock market has a Situational Awareness moment. At least, that's the worst-case scenario being mulled by some analysts on Wall Street, who have increasingly turned their attention to one eye-popping statistic in the market: Margin debt held by investors has swelled to records and grown at a pace recently that's only been seen leading up to major corrections. The fear is that a steep tech sell-off could be the spark that causes the record amount of borrowed cash to combust, triggering margin calls and resulting in a wave of forced selling that derails the bull market. It may sound like an unlikely scenario, but it's a growing risk investors need to contend with, especially considering how concentrated the market is in tech and how exposed US households are to a sudden drop in equity prices, investing pros told Business Insider. Investors who trade on margin can buy stocks or purchase investment products by borrowing funds from a broker. But if the value of their positions falls below a certain threshold, investors get hit with a margin call, demanding they deposit more money into their margin accounts. If they can't, brokers can sell their positions, sometimes at a loss to the investor. It's what caused South Korea's stock market to tank this summer. Retail investors in the nation were highly levered and hit with a wave of margin calls when chip and memory stocks began to drop this summer, triggering a spiral of forced selling. The same dynamic also led to the implosion of Situational Awareness, the highly levered hedge fund run by AI wizkid Leopold Aschenbrenner that bet heavily on chip stocks before being hit with margin calls this summer. Debit balances in customers' securities margin accounts hit a record $1.5 trillion in June, according to FINRA data. Levels have fallen slightly since the summer, but remain elevated. Margin debt clocked in at $1.4 trillion in August, up around 27% over the last year. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get. Margin debt falling from elevated levels has historically been a warning sign for markets, Peter Berezin, the chief economist at BCA Research, told Business Insider. When margin debt starts to fall, it generally signals low future returns for stocks, he said, adding that he would be worried about a deleveraging wave if margin debt were drop significantly from its summer peak. "Once that starts, it tends to feed on itself. Because as investors de-lever, that means they have to reduce their exposure to stocks; that pushes down stock prices, which leads to another wave of selling," he said. Berezin said investors may be uniquely vulnerable to such a sell-off in ways they haven't been in the past. He pointed to a few coexisting vulnerabilities that have the potential to make the scenario more dangerous: "From that perspective, this is a more risky stock market than it was even in 2000," Berezin said. Ross Mayfield, an investment strategist and vice president at Baird Private Wealth Management, told Business Insider he believed record levels of margin debt suggested that the rapid selling that tanked South Korean stocks this summer was also possible in the US. "I do think that there's maybe more fragility in the market structure just because of all of the different ways we've introduced leverage into the market," he said, though he noted that it wasn't an existential risk to markets. There are different ways to measure margin debt that suggest current levels of leverage are extreme from a historical perspective. As a percentage of the US's total market cap, margin debt remains near its historical 2% average, but as a ratio to M2 money supply, margin debt has reached levels comparable to those seen in 2008 and prior to the burst of the dot-com bubble, according to a March analysis from the financial services firm CGS International. Since 1997, there have only been three years when margin debt has grown as rapidly on a year-over-year basis: 2000, 2007, and 2021, which all preceded major market corrections, an analysis from Ameriprise Financial found. Anthony Saglimbene, Ameriprise's chief market strategist, outlined one scenario in which record concentration in tech stocks collides with record leverage, resulting in a "self-reinforcing" sell-off that hits the market's most concentrated names. "When leveraged participants all hold the same names, a factor that is growing, stress up or down can produce larger market swings that may seem out of step with headline developments," Saglimbene wrote in a note. There's no obvious place for investors to hide if forced-selling takes hold, Berezin said. He noted that the deleveraging that came as the dot-com bubble burst came in two distinct waves: The first, which came in early 2000, was a rotation away from tech stocks, in which investors were able to find safety by heading into other sectors of the market. The second was a broad-based market sell-off that began in 2001, where all areas of the market were badly hit. Markets look like they're moving toward the "rotation" phase today, Berezin said, pointing to the recent sell-off in the chips and memory space. He speculated that a broader market sell-off similar to 2001 might not happen for at least several more years. "It's probably too early to sound the alarm, but it's not too early to be worried about what happens once things begin to deteriorate. Because once they do, I think it will feed on itself," he said. This year's descent into fall has been more of a crawl, but I think we're all ready for some cozy weather. And what better accompaniment to a classic rom-com and your favorite sweater than a dish by Ina Garten? The "Barefoot Contessa" star has built a whole career on recipes that are easy and comforting. I've made dozens of Garten's dishes, so I decided to look back and find a few that I think are perfect for this busy season. From a Bolognese that's ready in 30 minutes to a cake packed with the flavors of autumn, these are Garten's best fall dishes. The start of fall is so hectic. Work ramps back up, school is back in session, and the prep and stress of the holidays begin to creep in. Travel-friendly and loaded with protein, a breakfast sandwich is just what you need. And Garten's version only requires five ingredients: English muffins, whole milk, avocado, bacon, cheddar cheese, and eggs that you can cook in the microwave. Everything in Garten's breakfast sandwich works so well together. She recommends using thick-cut applewood-smoked bacon, which provides a crispy contrast to the soft eggs. Spreading the avocado on the bottom adds both flavor and nutrients, and I love the tanginess of the sharp white cheddar. If you're making this sandwich for more than two people, I recommend cooking the eggs on the stove rather than in the microwave to save time. But this is a great recipe to teach your kids so they can make breakfast on their own. And if you're a college student, you could easily whip this up in a dorm. Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's bacon, egg, and cheddar sandwich here. I began testing Garten's soup recipes in 2023 and knew something was missing after I kept using boxed stock. "Store-bought is fine!" might be Garten's most famous catchphrase, but she believes homemade chicken stock is akin to "liquid gold." "Nothing available on the market has the depth of flavor or richness of stock you've made yourself," she wrote in "Go-To Dinners," her October 2022 cookbook. "It contributes such great body and aroma to so many dishes. Plus, having a big pot of chicken stock simmering away on my stove just makes me feel good." Garten's stock is packed with flavor because it involves simmering three roasting chickens for hours alongside carrots, onions, celery, parsnips, garlic, and plenty of herbs. There's no flavor left in the chicken once the stock is ready. If you'd rather save the meat for meals, you can always take the chicken out once it's cooked through and continue to simmer the aromatics. I also recommend freezing chicken bones so you always have some on hand for more stock. Garten's recipe provides nearly nine quarts of stock, and you can store it in the freezer for up to six months. My absolute favorite Barefoot Contessa soup to make with the stock is Garten's chicken pot pie soup, which I whip up anytime my fiancé and I are craving a bowl of comfort. Her ravioli en brodo is a delicious twist on chicken noodle, while her Italian wedding soup is light and bright. If you want to switch things up from soup, you can also use the stock to make Garten's one-pot chicken and orzo — another delicious meal for chilly nights. Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's homemade chicken stock here. Garten served traditional chili for two decades at the specialty food store she ran in the Hamptons before becoming a cookbook author and Food Network star. When Garten decided to switch up the chili and use chicken instead of beef, it became even more popular than the original recipe. The dish also features red and yellow bell peppers, fresh basil, and a variety of seasonings, including chili powder, ground cumin, and red pepper flakes. Garten serves the chili topped with green onions, cheddar cheese, corn chips, and sour cream. The tomatoes and spices build a rich broth, and each bite of chicken is so tender and juicy. It's also a great dish for hosting because you can lay out the toppings in individual dishes, allowing everyone to personalize their bowl to their own preference. Plus, who doesn't love a bowl of chili on football Sunday? Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's chicken chili here. My pasta cravings always hit when temperatures start to dip. And during this busy season, Garten's weeknight Bolognese is a perfect fit. The recipe includes ground sirloin, crushed tomatoes, heavy cream, Parmesan cheese, and fresh basil, but it's designed to be adaptable and pantry-friendly. Garten says you could easily swap the sirloin for any ground meat and skip the cream and basil if you need. And while she recommends using orecchiette, any dried pasta will work with this recipe. It's pretty incredible how much flavor Garten manages to create in a dish that traditionally simmers for hours on end. The rich sauce bursts through every bite of the small pasta shells, which I personally loved for this dish, and the freshly grated Parmesan cheese on top makes it feel extra comforting and indulgent. "It's a very meaty, very hearty pasta," my dad said before declaring that the dish was "perfect." We loved the dish so much that it earned the second spot in my ongoing ranking of Barefoot Contessa pasta dishes. Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's weeknight Bolognese here. The rigatoni pasta is paired with sausage and fennel, plus some onion, garlic, heavy cream, freshly grated Parmesan cheese, and a few additional ingredients. It all comes together in a big pot or Dutch oven, and you'll have dinner on the table in an hour. "You can make the whole thing in one big pot, bring it to the table, and everyone loves it," Garten told her viewers in a 2017 episode of "Barefoot Contessa." With its beautiful golden hue and rich, meaty sauce, Garten's one-pot pasta is the kind of dish that lifts your spirits. There's also lovely depth to the flavor, thanks to the sweet sausage, salty Parm, and the bite from the fennel. Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's rigatoni with sausage and fennel here. "We used to have all kinds of cakes like this out on the bakery counter, and you could come buy a whole cake, but you could also buy a piece," Garten said in an early episode of her Food Network show. "It's not fancy, just really delicious and earthy, and you always want to come back for more." The recipe includes Granny Smith apples, rum, raisins, pecans, and plenty of sugar and spice. Soaking the golden raisins in rum gave them a flavor that almost reminded me of caramel, and their sweetness helped temper the Granny Smith apples' sourness. All the spices infused the moist cake with a warm nuttiness, while the pecans added some delicious crunch. I followed Garten's advice and tried the cake with some ice cream and caramel, which were delicious additions. But the cake isn't super sweet, so you could also enjoy it on its own with some tea or coffee for breakfast. Now it's really starting to feel like fall. Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's apple spice cake here. Is there a dish you love making in the fall season? Share it with us in the comments. And check out more easy recipes here. You can’t really talk about smart glasses without bringing up Meta. HTC, the company behind 2010-era virtual reality headsets and a failed smartphone business, seems quite eager to tackle that comparison directly. In September, HTC started selling its $499 Vive Eagle smart glasses in the US. The Eagles have lots of the same features as other glasses on the market—cameras for capturing photos and video, speakers in the frames for music playback and calls, an embedded AI agent you can ask questions of and even get recipes from by taking pictures of stuff in your fridge. But HTC also wants to steer clear of the ongoing debate about privacy in camera-equipped smart glasses. Meta has been dogged by controversy for its smart glasses, with people worried about the company’s interest in enabling face-recognition features, and calling the people who wear them creepy. HTC is aware of that discourse and thinks it is completely possible to make smart glasses that aren’t a privacy nightmare. “It's not just about protecting the consumer, but it's also about protecting people around the consumer,” Dan McDowell, HTC Vive’s head of enterprise sales, tells WIRED. “People can usher in, I think, what are really tremendous experiences with a new layer of confidence and protection.” I’ve been wandering around with the glasses for a couple of weeks, and so far they meet my expectations for what smart glasses have become. They protect my eyes from the sun. They snap good photos and videos. You can record and transcribe voice notes. The music playback has decent sound quality. (I’ll always prefer a solid pair of headphones if I’m actually trying to listen to music, but the speakers work just fine.) They come in two styles—one with square Wayfarer-esque lenses and the other more rounded. The Vive Eagle glasses can get 4.5 hours of battery life on continuous music playback. They can last 36 hours on standby. HTC also sells a companion clip-on battery pack called Power Boost that costs $49. It clips right onto the frame and is noticeable but not as obnoxious as you might think. Don’t forget the AI assistant, Vive AI, which can utilize OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini. It doesn’t require a login, so users are “de-identified” in a way that keeps the services from retaining personal information. (That also means, by default, you won’t be able to enjoy many of the personalization features these chatbots offer by gleaning information from your emails and messages.) The glasses come with Vive’s AI Plus, free for the first two years. After that, users must pay a monthly $2.50 subscription fee. Right by the cameras is a bright indicator light. If you cover the light, it won’t record. If someone around you says stop recording, that will stop the recording. Video footage you capture is encrypted and stored on the glasses—it’s not automatically sent to the phone or cloud. If you want to import photos or videos, you have to do it manually in the app. Meta has faced scrutiny over the indicator light before, as some users have blocked the LED with stickers or broken into the hardware to turn it off. Meta has responded with software updates that disable the camera if someone tampers with the indicator light, along with other privacy-focused measures. I ask McDowell how HTC, and really any smart glasses maker, can get past the “trust me, bro”–style privacy promises companies tend to make. “We're not a social media company,” McDowell says. “There's no benefit to me to have any of your info. We don't train our AI model or any third-party AI models with any of the information that is used on the glasses.” The real problem may be that with cameras on the frames, smart glasses are hard to distinguish between brands. The Vive Eagles look a lot like Meta glasses, and people worried about those privacy issues may not know that the Eagles are different and not tied to Mark Zuckerberg’s company. I’ve had friends see me wearing them and ask if they’re smart glasses. Yeah, I replied, but not the ones they’re thinking of. That didn’t seem to dispel any of their suspicions. The hope, at least how HTC frames it, is that more players with better privacy practices will help shift cultural disdain for smart glasses. A bunch of other companies are going cameraless, like Even Realities, Viture, and Halliday. Others are building theirs with privacy shields or focusing on virtual displays instead of capturing the world around you. That said, no one has captured the market quite like Meta. “We'd like to make sure that our technology adapts to society's expectations, not the other way around,” McDowell says. “I hope that everybody that's making products like these takes steps in the right direction.” Introducing the app: More ways to make the most of WIRED Meta failed to catch hundreds of AI child abuse ads Big Story: The search for Silicon Valley’s most powerful woman Hackers got inside a Flock camera—its data shows how the system really works In your inbox: Go inside the world of digital security with Kernel Panic Take 10% Off Legal Services with This LegalZoom Promo Code 10% Off Canon Promo Code + Up to 30% Off Best Verizon Smartphone Deals Save up to $420/year when you bundle AT&T Fiber® internet and wireless Take Up to 25% Off Custom Prints with VistaPrint Promo Code Save With a Peacock Promo Code: 3 Months Free More From WIRED Reviews and Guides © 2026 Condé Nast. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kiley Pulley, a 23-year-old Walmart store manager in Buckeye, Arizona. It has been edited for length and clarity. In 2019, when I was 16 years old, I started working at Walmart as a part-time cashier. I wanted my own money, and figured, why not just get a job? My sister and my mom were already working there, and it was also right down the street from my high school. It was easy for me to get out of school and walk to work. Over the next few years, I moved through different roles, from cashier to stocker to online fulfillment. Then, when I turned 18, I became an academy trainer, and six months later, a digital team lead. When I became a team lead in mid 2021, it hit me that I wanted to stay at Walmart full time and make it my actual career. At 19, I became an operations manager, and right before I turned 22, I became the youngest store manager at Walmart in the US. People ask me, "How did you do it?" My answer is to show up and learn something new every day. Here are six things I've learned along the way. Originally, I wanted to start either my own nonprofit or my own business and help out the homeless population; then I realized that I could do all that through Walmart. I could make a difference through the people that I hire and the impact that I have on my associates at the store. When I became a team lead, I was making good money, and I also really liked it. I started actively working toward becoming a store manager. I got on succession plans and was on monthly calls with our market manager. When I became an operations manager, I led multiple projects in our market to get myself ready to become a store manager. Create a BI Job Scout and get opportunities matched to your goals. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    I'd also ask to cover for store managers when they'd take off work; that way I could gain additional experience that was needed to be promoted. I remember thinking, I'm going to be a store manager at 21. I'll be the youngest in the company. As an associate, I was friends with everybody. I could joke around with everyone. When I became salaried, everything changed. One of the biggest learning points for me has been the way I talk and how to engage with people from different cultures. Changing my tone and limiting the joking and playful attitude felt necessary as a leader in the building. At the time, setting new boundaries for myself made me feel more confident in my new role and even now in my current role. I was a little nervous when I first went into a salaried position. People said I might have issues managing those older than me, but I've never had problems with my team not respecting or listening to me. I also made my social media profiles private. I think connecting on social media can make it harder to separate between being someone's manager and being their friend. Getting out of the "if I want it done the right way, I'll do it myself" mindset was a big learning. I realized not everyone's going to know everything that I know, and if I really want to delegate and get tasks done, I'm going to have to teach and train. A big part of being an academy trainer and team lead is training your associates. Once you get to operations manager, you kind of have to step back and expect your team leads and academy trainers to do that same thing. I had to learn that if I delegated, things could get done faster or more efficiently. When it comes to my associates, if they need something, whether that's ordering the supplies or putting in tickets for them, I want to do that. I want to advocate for them. I know it makes them more productive, but they'll probably be happier coming to work, too. Also, everyone likes the appreciation of, "Hey, thank you for doing this today," or "Thank you for going above and beyond on this." When I first became salaried, I was always on the clock. I stopped going to the gym, and I sacrificed some time with my fiancé and family. I'd stay at work and say, "They need me." It was my fault; the team didn't need me that badly. Now, I'm doing better. When I get home, I'm not spending the whole day looking at metrics or constantly texting my team. I've gone back to the gym. I learned to take a step back and trust my leaders to do what they need to do. I trust that they know what they're doing. I think there's always going to be some event you could miss out on. That can be hard to juggle sometimes, but I'm lucky enough to have a fiancé who's also career-focused and driven, so we kind of use each other as motivation. I went to college for business and ended up dropping out when I got my salaried position. I told myself that I'd get back into college when I got my first store. My old store manager was the one who promoted me through all of the hourly supervisor roles. She even prepped me for my first salaried role. She sat in the office reading interview questions with me. Every time I'd say the word, 'um,' she'd say, "Nope, restart." She was constantly there for me, and even still having her as someone to go to has been great. My market manager has also known me since before I started promoting. Every time I think I'm too young to be in this room, he's always in my corner. I'm now enrolled in Live Better U, a program where Walmart pays for certain bachelor's degrees. I'm getting some of my foundational courses, and then I plan to get my college degree. For teenagers starting out, I encourage them to do a good job and learn as much as they can. Companies are constantly changing, especially with technology. It's important to adapt and not be comfortable with what you already know. When I look at my future at Walmart, I told myself I'd get to market manager at 27 or 28 — that's my short-term goal. Then, long-term, my goal would be regional EVP. One thing I always remind myself is that I worked hard to get to this life, so I can't be upset now that I have it. Maybe we don't have time to do all the fun things right now, but if we work hard through our 20s, thinking about where we might end up when we're 30 or 40 keeps me motivated. According to a new report from MacRumors, Apple employees are being told to warn customers that iPhone Duo likely won’t be available for purchase on launch day if you didn’t already place a pre-order. Right now, Apple’s website suggests that you can check back for iPhone Duo availability on October 24th. However, this isn’t a guarantee of any stock actually being available, per MacRumors: Apple Store employees told MacRumors that they have been advised that there will likely be no ‌iPhone Duo‌ stock available for walk-in purchases on launch day. Staff have been instructed to discourage customers without pre-orders from coming in expecting to buy the device, warning that they will be disappointed. This isn’t necessarily a surprise, given the fact that Apple stated yesterday that iPhone Duo demand is “extraordinary,” and we’ve long known that there were production constraints that’d lead to limited iPhone Duo supply around launch. However, this still serves as our first true sign that even if you line up at an Apple Store the night prior to the iPhone Duo launch, you might not actually end up getting a device. Some stores might receive no additional shipments beyond what was already pre-ordered. As of now, iPhone Duo is sold out through January. If these supply constraints remain, it’ll probably be challenging to buy a device for the foreseeable future. Scalpers have also been charging absurd markups on iPhone Duo orders close to launch day. If you truly want an iPhone Duo sooner than later, carriers and Best Buy seem to be a decent bet, at least in the US. Most of my losing bets, in both business and investing, were driven by narrative reasoning: short compelling stories about the world that sound smart. “Marijuana is about to be legalized in Canada. This is a rare opportunity to invest at the ground floor of a new industry.” “I’m going to invest in a cobalt mining company because they won a contract with Tesla.” Before we launched Spellbook, we thought: “Let’s launch Shopify for Lawyers, because hourly billing lawyers care more about getting business than efficiency” We love stories. Narratives are like a virus and a mind-altering drug. When they hit our ears we feel: “Ah! That makes sense”. They add clarity in an overwhelming world. And then we feel compelled to share the story with others. The clarity felt good and we want to share that feeling. More importantly, sharing the story makes us feel smart. This contagiousness makes narrative reasoning extremely dangerous. Because simple stories often make horrible bets. Concise stories don’t work well to drive action in the real world, because the real world is so multi-causal. There are hundreds, or even millions of factors that cause a bet to have a good outcome. Imagine the best chess AI engine in the world: for any board state, it has to consider hundreds moves, and then a huge number of branching futures. Great chess engines can’t simply use narrative reasoning like: “a good offense is the best defense” to win. These engines are more like spreadsheets: massive matrices of numbers and probabilities. They can make moves that are impossible for us to comprehend using language-based reasoning. The worst part? Real life is way more complex than chess. From this we can conclude that the most optimal way of strategizing about the world is definitely not by using a short sequence of words. Raw reality is not very legible. That is, it’s not simply structured and easily comprehensible by us. Although narratives make us comfortable, they’re not enough to capture the essence of reality. Reality is messy. One of the most impactful things I’ve ever read is Venkatesh Rao’s “A Big Little Idea Called Legibility”. It talks about how we are drawn to orderly, legible systems—but how those systems often fail. We even tear up messy, working systems, replace them with nice orderly systems, and see the order fail terribly. We put too much value on legibility. Let’s call this legibility bias. For instance, in the image below there is a legible “scientific forest” and an illegible organic forest. “Scientific forests” were a failure, even though their legible structure made us feel confident in the approach. Messy illegible forests remain successful. Why does legibility bias persist across society, even when we are aware of it? One answer is: it soothes people. We are conditioned from kindergarten onwards to believe that there is a crisp, clear structure to the world. That there are crisp reasons why things happen. In the world of startups, that illusion is demolished if you stick at it long enough. But large organizations “cast the illusion” of legibility to soothe and create a sense of order among employees, while those in the inner circle of upper management face messy reality head-on. Also in organizations, communication bandwidth means that you need crude, simple stories to get the ship headed in the right direction. Simple stories are a necessary evil in management. But big decisions at the top of an organization are not actually being made this way. Simple stories are a tool to motivate and direct people in approximately the right direction. If someone has spent years at a large company, and has not been in the “inner circle” of management—it is easy to see how they might confuse the tool that is being used to motivate them with the process in which effective decisions are actually being made. People misunderstand the utility of simple stories. They’re more of a management tool, a political tool, a motivation tool, and a marketing tool than a decision making tool. Good bet making is about “finding alpha”. That is, betting on opportunities that others have underestimated. Since humans have a strong bias for legibility, highly legible bets get bandwagoned. For example: “Since marijuana just got legalized in Canada, I’m going to buy $WEED stock to get in at the ground floor of a new industry” Here’s how that worked out: Even if these narratives are correct, they are too visible to markets and get quickly over-bought. In other words: The stock price gets too high before you make your bet. Or too many competitors get to the business idea before you. Or too many musicians make similar sounding songs. This reasoning works across any competitive domain. A really good place to find bets that are underestimated is in the illegible. If stories don’t work, how do we survive at all in a world so complex and multi-causal? Well, simple stories can work for basic survival: “I need to eat to survive”. But to find good bets that others don’t see, we need to leave crisp stories behind and think more like a chess engine. We need to digest raw hyper-dimensional reality. But how do we do that without putting our situation into a 100,000 x 100,000 spreadsheet? The first answer is: intuition. We already have 86 billion neurons in our brain that are doing something similar to a chess engine. We can’t see exactly how it works, but it can send us much more valuable signals about the world than narratives do. If we digest enough data, our brain starts pattern matching automatically. Pattern matching is how we position ourselves to throw a basketball and recognize our friends faces. Those are not things we think about in words. Running fast using intuition to make decisions can be extraordinarily effective. But what if our intuition is bad? What if our intuition differs from that of our team? That’s a lot of words to say: “trust your gut!”. But what if you haven’t developed intuition? Or what if your intuition disagrees with the intuition of your team? There is a slightly more legible approach that I’ve found effective: Look at your past bets and ask yourself: what are the 10-20 attributes that mattered? List them out, and then go through each of your winning and losing bets, noticing which attributes they had. We did this for all the product feature bets we made at Spellbook, and were able to correlate 16 attributes with what made a successful product bet. And many were surprising. Almost none of our correlated attributes had to do with the narrative of the feature itself. We discovered a bunch of other things that mattered: Can a lawyer get value from the feature instantly with absolutely zero configuration? Was someone on the team so inspired to build something that they “started without permission”? Is the feature “whole” rather than a stepping stone to get somewhere else? Can the feature be fully prototyped in 2 weeks? We ended up with a framework that is a middle ground between legible, narrative based reasoning and intuition. And the best part is we could objectively score prospective bets in this framework. It brings us a little closer to reasoning like a chess engine. These signals increased our hit rate significantly when we used to not hit at all. For years we had been listening to the gospel: “talk to your customers! Build what they ask for!” This was helpful, but it had an catastrophic blindspot that was causing us to make losing bets for years. We were missing an entire universe of patterns outside of the tunnel vision of stories. This approach also helped dramatically improve my performance in investing. When I started noodling in active investing almost 20 years ago, I relied on narrative “reasons” and news headlines to make bets. My active portfolio produced neutral returns for nearly 10 years (adjusted for inflation, that’s a big loss). Those narratives simply didn’t capture the thousands of factors that impacted stock price. And if they did: well everyone else was jumping on the same bandwagon and pushing up the buy price where the bet became too expensive to make sense. Over the last 9 years I switched to a pattern matching approach. My active portfolio has performed ~20x better than my passive portfolio over that period. To improve my ability to pattern match, I really like to “soak” in data. I read lots of charts and try to make written predictions on them regularly. I check back on how my predictions fared. Eventually making trades started to feel like throwing a basketball. My brain started to develop a deep intuition for technical and fundamental signals, and how they combine to make a “swish”. Pattern matching is not hard. Our brains are wired to do it. The hard part is being independent-minded enough to believe your own conclusions.  To do that, you need to escape the universe of simple stories we are surrounded by. Stories are the threads that hold society together. We are fish and stories are our water. Repeating popular stories grants us head nods and social acceptance.  For example, “You can’t beat the market, dollar-cost average into index funds!” is the kind of viral story that will earn you nods of approval from millennials and upvotes on Reddit. Pattern matching, on the other hand, can drive you to make moves like an advanced chess engine. Moves that others find alien and incomprehensible. If your bets don’t generate some confused looks, they’re probably too obvious, and thus overdone.  “To believe that what is true for you in your private heart, is true for all men,—that is genius” —Ralph Waldo Emerson, Self-Reliance  Thanks for reading Competitive Philosophy! Rapid Support Forces accuse army of killing 30 civilians in attack on Nyala’s busy livestock market. Save Share The Sudanese army says it has killed dozens of fighters from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in a series of air attacks on the southwestern city of Nyala, but the paramilitary group says the military has killed civilians. The targets of Friday’s attack were RSF positions and command centres in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state and the seat of the paramilitary group’s self-declared administration, the army said in a statement. However, the RSF said the army carried out a drone attack on a busy livestock market, killing 30 civilians, including 17 women and five children. The group has not confirmed or denied whether separate attacks by the army killed some of its fighters and destroyed its command centres. Separately, the human rights group Emergency Lawyers said in a post on X that a market was hit on Friday in Nyala and the drone used was “affiliated” with the Sudanese army. Reporting from the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, Al Jazeera’s Almigdad Alruhaid said on Saturday that the fighting between the army and RSF has “intensified”. “In South Kordofan, a source in the Sudanese government told Al Jazeera that the RSF carried out drone attacks on mining sites with the exchange in fire intensifying in many parts of Sudan in the past 24 hours.”      The army has repeatedly targeted the Darfur region in western Sudan with drones to try to retake territory controlled by the RSF, which holds most of the area. This month, Sudanese military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan promised to seize “every inch” of territory under RSF control. The Sudanese civil war began in 2023 and has killed tens of thousands of people. The United Nations has described the situation in Sudan as the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. Itâs difficult to imagine the legendÂ Arthur MillerÂ as anything other than an intellectual playwright with biting social commentary.Â We all have to start somewhere, however, and Miller wasn't always one of the great American writers. He was once a gawky teenager trying to earn money for college. Miller grew up in a wealthy family, but after the stock market crash of 1929, he found himself thrust into the working class. In order to achieve his career goals, Miller worked several different jobs before and after university. But all of them gave him experience to one day write about the true meaning of success and failure in the life of the everyday man. Miller's father had shown him how to be a successful businessman with his clothing manufacturing company. But when the Great Depression hit, the Miller family lost almost everything and was never able to rebuild their wealth. Arthur Miller had not taken school seriously until it was time to prepare for college, and he realized that he would need to work to pay for all his expenses. While still in high school, Miller worked as a delivery boy for a bakery, helped in his father's business, and drove a delivery van for an auto-parts store. After high school, Miller found several other jobs, including a radio singer, truck driver, and worker at a box factory. But the job that he would remain at long enough to earn the $500 needed for college tuition was a clerk for an auto-parts warehouse. When Miller started at the University of Michigan, he wanted to study journalism. He got a job as a reporter and editor for the student newspaper, The Michigan Daily. While in school, Miller wrote his first play, No Villain, which, after winning an award, had him reconsider his career. He switched from journalism to English. After graduating in 1938, Miller worked for the Federal Theater Project, writing and reading radio plays. The FTP was shut down one year later due to government fears of Communism, and Miller went to work at the Brooklyn Navy Yard during World War II. He was exempt from fighting in the war because of an injury sustained in high school. While working at the Navy Yard, Miller continued writing radio scripts, some of which were produced by CBS and NBC. The Great Depression and its effects on not just the economy but the psychology of the working man were huge inspirations for several of Miller's plays. His diverse experiences in all of his jobs also played a big role in how he wrote. A Memory of Two Mondays (1955) was based on Miller's co-workers at the auto-parts warehouse and their struggles to make a living during the Depression. While working with his father to try to open a new clothing factory, Miller witnessed the poor treatment of the salesmen there. This led to his short story In Memoriam, which he would later turn into his most famous play, Death of a Salesman (1949). His many odd jobs opened his eyes to a different world than the well-to-do one he knew growing up, and prepared him to write some of the greatest and most relatable American tragedies to date. I've lived in Colorado for over a decade. If I had just a single day to show someone what I love about the state, I wouldn't take them to our capital city, Denver.  Instead, I'd bring them to the much smaller city of Golden.  Golden gives has a little bit of everything for visitors: mountains and hiking trails, a creek running through town, a historic downtown made for wandering on foot, and plenty of places to eat and drink. It's located just about 15 miles west of downtown Denver, or about a 25-minute drive, and typically less than an hour's drive from the Denver International Airport.  Here's why I love bringing out-of-towners to Golden — and where I'd take them when they visited.  Golden has several coffee shops, but I'd start my perfect day here at Sogo Beans and Boards.  The family-owned coffee and skate shop is just minutes from downtown. I love that Sogo air-roasts its fair-trade coffee and makes its own syrups and pastries.  Its plant-filled room, free Wi-Fi, and garden patio make it easy to linger over a latte, and it's the kind of independent shop that makes a morning feel unhurried. The city makes it easy to go from a coffee shop to a trail without a long drive.  Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get. For a leisurely morning, I'd rent an e-bike and follow the paved Clear Creek Trail, which winds alongside the water through parks and greenery. For more of a workout, I'd hike North Table Mountain, where the initial climb stings but rewards you with sweeping views of the city and surrounding mesas. In warmer months, tubing on Clear Creek is another way to take in the town's outdoor culture and scenic views.  If I had more time, I'd take the short drive from town to visit Golden Gate Canyon State Park, a beautiful place to enjoy aspen groves and mountain scenery. Come winter, the same park is a serene place to snowshoe through snow-covered trails. After working up an appetite, I'd head to The Golden Mill, a food hall and community gathering space along Clear Creek.  It offers several food concepts — from sushi and tacos to fried chicken, barbecue, and New Zealand-style ice cream — which means a group with different tastes can all leave happy. More than 50 self-pour taps offer beer, wine, cider, and more.  The best part is the setting. Large creekside and rooftop patios have mountain views, which makes it an ideal spot to settle in after a morning outside. My sister and I recently spent a morning there for rooftop yoga led by a local teacher, then walked around town afterward before returning for lunch.  It was peaceful, and it reinforced what makes the place work: It feels less like a traditional restaurant and more like somewhere you can spend a few hours eating, drinking, and watching Golden go by. The yoga is a summer series that typically returns in May, and the event lineup rotates with the seasons. Past offerings have included rooftop barre and Keg Conditioning, a workout that uses empty kegs as equipment. Washington Avenue is lined with locally owned boutiques, galleries, and Western outfitters, and a seasonal Saturday farmers market adds to the scene.  Kayakers can play at Clear Creek Whitewater Park and beer fans can tour the Coors Brewery. Coors began brewing beside the creek in 1873. One year later, the Colorado School of Mines was established nearby. It's part of an industrial past you can still sense as you walk. I'd leave some of the afternoon unscheduled, too. Part of Golden's appeal is simply walking along the creek, looking up at the foothills, and stopping wherever something catches your attention. All of the above is ultimately why I'd choose Golden for someone's first taste of Colorado.  Denver has plenty to offer, but Golden gives you a concentrated version of the state I'd want to share with a first-time visitor: mountain views without a long mountainous drive; outdoor adventure alongside a walkable downtown; and enough food, beer, and local character to fill the day. Sometimes it's not the most extravagant destinations that create the most meaningful memories. Some of my favorites in Golden have been the simplest, like that quiet morning with my sister. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jen Podany, founder of Bluestone Sunshields. It has been edited for length and clarity.Near the end of 2024, my family of five had once again escaped Los Angeles for the quiet we found 10 hours south in Snowflake, Arizona. We'd been doing it for years, renting an Airbnb in Snowflake, a town of 6,000 in the middle of nowhere, switching off amid the miles of empty land. It had started as a stopover on our way to visit my husband's family in New Mexico. We fell in love with the town, and from then on, we'd visit whenever we needed to get away from the busyness of LA. In Snowflake, we felt like we could catch our breath. Our souls calmed each time we arrived and ached to stay each time we left. Back in LA, specifically Burbank, the five of us — my husband and our three children, whom we homeschooled — lived in a duplex made up of two connected apartments. We lived in one of them, which had two bedrooms and one bathroom. From the other apartment, my husband and I ran our two separate businesses. The duplex was in a neighborhood near a busy street, and we had to be cautious about letting the kids go outside to play because of the cars. I was always holding someone's little hand when we were out, just in case. You could hear planes flying back and forth into Burbank Airport. As our kids and businesses grew, we felt increasingly confined. Then we saw a house on the market in Snowflake, and I felt in my bones that we should put in an offer. It was a four-bedroom house surrounded by land, chickens, cows, and a crazy turkey. We could buy it and have our own place to stay when visiting, rather than always renting an Airbnb. We bought the house for about $500,000, and on our first visit to stay in it in January 2025, none of us wanted to go back to Burbank. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    We knew then that we'd make Snowflake our home. And so we did. In so many ways, our life looks exactly like life in LA. Our routines have remained the same. Every morning, just like in LA, we start our day at a coffee shop. Except in Snowflake, there's only one place to go instead of 20 choices. We work, we homeschool, we eat our meals, and we go to sleep — just like we did in LA. But by transplanting our lives to a quiet town, we all feel calmer and more peaceful. Personally, my nervous system has regulated. In LA, I felt like the world was constantly coming at me, like I was being bombarded and reacting to everything around me. Here, I feel like I'm in the driver's seat, with a clear head. Not only has it been good for my well-being, but it's also been good for my business. The move has given me the mental space to think bigger. It's led to greater creativity, paving the way for business growth. My kids love Snowflake, too. I didn't have to convince them about the move. They have the freedom to be out of the house without worrying about cars and crime. Just a bike ride away are other kids with whom they are often found playing. I think kids grow up quickly in cities, and living here, I feel like my kids get to just be kids. It's like going back to being a kid in the '80s, and I love that for them. The house is bigger, so we aren't living on top of each other, but they've also got endless outdoor space to explore. Even though I lived in LA for 20 years, we never experienced friendship and community as we have in just over a year in Snowflake. We can't leave the house without seeing someone who wants to stop and talk. Everyone here is on "mountain time" — slowing down. No one is rushing around, head down, looking at their phones, too hurried to have a conversation. Everyone is present and friendly. My husband and I still occasionally have to go to LA for work, and each time we come back home to Snowflake, I take a deep breath and know we made the right decision to relocate our family. Some Apple retail employees have been told to warn customers against visiting to purchase an iPhone Duo without a pre-order on Friday, October 23. Apple Store employees told MacRumors that they have been advised that there will likely be no ‌iPhone Duo‌ stock available for walk-in purchases on launch day. Staff have been instructed to discourage customers without pre-orders from coming in expecting to buy the device, warning that they will be disappointed. Apple's online store tells customers to check back on Saturday, October 24 for pickup availability. Pickup reservations were briefly available when pre-orders opened before the option was disabled. The October 24 message does not guarantee stock will be available that day, and it remains unclear how firm the warning shared with employees is and whether it applies worldwide. If the guidance is firm and widely perpetuated, it closes off a potential route for customers hoping to bypass the device's lengthy online wait times, at least at the stores concerned. Warnings about a constrained launch began well before Apple announced the ‌iPhone Duo‌. In early September, Nikkei Asia reported that production had reached only a few hundred devices per day in late August. Further production problems emerged in late September. Earlier this month, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman said Apple had at one point believed production constraints could push the start of sales into November. The company subsequently assembled enough inventory to proceed with the October 23 launch, although supply remained very limited.  The extent of the shortage became apparent when pre-orders opened earlier this week. Delivery estimates moved beyond launch day within minutes, and within 30 minutes, all configurations in Apple's U.S. online store showed January 25 shipping estimates. The device is now effectively sold out for Christmas through Apple's online store. Apple subsequently described demand as "nothing short of extraordinary" in a statement to the Financial Times, adding that it was working to get devices to customers as quickly as possible. Apple has not publicly specified whether any stores will have stock for launch-day walk-in purchases. Over 20 years of combined experience and the latest in technology, AI,… New Jersey’s Senate Judiciary Committee has advanced S597 with bipartisan support, proposing to replace criminal penalties for gambling by people under 21 with civil fines of up to $500 for a first offense, $1,000 for a second and $2,000 for a third. The bill would direct the money collected to compulsive-gambling prevention, education and treatment programs. The proposal changes the legal framework but does not remove penalties. It would cover under-21 gambling at casinos or simulcasting facilities, as well as adults who allow someone in their legal care or custody to gamble and casino licensees or employees who permit underage gambling. S597 applies to people who gamble at a casino or simulcasting facility before turning 21. Its scope also reaches people responsible for a minor and casino licensees or employees when they allow underage gambling at those facilities. The bill therefore concerns more than the young person placing a wager. For casino operators, the proposed framework retains a direct compliance consequence where a licensee or employee allows someone under 21 to gamble. The available reporting does not describe changes to age-check procedures or other operator requirements, so the proposal’s stated effect is the change in penalties. That distinction matters: S597 does not simply eliminate consequences for underage gambling. It would replace a disorderly persons criminal offense with escalating civil fines, while preserving accountability for the categories of conduct identified in the measure. Age-verification enforcement has also featured in other jurisdictions’ gambling regulation. In Ontario, the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario fined Betty Gaming over underage-gambling issues, a separate case that illustrates how regulators can address age-related compliance concerns through operator enforcement. Under S597, the proposed maximum fine would rise with repeat offenses: up to $500 for a first violation, up to $1,000 for a second and up to $2,000 for a third. The source reporting describes those amounts as the proposed civil-fine schedule, rather than criminal penalties. Money collected would support programs for compulsive gambling, including prevention, education and treatment. The Press of Atlantic City reported that the funding could go to programs such as those provided by the Council on Compulsive Gambling of New Jersey. The funding arrangement is part of the bill’s approach to enforcement: penalties would remain, but their proceeds would be directed toward efforts intended to address gambling-related harm. The proposal does not specify in the available reporting how funds would be divided among programs or how the state would assess their results. That focus on prevention sits alongside the bill’s provisions for casinos and their staff. Casino licensees and employees are among the parties the measure identifies when they allow an underage person to gamble, so the proposed civil framework would continue to make operator conduct relevant. New Jersey regulators have separately taken action against licensed operators over responsible-gambling requirements. The state’s fine against Caesars Sportsbook provides context for the regulator’s use of enforcement in the market, but it is distinct from S597 and does not establish what penalties would apply under the bill. Sen. Vince Polistina, a Republican from Atlantic County and one of the bill’s sponsors, has argued that casinos must follow the law while describing a criminal offense as too severe a consequence for a young person who makes a mistake. He also cited young people’s exposure to gambling through sports broadcasts, advertising and social media as a reason to reconsider how violations are handled. Polistina’s stated position combines continued enforcement with a different form of penalty. Under the proposal, repeat offenses would carry higher civil fines, and collected revenue would go toward gambling prevention, education and treatment rather than leaving the matter solely within the criminal system. Sen. James Beach, a Democratic sponsor, has emphasized the risk of gambling problems among young people and the possibility that criminal punishment could leave them with records. He has argued for focusing on behavioral changes and prevention instead. Those positions frame the debate around how to respond when underage gambling occurs: the bill’s supporters say young people should remain accountable, but that a civil penalty linked to prevention and treatment is a more constructive response than a criminal offense. S597 would apply that approach to the covered gamblers, responsible adults and casino personnel specified in the proposal. The measure now goes to the Senate Budget and Appropriations Committee after advancing from the Senate Judiciary Committee. Its progress is not final approval by the Senate, and the proposal has not become law. The bill mirrors a measure that was debated and received preliminary approval in the previous year but was ultimately not enacted, according to the reporting. That earlier effort did not result in the proposed change taking effect; S597 must still complete the legislative process. As reported by the Press of Atlantic City and PlayUSA, the bill must pass the relevant committees in both the Senate and Assembly, win approval from the full membership of both chambers, and then go to the governor for action. Until those steps are completed, New Jersey’s existing criminal-penalty framework remains in place. Copied to clipboard  		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 In the pursuit of greater productivity and profit, companies see AI as a glow on the horizon. For many workers, however, the AI revolution has already arrived in the form of a pink slip. In January, Amazon announced nearly 16,000 job cuts to reduce organizational layers and bureaucracy. CEO Andy Jassy had previously predicted that generative AI and agents would mean fewer people doing some existing jobs. Meta soon followed with plans to eliminate about 8,000 positions, close to 10% of its workforce, in pursuit of greater efficiency while directing more resources toward AI. Financial technology company Block announced more than 4,000 cuts, nearly half of its workforce, as CEO Jack Dorsey explained that intelligence tools, combined with smaller and flatter teams, are changing how companies operate. These tech heavyweights are hardly alone. Reuters has tracked AI-linked cuts or restructuring at companies ranging from Allianz and Nike to Telstra and British American Tobacco. In its monthly Challenger Report, outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas attributed 7% of U.S. layoffs announced in January to AI. By the end of September, AI had been cited in more than 120,000 announced job cuts in 2026, about 21% of the total, making it the leading reason for layoffs so far this year. Some of those workers will find another job or retire early. But if the data points to a trend, others may be turning lemons into lemonade through entrepreneurship. New business formation has been unusually strong this year, with nearly every month setting a record compared with the same month in previous years. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, business formation statistics, nearly 4.2 million business applications were filed nationwide in the first eight months of 2026, up about 17% from the same period in 2025. On their own, these numbers don’t prove that AI, layoffs or both are driving the surge. Business creation rises and falls for many reasons, as it did during the pandemic, and not every new registration becomes an operating company. Still, the convergence turns heads. Even as large employers aim to accomplish more with smaller teams, backed by the muscle of AI, workers have access to many of the same productivity tools. In their hands, those tools offer a supercharged way to combine specialized knowledge, an idea for a product or service that solves a problem or fills a niche and a passion for bringing it to market. Not everyone affected by layoffs is being replaced by an AI agent. Companies cut jobs for many reasons, including industry pressures and narrowing margins. But AI is putting its thumb on the scale. Amazon, Meta and Block have all announced major reductions as they embrace AI, though each has described its role differently: Amazon emphasized cutting layers and bureaucracy, Meta pointed to shifting resources toward AI, and Block said AI-enabled productivity calls for a smaller workforce. Rather than curse AI for eroding jobs, aspiring entrepreneurs should embrace what it can do for them. The same technology that helps a large corporation accomplish more with fewer employees can help a one-person venture tackle tasks that once required an entire team. AI can help research markets, develop business plans, create marketing materials, handle basic customer inquiries and automate routine administrative work. When you’re getting a new business off the ground, every task you can handle without adding fixed payroll lowers the revenue your business needs to survive its lean years. Just as the internet and smartphones transformed business a generation ago, AI can transform yours. A layoff can make years, or even decades, spent building a career at one company feel suddenly devalued. For a would-be entrepreneur, however, that hard-won experience may be the most valuable asset. Let’s be honest: Employees know their industry’s problems because they’ve lived with them. They know what customers complain about, which processes waste time, which services cost too much and where existing products fall short. Unless you’re set on doing something completely different, like leaving a civil engineering job to open a scrapbooking shop, you have an opportunity to analyze those issues and, free of corporate baggage, create real solutions. You don’t have to reinvent the wheel. A specialized consulting practice, service business or niche product that addresses a problem you already understand may offer a natural, inexpensive path to entrepreneurship. One of AI’s biggest benefits for new entrepreneurs is the ability to test an idea before making a major financial commitment. You may not need to lease an office, hire employees or buy expensive technology right away. Start with a small, workable version of your idea. Interview potential customers. Build a basic website. Test different pricing structures and marketing offers. Use AI for research and routine work, but bring in human experts when needed. Spending doesn’t make you a successful entrepreneur — revenue does. And revenue validates a business idea better than a glitzy launch party or a wood-paneled office. If you’re leaving salaried employment, protecting your personal cash matters too, even if you received a generous severance package. Add up your household expenses alongside your business costs, and know your full runway before taking on serious financial risk. AI may be eliminating jobs — it may have eliminated yours. Entrepreneurs can use these tools to keep startup costs low, including labor costs. But don’t take that as a sign to cut people out of the picture. The surge in new businesses may partly reflect corporate America devaluing human work and putting profits ahead of people. As layoffs continue to reshape the workforce, traditional employment may keep shrinking while the ranks of people who recognize the value of their own expertise grow. Building a business means building a trustworthy brand, and that requires human interaction. AI can create content, analyze data and automate repetitive tasks, saving time and money. Where it falls short is in building person-to-person relationships. For entrepreneurs, AI’s role is to free you up to apply your expertise, judgment and creativity. After all, those uniquely human traits are what will help you connect with customers and establish your brand. By Ed Hardy • 11:14 am, October 17, 2026  As Apple already immediately sold out of iPhone Duo units through January 2027, the company likely just sold at least 6 million of its foldable in a couple of hours. And the number might approach 10 million. That means Apple may have just claimed a third of the global foldable market.  The iPhone Duo went up for preorder on Friday morning, and Apple ran out of its prelaunch stock in minutes. Well before noon, anyone placing an order for the foldable from the U.S. Apple Store was told their product wouldn’t ship before January 2027. “Demand for iPhone Duo, our first foldable iPhone, has been nothing short of extraordinary. We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers’ hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online,” according to a statement from the company gave to a variety of news sites on Friday. While Apple claims extraordinary demand, judging actual demand for a product based on preorder sales is a dicey business. It depends on how many units of the product are available at launch. For example, if Apple had only made 100 iPhone Duo units, of course they all sold out. That would reveal nothing about demand for the product. But Cupertino made far more than 100 iPhone Duo units. More than a few thousand. Analysts estimate it produced millions of them and continues to make more… and they all sold out in a couple of hours. Apple did not reveal how many units of its new foldable it is producing. That’s a figure the company never makes public for any of its smartphones. But analysts fill in the gap. “Apple is expected to achieve over six million shipments of iPhone Duo by the end of 2026,” said the analysts at Omdia in September. Counterpoint analysts agree on the 6 million figure. And considering the wait time for the foldable is now January 2027, those units aren’t sitting in warehouses hoping to someday be sold. They are already sold, including the pre-launch units as well as the ones that will be assembled between now and January. Android manufacturers launched the first foldable smartphones years ago, with Samsung introducing its original Galaxy Fold in 2019. Apple waited until 2026 to enter the market with the iPhone Duo, yet analysts already expect the device to account for roughly a third of global foldable phone shipments this year. Omdia estimates that manufacturers shipped 18.2 million foldable smartphones worldwide in 2025. The analysts at the rival market analysis firm IDC approximate the total at 20.6 million. So if Apple really will ship 6 million iPhone Duo units before the end of 2026, that will equal approximately one-third of the entire foldable market in 2025. To be clear, even if analysts are correct and Apple ships 6 million iPhone Duo units in the next few months, the foldable will represent only a small slice of the company’s overall smartphone business. Analysts at GF Securities predict the company will ship around 257 million iPhones worldwide this year, meaning the Duo’s projected shipments would account for just over 2% of the total. That would still be a significant debut for Apple’s first foldable, but it puts the device’s expected sales in perspective: Apple’s conventional iPhone models will continue to account for the overwhelming majority of its smartphone shipments. Foldables in general remain niche products. Omdia estimates that manufacturers shipped approximately 1.25 billion smartphones overall in 2025, of which 18.2 million included folding screens. That means foldables accounted for just 1.5% of global smartphone shipments.         Ed Hardy has been writing full-time about tech for 26 years, and using it for much longer than that. His intro to Apple was a Macintosh SE/30 (which he still has), but now he uses a 13-inch iPad Pro as his primary computer. That’s because he’s a “tablet first” type of guy. Rather than use a Macbook, he connects a keyboard case to the iPad. And instead of a desktop Mac, he connects his tablet to a 27-inch display and full-size keyboard. (So don’t try to tell him that everyone has to use a Mac to be productive.) Before coming to Cult of Mac, Ed wrote for NotebookReview, TabletPCReview and Brighthand, as well as other sites. Ed – think you might want to recheck the math. It's that time of year again. Temperatures are dropping in the northern hemisphere, the leaves are falling off the trees, and RVers are breaking out their four-season campers to prepare for what is shaping up to be a hectic El Niño winter. You can also find all your fall favorites, from PSLs to those Oreos with the orange filling that definitely tastes different than the normal filling. But all of that fall coziness is technically just performative autumn if you don't balance it out with the appropriate number of scary movies to make your skin crawl. Here at Jalopnik, we don't settle for just any old horror movies, either. No, we like to keep things on theme 365 days a year, and that's why our October is going to be packed to the brim with the many delightful scary movies that feature cars and trucks as central antagonists, frightening foes, and ruthless killers. There might be more of them than you would have guessed, and they range from all-time classics to so brutally corny that you can't help but love them. In the run-up to Halloween, you'll find my TV tuned to films like Stephen King's "Maximum Overdrive," John Carpenter's "Christine," and Quentin Tarantino's "Death Proof." There are honestly so many horror movies that center around road vehicles, though, that it can be hard to pick a favorite. What killer car movies are you most excited about watching and rewatching this Halloween? We all know what Rivian is watching this year, seeing the brand's annual Halloween mode beautifully recreate Ecto-1 from Ghostbusters. John Carpenter is a name you should know, if you don't already. He's one of the most massively successful filmmakers of the last century, and his career spans over 50 of those years at this point. If his name doesn't ring a bell, he's the mind behind the oh-so-memeable "They Live" (1988) starring Roddy Piper and the haunting 1982 film "The Thing," starring Kurt Russel and Wilford Brimley. He also wrote and directed 1978's "Halloween," the horror classic that follows the murderous story of Michael Myers and which has spawned a massive movie franchise. Though one automotive mistake kind of ruins "Halloween" for many enthusiasts. While it hasn't seen the widespread and continued success of "Halloween," Carpenter also directed one of our favorite disturbing and scary car movies. "Christine" came out in 1983 and asks the question, "How do you kill something that can't possibly be alive?" "Christine" was written by Stephen King, making this movie a team-up between two of the GOATs of horror, and it features a sentient 1958 Plymouth Fury with a taste for blood. She starts her murder spree before she's even off the assembly line and, 21 years later, finds herself in the hands of a teen driver named Arnie, who becomes as obsessed with Christine as she does with him. "Christine" is, as movie critic Roger Ebert called it back when it was released, "utterly ridiculous," but it's also a hell of a horror film. It has chases, crashes, bad decisions, and scenes that will make your skin crawl. There's not much you can ask of a horror movie that "Christine" doesn't deliver. While "Christine" might be the foremost sentient, autonomous, and bloodthirsty car in most cinephiles' minds, she's not the only one. In fact, she's not even the first. Six years before "Christine" was released in theaters, a humble film with a simple name came out that also featured a beautiful, now-classic car with a dark and twisted side. "The Car" (1977) didn't have as big of names attached to it, and its Rotten Tomatoes score of 32% suggests that maybe it doesn't quite hold up, but it's still a silly, fun, and at times unnerving film with a sinister car at its core. "The Car" was directed by Elliot Silverstein, who was no stranger to film involving either cars or horror. In "The Car," a young James Brolin plays a sheriff and single father in small-town Utah, where a strange black car starts off a spree of hit-and-runs by killing some innocent cyclists. As the car racks up kills, the identity of its driver remains a complete mystery, and some believe the car might even be driving itself. The movie's tagline says it all: "Is it a phantom, a demon, or the Devil himself?" The only way to find out is by watching. What makes this film all the more fun is the eponymous car itself. It's "played" by a 1971 Lincoln Continental Mark III, but it's no stock model. It was customized by car customizing legend George Barris, who added new fenders and a hand-made grille, recessed the headlights deeper behind the fender, cut a few inches off the top, and finished the project off with 20 coats of black pearl paint to achieve the car's signature look. The result is a Continental that looks straight out of the uncanny valley. Real horror heads know that an integral part of the culture is watching movies that are admittedly pretty terrible. There's no excusing a movie as corny and forgettable as "Wheels of Terror" (1990), but it might still be fun to put on the TV on a cool October night and watch in the background. This one didn't have any big names attached to it, it didn't introduce any young stars who would later take cinema by storm, and its only award nomination was for Best Young Actress in a Cable Special at the Young Artist Awards, which it didn't win. In other words, it barely made a ripple in Hollywood. "Wheels of Terror" has a plot strikingly similar to that of "The Car." After Laura and her tween daughter Stephanie make a big move to a calm suburb in Copper Valley, Arizona, they discover that it's being terrorized by an evil Dodge Charger — surely many of us have had traumatizing experiences involving a Charger. It's just par for the course. This particular 1974 Charger is seemingly driverless and has been tormenting people about town. When the protagonist watches her daughter get abducted by the malign muscle car, she sets off in desperate pursuit to save her. What's so amazing about the evil Dodge at the center of this film is that it's clearly multiple different cars. The models they used for the Charger terrorizing Copper Valley flip from 1971 to 1974 Chargers all willy-nilly, and they're not even always the same color. The characters even refer to this Dodge coupe as a sedan multiple times. If you love to lampoon a movie as you watch it, this is an unbeatable choice. This year celebrates the 40th anniversary of "Maximum Overdrive" (1986), written and directed by Stephen King, and it deserves a spot in your Halloween rotation for its over-the-top technological violence and cars coming to life. Despite King's legendary status in the horror world and his dozens of extremely popular books, this is his only directorial effort, and there might just be a reason for that. The film stars Emilio Estevez and Pat Hingle, and it's a fever dream of epic proportions that was nominated for not one, but two Razzies in 1987: one for Worst Actor and one for Worst Director. The premise is that a passing comet causes all machines on Earth to come to life and start killing indiscriminately. If that's not enough to reel you in, King's comment on his own movie when speaking with The Kingcast is, "I was doing a lot of cocaine, and I was drinking a lot. You can tell!" Sold yet? All kinds of machines start murdering in this movie, from lawnmowers to a semi with a massive Green Goblin mask for a grille, and the only explanation for why seems to be, once again, cocaine. The main action follows a group of survivors holed up at a truck stop in North Carolina called "Dixie Boy," and they're none too skilled at surviving. In fact, they die so gloriously that the film reportedly had to see major edits to avoid getting slapped with an X rating from the MPAA. There are even rumors that another horror legend, George Romero, was on set for much of the film's production and that the first cut threatened to make him sick. Unfortunately, the X-rated cut likely doesn't exist, so we'll never know how bad it really could've been. So far, most of the movies listed here are old enough to be grandparents. It seems the '70s and '80s were rife with filmmakers pondering the implications of autonomous cars that prefer to kill you rather than tell you what they're doing and why. Of course, a truly evil sentient car might even want to do both. Still, the cinematic exploration of cars with a taste for blood seems to have tapered off in the '90s. That's what makes Quentin Tarantino's 2007 film "Death Proof" all the more unique and compelling — along with the fact that it debuted in theaters as part of an anthology called "Grindhouse" that combined both "Death Proof" and Robert Rodriguez's "Planet Terror," which didn't feature evil cars but did star Rose McGowan fighting zombies with a machine gun leg. In "Death Proof," the car isn't sentient, but it is used by antagonist Stuntman Mike (Kurt Russell) to repeatedly cause deadly accidents that allow Mike to walk away unscathed. It's as if he's feeding some kind of ravenous beast. The movie has some excellent chase scenes, including an extended chase sequence that makes up a good portion of the second half of the film, and Kurt Russell is excellent as always. There's also a highway massacre or two, just for extra thrills, you know. The title refers to Mike's car, a 1970 Chevy Nova that he's death-proofed by reinforcing it and modding it over the years to make it a perfect killing machine. Mike eventually targets and faces off against a group of stuntwomen, including Rosario Dawson and Zoë Bell. The year 2001 saw the first installment of "The Fast and the Furious" franchise, which skyrocketed Paul Walker to street-racing superstardom and kicked off a massive ongoing franchise. However, many people don't remember that Walker actually starred in a second car-focused movie that year. The oft-forgotten "Joy Ride" has all your favorite horror tropes. College freshman Lewis (Paul Walker) is on summer break and embarks on a road trip from California to New Jersey, joined by his crush Venna and older brother Fuller along the way. Things go awry when Fuller cajoles his baby brother into pulling a prank on a trucker over the CB. The trucker, because of course, turns out to be a rampaging murderer whose only goal now is to kill the young adults who pranked him. Oh, and the trucker goes by the name Rusty Nail, which totally isn't a silly handle. "Joy Ride" had J.J. Abrams on the writing team, and while it hasn't seen nearly the success that "The Fast and the Furious" did, it was at least successful enough to earn a couple sequels, albeit with an entirely new cast and an expanded writing team sans Abrams. The semi truck that Rusty Nails drives in this movie is, once again, not actually sentient or ontologically evil, as we've seen in many other films on this list, but it sure is menacing as hell. Rusty Nail and his big rig pursue Paul Walker and crew across the country and against all odds, and that truck just won't quit. This is a solid thriller for anyone who wants to indulge in a little nostalgia and pour one out for the late, great Paul Walker. Last but not least on this year's list of movies with killer cars to watch for Halloween is the 1971 movie "Duel," directed by Steven Spielberg. Even though "Duel" came out when Spielberg was only 24, the now-iconic filmmaker had already directed several short films and episodes of TV by then. This was, however, his second full-length film after 1964's Firelight, which inspired what would eventually become "Close Encounters of the Third Kind" in 1977. "Duel" was a TV movie based on a short story of the same name by Richard Matheson, better known for his novel "I Am Legend." Matheson also wrote the script for "Duel." "Duel" stars Dennis Weaver, a lone traveling salesman who finds himself being stalked and followed by a tanker as he travels across desert highways to his next appointment. Most of the movie takes place as Weaver's character drives his Plymouth Valiant through desolate stretches of highway and features tense scene after tense scene of a menacing Peterbilt 281 trying to run him and various other interlopers off the road. The premise is simple, and the film might seem repetitive or boring by today's standards, but in actuality, it's a tense thriller that's well worth the watch thanks to great solo acting on Weaver's part and a lot of beautiful, long shots of the landscape whirring by as Weaver tries to get to safety. This is the kind of movie you couldn't make today, and not only because the world's oil reserves are quickly dwindling.
