As prices skyrocket on virtually everything else, Walmart’s $60 Onn 4K Pro streamer with Google TV might be the only good deal left — if you can find it in stock. Prices on streaming hardware have exploded in recent months. Just a few examples include: It’s rough out there folks. AI is totally worth it, right? Anyway, all of those price hikes have had me revisiting the Walmart Onn 4K Pro that launched earlier this year and that I’ve been using in one of the rooms in my house for the past few months. Put simply, it gets the job done very well, and is a tremendous deal compared to everything around it. The most direct comparison to the Onn 4K Pro is the Google TV Streamer, and they are pretty close across the board. They have virtually identical software, though Google’s first-party release obviously gets updates and new features a bit quicker. Performance is also nearly identical, with the only big difference being 4GB of RAM in Google’s streamer vs 3GB in Walmart’s. Most of the time, it doesn’t matter. Walmart’s streamer continues to be a good performer day-in and day-out, and there are little things I actually prefer over Google’s. Topping that list would be the remote, which is a bit more comfortable and backlit, the latter being invaluable in a dark room at night. I could do without the slightly obnoxious “Free TV” button, but I’m overall quite happy with the remote, and even more so with the find remote button on top of the actual streaming box. The hardware itself is unassuming with a fabric top and a footprint similar to any other streaming box. That fabric top won’t be a problem for most but, crazy tip, don’t spill anything on it! It’s basically impossible to clean if it gets dirty. As far as ports go, you’ve got HDMI, Ethernet, full-size USB-A, and the whole thing draws power from USB-C instead of a barrel plug like the last generation — dreams do come true! All of that comes together for just $60. It’s nothing ground-breaking, sure, but this is just a good streamer in every meaningful way without costing an arm and a leg like virtually everything else does right now. The biggest headache is just finding the thing in stock. We’ve been tracking stock for months and, finally, Walmart seems to be more consistently selling Onn 4K Pro both in stores and online, but your results may still vary depending on when you go to buy and where you live.  If you can’t find the Pro, Walmart also has its Onn 4K Plus dongle that costs just $50 and, in most ways, matches up with the Pro. The main things you’re giving up are the Ethernet port, USB-A port, and a bit of performance.  What do you think of Onn 4K Pro? Have you tried one? Have you been able to find it in stock? For years, I assumed every Ryobi purchase ran through Home Depot. A recent shopping trip on ryobitools.com seemed to prove it. I added an attachment kit for my oscillating multi-tool to the cart, and the only button waiting for me read “Checkout At The Home Depot.” One click later I was on Home Depot's website. What I’d missed sits in the site’s Support menu: a Replacement Parts link that opens the official parts store: Ryobi Power Ordertree. It has its own cart, its own checkout, and thousands of pieces no retail aisle carries. Since the battery was the real investment in my setup, keeping the tools around those batteries alive is the cheapest move I have. The parts store makes that possible, and it isn’t the only direct channel Ryobi’s parent company runs. Ryobi’s site looks like a store. It has categories, prices, a Savings tab, and an Add to Cart button under every tool. The cart tells a different story. Mine showed an estimated subtotal, a note that prices may vary by local Home Depot, and a line reading “Sold Exclusively at the Home Depot.” That handoff isn’t bad news. My Home Depot credit card, its financing offers, and its year-long return window all still apply, because the sale happens on Home Depot’s side. Treat ryobitools.com as a well-organized catalog with a shortcut to the register. For tools, batteries, and kits, the orange store remains the only door. You can use your power tools batteries on more devices and gadgets than you think.  Replacement Parts lives under Support, away from the shopping menus. It opens a Ryobi-branded storefront with two ways in: type a part number, or enter your tool’s model number and browse its schematic. The model number is printed on the tool’s data label. My drill’s reads PCL206. The schematic view surprised me most. Each tool breaks down into numbered pieces, from housings and triggers to backing pads and the smallest screws. Home Depot sells Ryobi blades, bits, and batteries, but it won’t sell you the trigger assembly for a five-year-old trimmer. This store will. If you’d rather talk to a person, Ryobi lists a parts order line at 1-877-634-5704.  Prices on the day I browsed made repair look obvious. A blade adapter was $4.20. A corner sander platen was $4.10, a trigger handle assembly $18.58, and a dust bowl assembly $23.75. Set those against a new tool and the math is short. I’ve written that the blade matters more than the saw, and the same logic covers worn pads and cracked guards. Shipping changes the picture. The store charges $9.99 on orders under $20, $11.99 from $20 to $49.99, and $13.99 from $50 to $99.99. In-stock parts generally ship within a week and arrive in seven to 10 business days. Batch your order. If one tool needs a part, check the rest of the shelf before you pay that fee.  Amazon and eBay often list the same part numbers for less, sometimes with free shipping. Some of those listings are real. Others are lookalikes, and nothing in a product photo tells you which. I already run five checks to spot counterfeit Ryobi batteries, and I’d rather not audit every spool cap too. The official store has its own fine print. Returns must be new and in original packaging, shipping charges aren’t refunded, and a 20% restocking fee may apply. Parts under $5 can’t go back at all. Confirm the part number against the schematic twice, because a wrong guess costs more here than at a big-box return desk.  Parts aren’t the only thing sold outside Home Depot. Techtronic Industries, the company behind Ryobi, operates Direct Tools Factory Outlet online and in outlet malls. My handheld tire inflator, a flashlight, and an angle grinder all came from there, and each cost less than retail. The stock comes in two conditions. Factory blemished tools are unused, with a cosmetic flaw and the standard warranty. Factory reconditioned tools were returned, repaired, and tested, and they carry a one-year warranty. It’s the one place I know of to buy a complete Ryobi tool from the manufacturer’s side of the counter. Home Depot still gets my money for new tools and batteries, and Ryobi’s own website will walk you there whether you planned it or not. The official parts store handles the gap after the sale, when a pad wears thin or a guard cracks and the rest of the tool is fine. Look up the model number, batch a few parts into one order, and weigh the shipping fee against a replacement. The outlet is worth a look when a bare tool is on your list. None of it changes the one tool I refuse to buy from Ryobi, but it has kept several others off the curb. We want to hear from you. Oppo is under no illusions about its current market share in Europe — but it's not shy about its growth ambitions, either  When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.  Recent data published by Counterpoint Research paints a bleak picture of the smartphone industry as it stands today. Q3 2026 (that’s the period between July and September) marked the lowest Q3 for smartphone sales in 14 years, with challenger brands like Oppo, Xiaomi, and Vivo all experiencing declines in market share versus the same period in 2025. Skyrocketing component costs have wreaked havoc on the budget and mid-range tiers, while consumers are holding onto their devices for longer and have become more discerning in how and where they spend their money. What, then, are growth-hungry smartphone manufacturers to do? Oppo, for its part, plans to pursue an aggressive premiumization strategy in Europe. “The European premium market is dominated by two brands,” Elvis Zhou, CEO of Oppo Europe, explained to TechRadar in a recent roundtable interview. “I believe local European consumers would be interested in a third, good option.” Zhou didn’t mention Apple and Samsung by name in our discussion, but those two companies were the only two smartphone manufacturers to grow their respective market shares during that aforementioned Q3 period (though they, too, suffered year-on-year sales declines).      “We are not here to say we will replace one of these established brands. No. We are here to offer a differentiated third option [...] I believe, in the future, the competition between flagship products [will not be] about price; we are not here to sell a more affordable smartphone. We are here to offer a differentiated experience for the premium market. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. “And we heard the same [sentiment] through our market research — most premium users would be happy to try a third premium brand.” The European market is not as wedded to Apple and Samsung as, say, the US market, but these companies still account for 68% of the entire European smartphone market (34% each). By contrast, different sources put Oppo’s share of the European pie at between 1 and 4%. That’s a sizable mountain to climb for any brand — but Zhou and Oppo have identified three emerging trends that could turn the tide in the Chinese company’s favor. “I'm quite aware that these two established brands in the European market do still lead the market in terms of brand awareness, sales channels, and even retail channels; they still do have a lot of advantages,” Zhou explained. “But through our market research, we have identified three trends that might be beneficial to us. “First of all, young consumers here in Europe are ready to buy smartphones online. That offers us an opportunity to engage them directly. “The second trend is that the young generation is dubious about advertisements. They prefer to believe real user experiences that they see [relayed] on social media platforms. And if they believe [those testimonies], then it must be good experiences that people are sharing organically on social media — that's more convincing, and only good products can do that. We are not here to say we will replace one of these established brands. “The third trend is that younger consumers ask questions to AI tools during their decision-making process. These AI tools can help our brand because they focus more on the features of these products — on the user experience of these products — without other interference. And according to our market survey, more than 40% of young people ask questions to AI tools when they want to purchase a new phone. Based on these three new trends, I believe that the value of our products is better respected nowadays.” That last point is a particularly interesting one. Chatbots like ChatGPT have quickly become a primary search engine for millions of young people globally; if these consumers ask an AI platform for information on the best phone to buy, Oppo’s handsets are likely to be surfaced on a numerical specs basis alone (the Oppo Find X9 Ultra, for instance, has better camera specs than the iPhone 18 Pro and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra). Oppo doesn’t enjoy the same visibility via traditional Google searches, as I proved by searching for the “best phone for photography” on ChatGPT and Google. The former displays Oppo Find X9 Ultra as the number one choice; the latter doesn’t reference Oppo at all until you manually click through to a dedicated best camera phones guide. View Original View Original Of course, young consumers aren’t so naive as to instantly buy the first product recommended by ChatGPT, but Oppo’s increased visibility on the platform can only be a good thing for its brand awareness and, ultimately, sales.      In our roundtable interview, Zhou was also asked whether Oppo and other Chinese companies face a perception problem in the West, particularly surrounding privacy, and the CEO was keen to credit consumers’ ability to decide for themselves which brands they trust. “We face all kinds of challenges in our work, but for Oppo, since we are here in an overseas market, our focus is more on market surveys. I've met a lot of young consumers here in Europe, and I find that they are quite open-minded. They're well educated, reasonable, and rational. They are independent in their decision-making process. “These young consumers, when they purchase their personal items, focus more on the product itself. Is this experience good enough? Is it good value for money? And through our market surveys, we found that young consumers are more interested in good imaging [capabilities], AI [features], and also battery autonomy. “In addition,” Zhou continued, “the European market pays great attention to data privacy, so we pay great attention to our compliance policy. We want to make sure that when we design our products, we can meet all these compliance regulation demands. We are very confident that our products can stand the test of time, and one day, our local European consumers will understand that our products can not only meet their requirements, but exceed their demands.” Oppo, then, is putting all its eggs in the premium basket for the foreseeable future — and its next pair of flagship phones, the camera-focused Oppo Find X10 and X10 Pro Max, will be the first test of the company's new premiumization strategy. We’re expecting both devices to be more expensive than their predecessors, but if, as Oppo suggests, young European consumers really do value imaging, AI, and battery life above all else, the Find X10 series has every chance of making a splash on the continent. For a company that only completed its first successful rocket launch in 2008, SpaceX has made remarkable strides in the spaceflight industry. Set up by the flamboyant tech entrepreneur Elon Musk six years before that launch, SpaceX has become an integral part of the American spaceflight industry, launching satellites for governments and organizations globally, transporting astronauts to and from the International Space Station, and developing the next-generation Starship, the world's most powerful rocket that could one day take crew and cargo to the moon, Mars, and possibly beyond. Its success has been propelled in part by its ability to cut costs by reusing the first stage of its trusty Falcon 9 booster, as well as other parts of its spaceflight system such as the Crew Dragon spacecraft and rocket fairing. But SpaceX isn't the only company seeking to make its mark in the spaceflight industry, with several rivals, Blue Origin among them, looking to challenge its growing dominance. As SpaceX knows well, for those that succeed, the rewards could be substantial — with everything from lucrative government contracts and commercial launch deals to satellite constellation deployments and deep-space missions with NASA, all offering a potential route to a larger share of the burgeoning space economy. So let's take a closer look at three of the big spaceflight rivals working to take on SpaceX. Founded by Amazon's Jeff Bezos in 2000, Blue Origin is perhaps the most significant challenger to SpaceX, with activities spanning reusable rockets, satellite launches, and space tourism running alongside ambitions in lunar exploration. While its pace of development has been slower than SpaceX's, Blue Origin has, in recent years, been making notable strides in launch technology. In January 2025, for example, it conducted the maiden launch of its first orbital rocket, the New Glenn. The rocket has now flown three times, with its second flight launching NASA's ESCAPADE Mars mission in November 2025. In the same mission, it achieved its first landing of a first-stage orbital booster — the same booster that it used in the third mission, proving its ability to reuse a rocket. But the New Glenn's fourth flight has been delayed after the rocket exploded on the launchpad during a ground-based test in May 2026. Blue Origin has also been conducting tourism flights to the edge of space using its suborbital New Shepard, a more basic rocket that it's also been able to land and reuse.  Blue Origin is taking on SpaceX by competing for some of the same contracts for satellite launches and government programs. It's also developed a powerful BE-4 rocket engine, which it supplies to other companies to power their own launch vehicles. This gives Blue Origin a separate commercial presence in the launch market, strengthening its position in the American space industry. Like SpaceX, Blue Origin is also developing a lunar lander for NASA's Artemis program. In 2023, it was awarded a $3.4 billion contract to develop the Blue Moon lander for Artemis V, currently set for late 2028, which will follow SpaceX's Artemis IV lunar landing targeted for early 2028. Both missions aim to put humans on the lunar surface. Rocket Lab was founded in 2006 by Peter Beck. While most of its rockets continue to launch from New Zealand, it's also utilizing a launch site in Virginia and has its headquarters in California. Rocket Lab made its name with the Electron, a two-stage orbital rocket that debuted in 2017 and reached orbit the following year.  Rocket Lab is developing a rocket much larger than the Electron designed to carry bigger payloads to space. The Neutron is designed so that the first stage can be reused. The company is also developing spacecraft and satellite components, while providing launch services and infrastructure for hypersonic technology development with its HASTE rocket. This allows customers to test experimental vehicles and systems at hypersonic speeds. Elsewhere, United Launch Alliance (ULA) is a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin. Formed in 2006, ULA historically relied on Atlas V and Delta IV rockets, but is now transitioning to the Vulcan Centaur, a rocket that completed its maiden flight in January 2024. ULA competes with SpaceX for government contracts, including launches for the U.S. Space Force. In April 2025, the Colorado-headquartered company was awarded 40% of the missions shared between ULA and SpaceX under a new national security launch procurement. NASA is planning to use ULA's Centaur V upper stage on future missions of its Space Launch System (SLS) moon rocket. Unlike SpaceX, which has built its business around frequent launches and reusable Falcon 9 boosters, ULA focuses on high-value government and commercial missions. Its new Vulcan rocket is intended to strengthen its position in this market, although the vehicle's first stage is not currently designed for reuse. Rather than trying to replicate SpaceX's entire business, ULA is instead competing for a valuable segment of the market.

Back in the fall of 1987, a new show called Friday the 13th: The Series turned up in syndication, and anyone tuning in for Jason Voorhees was in for a long wait.  Created by Frank Mancuso Jr. and Larry B. Williams and distributed by Paramount, it ran for three seasons and 72 episodes, from October 3, 1987, to May 26, 1990, and the closest it came to a hockey mask was a rumor. Mancuso had a real claim to the name: heâd been on the Friday the 13th sequels since Part 2 in 1981, as a producer or associate producer on four of them. The show started out as The 13th Hour, and he told author David Grove, for the book Making Friday the 13th: The Legend of Camp Blood, that the switch was about selling it.  âI felt that it wouldâve been a lot easier to sell a Friday the 13th show than something called The 13th Hour,â he said, though âwhen I first started pitching a Friday the 13th show, people would cringe because the films had such a negative connotation to them. But yeah, from a commercial standpoint, it was a no-brainer to call the show Friday the 13th.â What he wanted from the movies, per Grove, was only âthe idea of Friday the 13th, which is that it symbolizes bad luck and curses,â and the show never mentions the filmsâ events, to protect âthe new world that we were trying to create.â  A hockey-mask tie-in was floated and dropped. What the show built instead was an antiques shop. The story goes like this: Uncle Lewis Vendredi (R. G. Armstrong) made a deal with the Devil to sell cursed antiques, broke it, and died, leaving the store to his niece Micki Foster (Louise Robey, credited simply as Robey) and her cousin Ryan Dallion (John D. LeMay).  They sell off the stock, then have to get every piece back, working alongside Jack Marshak (Chris Wiggins) and locking each indestructible object in the vault of a shop they rename Curious Goods. âVendrediâ is French for âFriday,â which is about as close as the premise gets to its title. The show was shot in Toronto and started out in late-night slots, until some stations gave it a spot in prime time. A few of its directors came with film careers attached.  David Cronenberg directed âFaith Healer,â a first-season episode from 1988 that lands between The Fly and Dead Ringers in his filmography; it guest-stars Cronenberg regular Robert A. Silverman, and its cursed object, the Sforza glove, moves an ailment from one person to another. Atom Egoyan directed an episode too, the first seasonâs âCupidâs Quiver,â in 1987. For a show that kept its distance from the films, it shared a surprising number of people with them. LeMay went on to star in Jason Goes to Hell in 1993, guest star John Shepherd had already played Tommy Jarvis in A New Beginning, and Cronenberg later appeared in Jason X. Composer Fred Mollin, Rob Hedden, and Tom McLoughlin worked on both the series and the movies. The end came without warning. By the third season, Steve Monarqueâs Johnny Ventura had replaced Ryan, and the season stopped at 20 episodes; the cast and crew reportedly learned of the cancellation while shooting the 20th, so no episode wraps the story up. Normally, America’s highest value exports are either oil, pharmaceuticals, or aircraft and their parts.  Not now.  Starting in October 2025, the value of gold exports has topped all other categories almost every month.  For information on U.S. nonmonetary gold exports through December 2025, go to https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IEAXGG That’s not just because the price of gold reached record high prices.  In February 2026, the tons of gold exported may have set an all-time record. The majority of gold exports are going to Switzerland, almost certainly to the refiners there.  The second greatest quantity is going to Hong Kong, which is the global destination for gold going to China.  The third greatest quantity of exported gold is going to the United Kingdom, where the London Bullion Market Association is the world’s largest gold trading exchange. The U.S. government is still reporting that its gold reserves are unchanged, so these exports look to be coming from current mine output and recycling operations. Why is this happening? There is no official explanation of why U.S. gold exports have soared in recent months.  But here is my speculation. When you put these factors together, my suspicion is that a high percentage of U.S. gold exports are going to China, though some must first detour through Swiss refineries to convert the gold into kilogram bars of acceptable purity.  It is possible that the U.S. government may have acquiesced in this form of payment in return for other political concessions having to do with a number of global uncertainties. Can I prove this?  No.  But it does make sense, much more than any other explanation. Last time I asked—Why did the Coinage Act of 1834 reduce the gold content in U.S. coins?  From the late 1700s to the 1830s, the relative value of gold to silver had increased.  As a result, pre-1834 U.S. gold coins contained a higher value of gold than their face value.  Many were being melted down.  In 1834, the U.S. government reduced the gold content in coins to match the face value to the international value of the gold they contained. Here is this week’s question. Which denominations has the U.S government issued in both coin and currency? Come back next week for the answer. Patrick A. It's no secret that I love handheld gaming, whether that's a small device emulating older games or using one of the most powerful gaming handhelds on the market. But some games deserve a larger screen, or just aren't playable on the handhelds you can carry around, especially if you want to play strategy games. That is fine; I'm a big believer in using the right device for the job, but sometimes I want to play those games from the comfort of bed or the couch without being tied to the desk I sit at for work. That's where I turn to an Android tablet with Steam Link installed, streaming games from my gaming PC onto the tablet on my lap. You can use pretty much any half-decent Android tablet, but I've been using the OnePlus Pad 3 with its glorious 13.2-inch screen, and it's almost as good as sitting at my desk, without having actually to sit there.  I've got Steam Link installed on all my TV boxes, which are Apple TV 4K devices. The Android client has historically updated more frequently, though they're more on par these days. Features like the new Pyrowave codec for Remote Play are a joy to use on the OnePlus Pad 3's 144Hz refresh rate, giving me a smooth gaming experience even over Wi-Fi. The Steam Link app works well, but it doesn't offer as many tweaks as Apollo and Artemis. The former runs on your gaming PC to encode the virtual display, while the latter decodes and shows the stream on your Android tablet. This pairing gives you automatically adjusting resolution, refresh rate, and aspect ratio to suit your device, and you can opt to turn off your PC's screen while streaming to your Android device. Again, the Steam Link app provides all of these (except the option to keep the display off), but I vaguely remember it couldn't at one point. Now you can set the Steam Link stream to match the host or client device's properties, and I change this depending on what game I'm playing. I don't have a consistent logic; Destiny 2 seems to look better at the tablet's aspect ratio, but I like playing more story-oriented games like Uncharted and Tomb Raider at ultra-wide with letterboxing. It controls everything inside the home from one screen. I want to start by saying I don't have an issue with the screen size on gaming handhelds. Well, maybe     on the MSI Claw, where the 8-inch screen is a little odd to hold. Other than that, I find most handhelds' 7-inch screens are just fine, whether they're at 800p or 1080p. They're designed to be large enough to see but portable.     I don't always need that portability when I'm playing from the other side of the house. Sometimes I want a big screen to play on, one that's bright and responsive enough for fast-paced action. I used to use an 11-inch iPad Pro before getting the OnePlus Pad 3, but it was an older iPad Pro, and the A-series chip was aging. Using an Android tablet gives me a larger screen to use and another option for finishing games in my backlog. I've come to terms with the fact that sometimes I want to play but don't want to move to do so, and having the tablet on the nightstand makes that decision-making process easier. The handheld I use most in my collection is the Steam Deck LCD, which has Wi-Fi 5. That's fine for downloading games, but it can struggle to stream Remote Play from my gaming PC. The Wi-Fi 7 chip in the OnePlus Pad 3 has no such issues, and never skips a beat while I'm playing Destiny 2 at high resolution, or anything else I want to slob out and play from the couch.  I've used most of the gaming handhelds on the market, and they all have ergonomic issues after a while. Some of that is just down to form factor and having to keep a 7-inch screen between the controls, but the grips, control placement, and weight also matter. And while I know I could pair a controller to them, that feels weird to me, because they already have built-in controller parts. My brain doesn't like that idea, but I can use anything with Bluetooth on an Android tablet. Sometimes I use an Xbox controller because it's familiar, while other times I use a DualSense because the symmetrical thumbsticks are comfortable. I can't use it all the time, though, as I really dislike the trigger design. I also don't have to worry about wearing out the controller parts, because they're not part of the tablet, and I can easily swap to another controller.  Okay, this isn't strictly limited to the tablet, because I could do this on the gaming handheld too. But then I'd have to find a stand to keep the handheld screen visible, while my tablet's keyboard also has a kickstand. The touchpad isn't my favorite way to navigate anything, but a Bluetooth mouse fixes that, so I can play resource management or strategy games without resorting to the touchscreen or a controller. Thanks to Steam Link, I can play my Steam library from anywhere in the house. That's a bigger deal than you might think, because I often want to play games but don't want to sit at my desk all the time. And playing on a larger screen, without dragging a laptop around, is great for games I want to play but don't want to play on a handheld's smaller screen. The OLED screen and design improvements are great — it's just that the Z2 Extreme is showing its age. We want to hear from you. This episode is a panel. Four guests join Michael Kennedy to compare the tools they actually use in 2026, from editors and terminals to databases and hosting. The episode moves fast across many tool categories. It helps to know where Python code lives on your machine and how developers have started handing work to AI coding agents. 1. AI has reopened every tool choice, and for some people the editor has become Slack The main idea of the episode is that the Python toolchain, which felt settled for years, is moving again because of AI. Michael used to ask every guest what editor they use. The answer became so predictable (VS Code or PyCharm) that he stopped asking. Sydney's answer this time was the surprise of the show: about 90% of her coding now happens in Slack. Tagging a coding agent there kicks off a task, she reviews the result on GitHub, and comments left on GitHub get picked up and addressed by the same agent. She only pulls code down locally when it really needs hands-on work. Her path there went from PyCharm to VS Code to Cursor, which added agents to the IDE early. Michael described something similar: dictating instructions on his phone to an agent and checking back later through chat without ever opening an editor. Reuven, who had thought Claude Code was as modern as it gets, said his brain was melting at the idea of Slack as the main coding tool. 2. Terminal-first editing: Claude Code, Pi, Vim, and Markdown specs Calvin doesn't even have VS Code installed. His coding happens in the Pi agent and Claude Code, with bat for viewing files and PyCharm as the "fallback fallback fallback" when deeper digging is needed. A lifelong vi user (vi, Vim, then Neovim), he once froze on stage at a PyCon lightning talk when vi mode got switched off in PyCharm. He now spends much of his time reading Markdown specs and plans produced with the Superpowers skills before telling the agent to implement anything. Reuven went from Emacs to some PyCharm to mostly Jupyter, and has spent the last year mostly in Claude Code. Pat uses VS Code for remote connections to AWS and VMware instances, Kiro (from AWS) for AI help, Vim for quick runtime tweaks, and Nano when a server's Vim defaults block pasting. He also still uses KEdit, a DOS-era PC editor modeled on the IBM mainframe editor XEDIT. For richer AI clients, Calvin mentioned the JetBrains agentic client, Codex, and the Claude desktop app, which now includes Cowork and Code. 3. uv won package management, and the panel agrees Every panelist uses uv. Michael expected the topic to take one sentence, and it filled a big part of the show. Calvin said uv simply packaged the opinions he already held: pyenv for Python versions, pip with lock files and pinning flags, and pipx for installing tools. uv added speed and consistency on top. Sydney compared uv's effect on package management to what AI agents did for coding. Reuven remembered years of PyCon packaging talks that ended with "if only someone would solve this mess." Then uv arrived and handled versions, packaging, uploads to PyPI, and Python installs, and it does all of that fast. Reuven also said uv hides the virtual environment activate/deactivate dance he always disliked. Michael argued uv's killer feature is that it lives outside Python and can be your way into Python: it can install the interpreter itself, so a script with dependencies runs on a machine with no Python at all. Calvin said that a few years ago he was considering a containers-only approach just to get reliable installs, and uv made that unnecessary. 4. PEP 723 inline script metadata and the uv run shebang Pat says 90-some percent of the code he writes is single-file DevOps scripts, so PEP 723 inline script metadata is a daily tool. The comment block at the top of the file declares the script's dependencies, and uv run builds the environment on the fly. Calvin described a shebang that calls uv run at the top of such a file. After chmod 755, the Python file is fully executable with nothing else needed. He had been prompting DevOps agents to use the PEP 723 section, and one of them added that shebang unprompted. Michael pointed out that this makes Python scripts feel almost like Bash scripts. Calvin added that uvx (run a tool without installing it) is even easier than uv tool install. His own example is the Talk Python CLI, installed with uv tool install and usable by your AI tools to query the podcast catalog without any authentication. Pat also noted a real-world catch: corporate machine policies can block installing Python, and uv runs into the same wall, so he works under WSL where the rules are looser. 5. Why AI agents love uv, and what Astral joining OpenAI changed Sydney explained why models work so well with tools like uv. Code is verifiable (it runs or it doesn't, a test passes or it doesn't), and models are post-trained heavily on code, so popular tools are familiar "at the weights level." uv was already the leading package manager before AI took off, which means models can use it well to control the environment where code runs. She also pointed out that general-purpose agents, not just coding agents, use code as a way to get things done. Recent models lean hard on that: in a Claude Code session you now see bash, bash, bash instead of read-file and write-file calls. Michael added that you also see python -c with giant strings. Calvin dislikes that pattern because each one needs approval and it makes session reports less readable. On Astral's acquisition by OpenAI, Pat said things carried on so normally that he had almost forgotten it happened. Reuven called Astral reliable stewards, and Calvin noted uv isn't tied to Python's own release cycle. Michael mentioned his recent conversation with Charlie Marsh about life inside OpenAI. 6. AgentsView: observability for your own AI coding sessions A side conversation turned up one of the most interesting tools of the episode. Calvin uses AgentsView to report on coding agent sessions and see how well he is working with the agent. It grades context window usage, scores bad behaviors and points them out, and shows things like how much of a session was spent on bash tool calls. Michael runs it as a daemon with a web view. All of his machines (a Mac Mini, a Mac Studio, and a MacBook) push to a central Postgres database in a Docker container so he gets one view of all his AI work. Calvin has the same multi-machine setup. Michael warned that the scariest part is seeing what your tokens would cost at true API pricing. Sydney, who thinks a lot about agent observability, framed the key questions: is the agent inefficient because of its structure, because of how you prompted it, or because it isn't equipped for the task? Pat said his team, which is watching token spend, will be looking at it too. 7. The terminal renaissance: Kitty, Ghostty, cmux, herdr, and Royal TS Reuven found it wild that people are still building new terminals in 2026, and figures AI is driving the rush. Pat added that they also have to be rewritten in Rust. Calvin uses Kitty, a cross-platform, GPU-accelerated terminal. He kept it through three years of running only Linux on the desktop (to get away from Apple's Touch Bar) and still uses it after returning to the Mac. He dropped tmux for Kitty's built-in window management, and now uses herdr, an "AI native" multiplexer for remote sessions and agent management. He connects to agents running anywhere with Mosh over a VPN. Reuven left iTerm2 for Ghostty after realizing he used about 10% of iTerm2's features, and fixed Claude Code flicker by switching to its full-screen TUI mode, which adds searchable scrollback and a diff pane. Michael moved from Warp to cmux, which remembers workspace layouts, restores SSH connections, has an iPhone version, and is built on Ghostty. Pat lives in Bash, uses WSL, and recommends Royal TS for saved SSH, RDP, HTTP, SFTP, and VNC connections on Mac and Windows. He also uses tmux so long-running tests survive dropped connections. 8. CLIs are becoming the interface for agents Calvin made the point that terminal UIs and CLIs now give LLMs and agent harnesses a rich interface. In many cases they work better than MCP servers for local tools. His example is the Spark email client, which now ships a CLI. He can tell an agent to use it, and can also use it directly without leaving the terminal to check email. He prefers this to the MCP option for local integrations. Michael tied it to the Talk Python CLI, which you can point your AI at to ask questions like "what did Sydney say on her first episode?" A tool that is easy for humans to script turns out to be easy for agents to drive too. The same idea comes back later with docs that serve Markdown and agent skills. 9. Web frameworks: FastAPI, Django Ninja, Flask, and Robyn in an AI-trained world Calvin just gave a DjangoCon talk with Frank Wiles comparing Django plus Django Ninja against FastAPI. FastAPI is still faster, but not by much. His rule: if something may grow into something bigger, start with Django. For quick, high-quality APIs, FastAPI fits. He noted you can change roughly one import and move FastAPI-style code to Django Ninja. Michael said FastAPI's "fast" is really about fast development done right, with Pydantic, OpenAPI, and validation. Calvin also praised Sebastian Ramirez's library skills project, which packages agent skills so your agent follows FastAPI best practices. Pat uses Flask at work because LLMs have seen so much Flask code, and uses Robyn (Flask-like, Rust-based, multi-threaded) for personal projects, though he has to "herd" the agent because there's less Robyn code for models to learn from. Michael's fix for less-known libraries: clone the repo, have Claude Code study the docs and code, and generate a skill for your project. Reuven settled on FastAPI for the back end of the practice system on his site and sees the volume of existing Flask, FastAPI, and Django code as a real advantage with LLMs. Calvin and Michael both miss Pyramid. 10. Pydantic is the bridge between LLM text and structured data Sydney got into open source by trying to make Pydantic work well with Django, and soon after started using FastAPI. Python isn't strongly typed, and Pydantic gives you a way to opt into strong typing for data modeling and validation. That's why it sits at the core of FastAPI, where requests and responses need structure. She thinks FastAPI first made Pydantic popular, and LLMs have made it more popular still. LLMs produce text, and Pydantic validates that text and turns it into predictable models that ordinary code can use. Reuven recently had the same realization from another angle: type hints are great, but Pydantic is like adding CHECK constraints to typed Postgres columns. You can say a value must be greater than zero or below some limit and really tighten what's acceptable. 11. Type hints: optional for humans, essential for keeping agents in line The panel split on hand-written types but nearly agreed on typing for AI-written code. Sydney is all in. The core team has made types much easier to write, ty makes checking very fast, and agents remove most of the boilerplate pain. Calvin came to Python for its clean, stay-out-of-your-way style and duck typing, and doesn't hand-write type hints. But he wants agents to add them for determinism and to catch whole classes of bugs before the code runs. Pat skips types in single-file DevOps scripts but uses them in AI-heavy side projects that may go public. Reuven went from "real programmers don't need types" to "all in." Teams make mistakes, people from statically typed languages want a safety net, and types keep LLMs "on a short leash." Michael types the public functions of a package, and requires every agent to pass ty, Ruff, and the tests with zero warnings before calling a task done. On type checkers: Sydney moved from mypy and Pyright to ty, Reuven still uses mypy but this episode may change that, Pat ends up with mypy because LLMs default to it, and Michael gave a shout-out to Pyrefly, wearing the shirt to prove it. 12. Databases: Postgres by default, with embedded databases on the rise Postgres is the default for nearly everyone. Reuven's answer was simply "Love Postgres, period." Sydney often pairs Postgres with blob storage, because agents produce large artifacts. She also thinks data models are "back in vogue," since data has to be structured well for agents to query it at scale. Calvin is Postgres too, with a nod to ZODB, the Zope object database that served him for decades. Pat's production is almost all Postgres, plus SQLite, DuckDB, and LMDB (Lightning Memory-Mapped Database) in a side project. Michael is on Team MongoDB because schema changes and code grow together without heavy migrations. Michael is also on a kick for small embedded databases: SQLite, with write-ahead logging, durability, and cross-process locking, is ready for a lot of single-machine production work. Calvin likes DuckDB's JSON features for quick CLI tools. Reuven uses DuckDB as a query engine over Pandas data, where it is "shockingly faster than Pandas itself." Michael also pointed to DuckLake, which puts Parquet files on S3 with DuckDB, SQLite, or Postgres as the metadata catalog. 13. Documentation goes AI-native: Zensical, Great Docs, and Mintlify Calvin's team uses MkDocs and loves it. Michael highlighted Zensical, the next-generation docs tool from the Material for MkDocs team, which now powers the FastAPI docs. Michael is especially enthusiastic about Great Docs from Posit, the team behind Great Tables, and thinks it doesn't get nearly enough love. He moved all of his small libraries to it. Great Docs generates agent skills per library with install instructions, serves any page as Markdown if you swap .html for .md, offers copy-as-Markdown, and produces llms.txt and llms-full.txt. Sydney recommended Mintlify, which LangChain uses. It adds copy-the-MCP-URL, copy-as-Markdown, and "copy this prompt" components to every page, and Sydney believes Pydantic has moved to it from MkDocs. Calvin made the point that beautiful docs are worth it even for personal projects. 14. Hosting: simple VMs, Kubernetes, Cloudflare Workers, and AI-driven price shocks Reuven runs simple DigitalOcean droplets. Michael pushed back on calling that small: if you run Docker on a big server, you can go a long way bringing your own stack instead of tying into cloud services. Calvin is all in on containers and works in two modes. One is full Kubernetes, either Talos Linux in large clusters or single-node K3s. For him, the killer feature is releasing code through the control plane without shelling into a box. The other is Cloudflare Workers, where Python is now a first-class language. He uses Workers to replace Zapier zaps. Pat's company runs 90% or more on AWS with multiple EKS clusters and an ECS cluster, has some workloads and authentication on Azure, and ended up on Oracle Cloud after Oracle bought Zenedge, which provides its CDN and WAF. Michael moved from DigitalOcean to Hetzner, but AI-driven hardware demand is changing prices: an 8-core, 16 GB Hetzner server he pays $35 a month for now lists at $130. By his math, DigitalOcean is now the better deal dollar for dollar. 15. AI tooling roundup: harnesses, models, memory, and token spend To close, each panelist shared their AI setup. Calvin mostly uses Pi plus Claude Code with the Superpowers skills, and prefers Sonnet 5.5 or OpenAI's latest model. He gets annoyed when a new release makes the latest Opus the default and it starts eating tokens. For self-hosting, he recommends a Qwen model that runs on most machines with 32 GB of RAM or more. Sydney's advice is broader: have a coding agent, an agent in Slack, and an agent wherever you keep documents (Notion, in her case). Sydney is bullish on MCP for connecting data and skills for capturing domain knowledge, and most excited about agents that improve over time through memory of your preferences and past reviewer feedback. Pat lets the tooling choose models automatically, uses Kiro and VS Code, watches token spend, and finds local models underwhelming next to hosted ones. Reuven uses Claude Code for about 95% of the work and compares it to the Mac, while OpenCode is like Linux: very extensible, but more setup. Michael also uses Claude Code, usually inside VS Code, and GLM models for personal automation through inexpensive hosted providers. 16. Python 3.15 is (nearly) here, and uv already has it The episode was recorded on October 1st, the scheduled release date for Python 3.15. When the panel checked, python.org still listed 3.14.8 as the current download. Calvin is excited about the release and had already used uv python install to run the release candidate for a Python Bytes "What's New" demo built around a dungeon crawler. Months earlier, Reuven made a YouTube playlist on getting ready for Python 3.15 and told viewers to install it with uv, which "just worked." It's a good example of Calvin's point that uv isn't tied to Python's own release cycle. You can try a new interpreter the day it ships, or before. "This would have sounded very odd like two years ago, but honestly, where I do most of my coding now is in Slack." -- Sydney Runkle "My brain is melting thinking of Slack as your main coding editor." -- Reuven Lerner "When I thought back in the day when I was doing Zope and we were coding into a text area on a webpage, that was bad... but to do it into a Slack agent, also kind of blows my mind." -- Calvin Hendryx-Parker "I got on stage once at PyCon to do a lightning talk and somehow VI mode got disabled on my PyCharm and I was absolutely petrified." -- Calvin Hendryx-Parker "Way back at Iowa State, I took Pascal on punched cards. So that was a little different." -- Pat Decker "Can I just say how wild it is that in 2026, people are still developing new terminals." -- Reuven Lerner "And you have to rewrite it in Rust, too." -- Pat Decker "If you use the word poetry in our Slack, there was a Slack bot response with a haiku that was not favorable to poetry." -- Calvin Hendryx-Parker "I feel like uv was the speed up for package management that rivaled what AI agents did for coding." -- Sydney Runkle "It took me a little bit of time to realize it was not just a super, super fast pip, but that was like the gateway drug to start using it." -- Reuven Lerner "I think one of its killer features is it lives outside Python, and it can be the way into Python." -- Michael Kennedy "LLMs produce text and Pydantic is kind of the bridge back into like, let's validate that data and turn it into a predictable model that we can then use in code driven applications." -- Sydney Runkle "One of the things that brought me to Python the language was the stay out of your way, get stuff done quickly, efficiency of the language." -- Calvin Hendryx-Parker "I sometimes say to people that the things we can tell agents and LLMs are the sorts of things that would get us like written up for being of abusive behavior as a manager if we were to do all these things to the software developers on our team." -- Reuven Lerner "You're going to run ty, you're going to run ruff, you're going to run the tests and you don't call yourself done... until all those things pass." -- Michael Kennedy "I feel like Claude Code is like the Mac and OpenCode is like Linux." -- Reuven Lerner Story: the duplicate cmux fan in the coffee shop. Michael and his friend Mark were looking at cmux in a coffee shop when a stranger walked over, apologized for interrupting, and showed off their own cmux setup. "So apparently at least three of us use it now." Story: three years of Linux over a keyboard. Calvin ran only Linux on the desktop for three years because Apple insisted on the Touch Bar. He came back to the Mac when Apple returned to a regular keyboard, and kept the Kitty terminal the whole time. Story: the haunted laptop. Calvin brought up the xkcd comic in which the artist's Python environment setup is so tangled that their laptop is declared a Superfund site. Michael explained the joke for non-US listeners. If this episode has you rethinking your own toolchain, these courses go deeper on the ideas the panel kept coming back to: working well with AI agents, using types to keep code (and agents) honest, and building a solid Python foundation. The striking thing about this conversation isn't any single tool. It's how much of the Python toolchain is moving again at once. A few years ago the answers were predictable: VS Code or PyCharm, pip and virtual environments, whichever type checker your team picked first. In 2026 the panel's answers ranged from Slack as a coding interface to GPU-accelerated terminals built for running agents, and the reason almost every time was AI. Some choices settled hard. uv is now the shared default, and Postgres remains the safe database. Others are wide open, with new terminals, new type checkers, docs that serve Markdown to agents, and embedded databases making a real case for production. The common thread is that tools now need to work well for both people and agents: fast, scriptable, well documented, and strict enough to keep generated code honest. You don't need to adopt everything this panel uses. Do take the episode's opening question seriously and ask which of your tools you'd still pick if you were starting fresh today. Last week, gamers still holding any hope that the GPU market would somehow stabilize had their hopes dashed. A while after Nvidia reportedly put the RTX 50 Super series on hold, rumors started flying that production of the already-rare RTX 5090 was stopping, likely to use precious silicon manufacturing capacity for more AI accelerators. Now, the company's senior VP Jeff Fisher reportedly said that card was not discontinued and would continue to be shipped. The statement comes after a myriad of websites, including Tom's Hardware, have asked the company for official comment, but to no avail. The information comes from Taiwanese websites including 4Gamers and SJTV, which both are quoting a purported post-event interview where Fisher offered a brief explanation of the situation. According to the VP, supplies of the GPU are limited, but Nvidia is seemingly going all out to get the product to market (paraphrased from the Taiwanese reports). "The supply chain (capacity) is indeed somewhat constrained, but NVIDIA is doing everything it can to get the product on the market. Although there are other variants of the RTX 5090 (chip), production has not been discontinued, and NVIDIA will continue to ship, which is very important," Fisher reportedly said to 4Gamers. He also reportedly reiterated a common quote from Nvidia execs, stating that without GeForce, Nvidia wouldn't be where it is today, and likewise, the AI market wouldn't exist as it does today. The claim that the card isn't gone after all merits some spot-checking, so we did a cursory browse of the common retailers. At Amazon, RTX 5090s are selling for about $8,500, but from third-party sellers. Best Buy has a grand amount of naught cards on offer, while Newegg lists 5090s for about $7,300, but from what are likely Chinese sellers, judging by the shipping time. The ever-famous U.S. tariffs would likely add quite a chunk of change to that price tag, too. Finally and perhaps most poignantly, the card remains absent from Nvidia's own marketplace and Micro Center as of this writing. Some would say that these statements are nothing but a means to keep the company in gamers' minds, even though gaming-related revenue is now a vanishingly small piece of Nvidia's ever-larger money pie. Jensen's firm isn't the only one seemingly keeping up appearances, as Intel has repeatedly stated that its long-awaited refresh of consumer GPUs isn't dead, and last year AMD said it still intends to deliver "the best mainstream gaming GPUs on the market." Yet there are no new GPU launches from any of the three, and their quarterly launch figures keep doubling down on AI. Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. Homelabs are quite the rabbit hole to delve into. There’s a ton of things to explore and customize, making the home lab truly your own. One of the more unconventional “upgrades” I’ve made this year is switching to an open-air PC case, and it's been quite the pleasant surprise. Most of my costly PC building mistakes are easy to avoid once you know what to watch for. While it houses pretty much any PC component you can think of, calling an open-air test bench a PC case is a bit of a stretch. After all, it's just two sheets of folded metal screwed together. That said, the ALAMENGDA DIY PC Test Bench is surprisingly well-built and seems to be cast entirely in iron. The box also came with a cute little single power switch, a set of screws to assemble everything, and a set of side plates. You can find clones of these cases online at varying prices. Get whatever is cheapest and has reasonable shipping — they’re all roughly the same. I’d have preferred a proper power/reset switch setup, but at around $30, I can’t really complain. Besides, it also leaves room for upgrades, as you’ll see later. Still, assembling the case was a nightmare and not a well-documented one, so here’s my walkthrough for the record. The ALAMENGDA DIY PC Test Bench case did come with a printed sheet of instructions, but the documentation was sparse at best. Trust me, I’ve tried. I went through a bunch of YouTube tutorials and the manual itself to come to the impossible conclusion: the plates must be facing at opposite ends. It makes no sense and defies all logic, and I spent a good hour or two scratching my head while I tried to assemble the case in all ways but the right one. Once that was sorted, it was time to place the PC parts on the case. I used a leftover B550-M MSI motherboard (the MSI B550M-P mATX) from my previous build as the base to start upon. An ATX-sized board would be much better, though, since you’d have way more expansion slots. As for the CPU, it was the trusty Ryzen 5 5600G, now replaced by a Ryzen 5 5600X on my main gaming PC. It came with 32GB DDR4 RAM, unfortunately not in dual-channel mode (8+8+16), and a 512GB NVMe drive for both boot and storage. I then paired this with a leftover Gigabyte 550W non-modular PSU and the RTX A2000 6GB GPU for some GPU acceleration. Assembling and wiring everything together was the easiest part of the whole process, and all that remained was to attach the power switch. The stock, bundled power switch is kind of useless, so I opted for an aftermarket option. This particular switch is kind of overkill, having physical buttons, lit for both power and reset. It also has 3.5 mm audio in and out, along with two USB-A ports. Once connected, it was time to turn on the PSU and test things out. To no one's surprise, the PC started normally, as if nothing had ever changed. Onto the obvious reason why you’d want an open-air PC case in the first place: easy access. Disassembling a PC case every time you want to test out a new hardware configuration (or just debugging issues in general) gets frustrating really quickly. A test bench solves this entirely and lets you swap out and monitor components to your heart’s content. As for how it's held up, I’d say pretty well. It also has the added benefit of lower temperatures, since there’s nothing to restrict airflow here. That said, an open-air PC case can quickly become a nightmare, depending on where you live. It’s particularly dusty over here, and I have to clean the case regularly. A small blower and a brush help, though I wish I didn’t have to do it so often. Open-air cases have no shielding, so it's wise to keep them in places with little movement. Make sure to tighten the hinges so they hold things better too. Assuming you can live with these (very minor) compromises, it’s a pretty solid buy and one I can wholeheartedly recommend. Pairing your rig with the right case can really elevate any custom-built desktop.  We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. Quota-carrying sales was spared across every region and department. Most of the growth came from demand. Management credited Workers and agentic workloads as key drivers of the quarter. Cloudflare is in the middle of the machine-to-machine traffic boom, and a smaller G&A team let it keep up with that demand at lower cost. Prince also expects Cloudflare to have more employees in 2027 than at any point in 2026. He’s planning to hire again, for different roles. My rough math: Q1 annualized revenue over 5,156 people works out to about $496K per employee. Q2 annualized over roughly 4,050 people works out to about $690K. That’s a ~40% increase in one quarter, nearly all from the lower headcount. Three things Cloudflare did well:  Atlassian cut about 1,600 people in March to put more money into AI and enterprise sales. More than 900 of those roles were in software R&D. The market wasn’t feeling good about Atlassian at the time. It had lost more than half its market value since the start of 2026, on fears about AI-native competitors. The stock rose about 2% after hours on the news. The June quarter: Cannon-Brookes also plans to buy up to $250M of Atlassian stock on the open market. The limits: fiscal 2027 guidance steps total growth down to about 13% and ARR growth to 18%, partly because Data Center revenue is expected to decline about 17% as customers move to cloud. And roughly a point of FY26 growth came from acquisitions. Atlassian cut 900+ engineers and product people, and the product side of the business sped up. MCP server and Teamwork Graph CLI usage passed one million monthly active users, more than doubling in a single quarter. Atlassian also split the CTO role into two AI-focused positions at the same time, so it changed how engineering works along with how many people do it. Bending Spoons is the extreme case, and since it’s now public, we have its numbers. It cuts deep at nearly every company it buys. Eventbrite announced major layoffs weeks after the deal closed, and Bending Spoons reportedly cut 75% of WeTransfer’s staff after buying it. Vimeo has been through two rounds since the $1.38B acquisition. The results: $2.57M per employee is roughly 4x Cloudflare’s post-cut number. Net revenue retention was 95% in 2025. The acquired base shrinks a little each year on average. Bending Spoons grows by buying more companies. So Bending Spoons shows you can run a mature, slow-growth product with a small fraction of the original team and make it much more profitable. It doesn’t show you can grow a product 30% at that headcount. Vimeo shows what gets given up. Right before the close, Vimeo had shown an ambitious roadmap, including a rebuilt review product with Premiere Pro integration and natural-language search. The January layoffs came soon after. Bending Spoons runs its products for margin. At a $20M ARR company growing 60%, the Bending Spoons model would hurt you. At a $15M ARR product growing 5% with 150 people, it’s worth studying closely.  Each plan fit its company. A 75% cut would have broken a business growing 34% like Cloudflare. Keeping all of Vimeo’s engineers would have cost Bending Spoons a lot of margin. 5 Interesting Learnings from Cloudflare at $2.8 Billion in Revenue: 36% Growth, a 20% Layoff, and a Stock at 50x Revenue  We’ve gone further than any of these three, at a much smaller scale. SaaStr runs at $15m-$20m in revenue with 3 humans and about 20 AI agents in production. That’s around $6M of revenue per human. The agent count peaked near 30. We’re consolidating back toward 20. About 6 do most of the daily work. What the agents run entirely: What humans still do: judgment calls, relationships, and checking the agents’ work. A recent 13-hour day with 10K went to checking, re-ranking, and fixing, with no new features built. We spend far less time doing tasks and much more time reviewing them. If you cut 50% and expect agents to run unsupervised, you’ll be disappointed. Someone has to own what the agents produce. At Atlassian, that’s the managers and engineers who stayed. At SaaStr, it’s me.  Back office, G&A, and ops: 50% or more. This was nearly all of Cloudflare’s cut. We run all of it with agents. Start here. Marketing ops and demand gen execution: 30% to 50%. Agents now handle campaign building, list hygiene, creative variants, and reporting. Humans still own strategy and brand. Engineering at a large, mature org: 10% to 20%, possibly more. Six months ago I would have told you to protect engineering. Atlassian cut 900+ R&D roles and cloud growth went up. Bending Spoons runs mature products with 90%+ AI-assisted PRs. Engineering orgs that grew fast through 2021 usually have room to cut. Engineering at a small, fast-growing company: keep it. On a 25-person team at a $20M ARR company growing 60%, each engineer is now 2x to 3x more productive. Keep them, and consider hiring more. Quota-carrying sales at a growing company: leave it alone. Cloudflare spared it explicitly. Atlassian cut elsewhere to invest more in enterprise sales. If the pipeline is real, the reps carrying a number go last. Customer success: depends on ACV. At low ACVs, agents can carry most of it. At $100K+ ACVs, customers expect a person, and large customers drive 73% of Cloudflare’s revenue. By John Gruber WorkOS: How SSO works and the fastest way to add it. I’ll start with a nomenclatural sidenote: Apple seems to be going with “Apple HomeView” as the product’s name. E.g., the URL slug for it on Apple.com is apple-homeview/, not just homeview/. Few people notice and no one who doesn’t work in Apple product marketing cares, but they actually do the same thing with Vision Pro — in Cupertino, it’s “Apple Vision Pro” (once again including the URL slug). Yet this week’s new HomePod Mini is just “HomePod mini 2” and the existing 2nd-generation HomePod is just “HomePod (2nd generation)” — not “HomePod 2” or “Apple HomePod”. I certainly intend to just call it “HomeView”. Apple introduced HomeView with a three-minute introductory film simulating a suburban family’s hectic before-school/work kitchen rush hour, with versions hosted on Apple’s site and YouTube. The most ridiculous aspect of it is that anyone would possibly make their kid French toast in that scenario. I’d have told my son to make his own goddamn French toast with that attitude. Or I’d have made a single serving and eaten it myself right in front of him. Bro. I do think the basic concept is an intriguing idea. But as an implementation of that concept, my initial impressions are threefold. First, I am unconvinced that anyone in a family would use this for anything other than playing music or podcasts, rather than just using their phones. And if that’s the case, why not just have a HomePod? Apple’s video shows family members taking turns to use the HomeView, rotating it on the kitchen island to face themselves. Why? Why does the mom check her calendar on this, rather than on her iPhone, while the dad is using it to follow a French toast recipe? There’s a real “Why do we need this?” question here and I don’t think Apple’s video answers it, at all. You need to think you want it if you’re going to buy it. And even if you already had a HomeView set up, I’m not sure how often you’d use it instead of your phone, or instead of just talking to it like a screenless HomePod. Second, all the touching and rotating — in Apple’s own demonstration — makes it seem awkward that HomeView must be tethered to a USB power cable. If you look closely in the video, they do show the USB power cable in some shots, but not many. And if you look really closely, this hypothetical family has drilled a hole in the center of their kitchen island to snake the cable through. The hero shot introducing the product, of course, does not show the power cable at all:   We see a wee bit of the cable when the dad reaches to touch the screen to start the French toast recipe:   And then a few seconds later, after the mom rotates the HomeView to the side, so she can check her calendar (despite the fact that she knows the dad was using it to follow a recipe), we get our most honest shot of the cabling situation:   The above shot is at 0:49. It’s followed by two quick cuts to the dad and then the younger daughter, then at 0:52 we cut back to the mom (curious about her daughter’s new boyfriend situation), and, lo, the shot is now framed in such a way that we no longer see where the cable goes:   If you think that slight reframing is happenstance, you should stay away from poker tables. Most kitchen islands I’m familiar with — including my own — have power outlets on the sides of the island. I’m sure some people have power outlets on the top surface of the counter, but I can’t recall seeing one. These are kitchen counters, not office desks. But either way, there’d be a long USB-C cable cluttering the countertop. And if you do happen to have a power outlet on the top surface of your counter, there’d be an adapter sticking out of it, all the time, to duplicate this HomeView setup. This family’s convenient hole in the center of their island countertop is a fantasy. Where does the cable go underneath? How exactly do they have a power adapter plugged in down there? What happens when something spills on the counter? When we custom ordered our kitchen, we weren’t asked if we wanted any holes drilled in our island countertop, and if we had been asked, it would have made me wonder if the guy asking the question had a hole or two drilled in his head. I know, it’s a marketing video. Marketing videos present products in ideal settings. But the power cable is an essential aspect of the standalone HomeView. I’m not suggesting that it should be battery powered. You’d still need to plug it in every few days, which would mean most people would just leave it plugged in, which gets us back to needing to live with an always-visible cable and power adapter in one of our living spaces. The countertop hole this cable disappears into in this video is less ideal and more dishonest. The wall-mounted option seems more appealing to me, but now you’re talking about a home improvement project and (for most of us) calling an electrician. And that raises the question of why the wall-mounted version costs the same $300 as the one with the connected base, even though the base provides the subwoofer. And it requires a mount, and the mounts cost $60 (USB-C), $80 (AC wired), or $130 (PoE — and this one is not available yet). So the wall-mounted version, when you include a mount, costs more but sounds worse? This doesn’t make sense. Those points make me skeptical that there’s a place for HomeView in my home. We have a stereo pair of HomePods in our kitchen. Neither is on the center island, because that would be dumb. They’re on the counters along the outside of the kitchen, each near an outlet on the wall. In the four days since HomeView was announced, I’ve tried to imagine when I’d want to look at something on a screen on either of them. My count remains at zero. My third early impression is that the display is surprisingly small. I saw HomeView in person in New York on Tuesday, and I think Apple’s video conveys its size very accurately. It’s small and cute. It’s much more like a HomePod Mini with a screen than a full-size HomePod with a screen. For some reason I was expecting the latter. This is not a complaint, simply an observation. I actually think that making it small and cute makes it about as unobtrusive as an ever-present screen could possibly be. That’s good. But because it’s small you need to be close to it to read anything more detailed than large glanceable widgets. The major difference between a device with a screen and one without is that you can watch video on a device with a screen. But HomeView clearly isn’t intended for that. It can play video but isn’t primarily meant to play video. If it were it would have a widescreen aspect ratio. But instead it has a square aspect ratio,1 which is decidedly unsuited to video, unless, I suppose, you want a screen that is equally unsuited for both widescreen and tallscreen video. So my skepticism boils down to the question of why anyone would want to add one (or more!) additional ever-present screens to our homes and lives. Phones can stay in our pockets until we need them. Watches remain on our wrists. HomePods can be tucked away unobtrusively in corners, and remain fully useful. HomeView needs to be in a prominent location for its display to serve any practical purpose. Apple’s initial pitch for it doesn’t earn that prominence for me. In my thoughts and observations column after Apple’s iPhone event last month, I wrote the following regarding the iPhone Duo’s clever 1:1.4 aspect ratio: Here’s the thing. If you take a 2 : 1 or even 2.2 : 1 aspect ratio phone display and turn that into a book-like foldable, the inner screen comes out square — or so close to square that we might as well just call it square. Nobody makes any device of any sort that just has a square display. Square is a terrible aspect ratio for a phone or a tablet or a laptop or a desktop display. The only square displays on the market are the inner displays for Android foldables from the last decade. Square being a shitty aspect ratio is half the reason almost no one has bought those things.  I will admit that I had the as-yet-unannounced HomeView in mind as I wrote that, given that its square aspect ratio had been rumored for months. HomeView is not a phone or tablet or laptop or desktop display. It’s not a TV either. So maybe square works for this nascent product category (status boards?). But if square does prove to be correct for this purpose, it’ll be the first category I can think of where that’s true. Apple Watch is the closest device I can think of whose screen serves primarily to display status, but even Apple Watch isn’t square. (It varies slightly by model, but Apple Watch displays are around 4 : 5.) ↩︎  Display Preferences  Copyright © 2002–2026 The Daring Fireball Company LLC.

By Joe Wilkins    					Published				  					Oct 17, 2026 2:51 PM EDT				  Can’t-miss innovations from the bleeding edge of science and tech Nearly a year ago, news began to spread of an experimental weight loss drug called retatrutide, under development by Eli Lilly. Though the drug hadn’t made it through clinical trials, nevermind been released by a federally licensed manufacturer, a rapidly-growing black market ensured interested customers didn’t have to wait for the real deal. Now, the bill on those black market knockoffs seems to be coming due. As CBS reports, the consequences of the unapproved retatrutide trade have now become deadly. According to the broadcaster, the Food and Drug Administration has received at least two reports of deaths related to the use of bootleg retatrutide in recent months — the first public accounts from health officials acknowledging that the knockoffs contributed to users’ deaths. Though CBS viewed documents related to the two deaths, it noted that the details haven’t been independently verified, and it remains to be seen whether the black market retatrutide was the principle cause of death in either case, or merely a complicating factor. Documents related to the death of a 41-year-old woman in July, for example, names retatrutide as a “suspect product” which the deceased obtained “from an unreliable source.” The woman in question was labeled obese, and died after going into cardiac arrest. Though more information is needed to determine whether the knockoffs were truly responsible for the deaths, the FDA’s interest is telling. In April, Medpage Today reported a case of retatrutide overdose which led to extreme side effects for the user which included kidney injury, extreme dehydration, and diarrhea lasting at least a week. And though the FDA is at least aware of the dubious retatrutide trade, the federal government’s lax attitude toward bootleg peptides throughout the second Trump administration is arguably a principle factor contributing to the rise of sketchy knockoffs. “It is concerning because of the breakdown of our drug-approval process in the United States of America,” associate professor at Harvard Medical School Pieter Cohen told CBS. Consumer hardware has come a long way, to the point where some data-center workloads are now being replicated at desktop scale. To play with local AI, desktop GPUs are ideal companions for complex parallel processing, especially RTX cards with dedicated AI hardware. However, a bulky card is overkill for smaller AI tasks that don't need a separate GPU. That's where newer specialized components come in to handle these lighter workloads, like a dedicated AI accelerator: a PCIe device that looks like a GPU and has the same form factor, but it doesn't output video and is built to handle lighter AI workloads much more efficiently compared to a GPU. These AI accelerator cards had a huge wave around 2023/24, but a market for them never really formed, and the hype quickly faded because they were trying to fill a gap already covered. PCIe everything! AI accelerators are specialized expansion cards that look like GPUs and are explicitly designed to run AI inference. They don't have input or output ports; they sit in a PCIe slot or come as M.2 devices. The processors inside an AI accelerator, in particular, handle parallel processing and matrix multiplication, operations used in AI workloads. An AI accelerator typically has onboard memory, but it's not a replacement for a GPU; it's meant to work alongside it by offloading AI inference to the accelerator while the GPU handles graphics and other AI tasks. Modern GPUs like the RTX series and newer RX cards already have dedicated AI hardware like NVIDIA Tensor Cores and AMD AI accelerators, so they themselves are technically AI accelerators. Overall, the term “AI accelerators” applies to GPUs, NPUs, and TPUs, but here it refers to dedicated PCIe AI cards. Most AI accelerators are comparatively less powerful than a GPU. Even though they pack a punch relative to their power draw, they're mostly advertised for light workloads like object detection, creating live models, transcription, or running small language models. On the other hand, they can also help with content creation by improving audio and video quality with background noise reduction using AI, image enhancements, and lighter video editing tasks, too. A GPU can already handle these workloads easily, but the pitch for AI accelerators is that they can handle the same mundane tasks that don't require a full GPU's attention, lowering the total power draw. A prime example of an AI accelerator that I'm talking about is the Hailo-8 PCIe, which packs up to 208 TOPS, depending on the number of processors inside. Individually, each processor inside outputs 26 TOPS while only consuming around ~2.5 W, making a PCIe card with up to 8 modules draw 20W in total. The main selling point for these cards over a GPU is the power savings. However, if you compare the price of an AI accelerator against a GPU, the pitch doesn’t quite land. The Hailo-8 PCIe card, for example, goes around $400, which is an awful lot for just 206 TOPs. In contrast, the RTX 5060 retails for the same price even after the price hike and inflated MSRP. The GPU features a total of 614 TOPs — triple the amount compared to the Hailo-8, and only consuming 145–150W. Therefore, a separate AI accelerator on your desktop wouldn't make sense if a GPU could already handle these tasks, unless you want to save a handful of watts that would barely amount to anything for your electricity bill. Where I see a practical application of AI accelerators is in robotics and other edge applications. Since there isn't an option to install a GPU on a single-board computer, an M.2 AI accelerator would fit fine. Even then, the use case is minimal because, individually, these AI accelerators aren't that fast, unless you opt for an add-in that fits into a GPU slot. In their current state, AI accelerators rarely solve any problem, regardless of their scale. For the desktop, a GPU alone should be a no-brainer, or an NPU can do the same job as an AI accelerator. Even then, NPUs are considered useless. Software support is another problem, and there are no proper benchmarks to showcase the performance of AI accelerators. In contrast, Nvidia’s CUDA ecosystem is already too broad, and no developer will be convinced to buy a separate chip because there are no equivalent tools. Unfortunately, I don't see proper support even coming in the near future because AI accelerators never really took off despite the initial hype. We want to hear from you.
