With Southeast Asia’s largest electricity bills rising even higher, Filipinos invest in rooftop panels. Save Share Philippines solar power boom: Iran war spurs demand for renewable energy sources Manila, Philippines – Keith Cantera and his family have been thinking about having their own solar power grid at home for years. But spending up to $5,000 for solar panels was nothing to scoff at, so they put the idea on the back burner. It all changed this year when the United States-Israel war on Iran rattled global energy markets and sent electricity prices soaring. From paying a monthly bill of about $150 before the war began in late February, Cantera said his family went to forking out as much as $220.     Eight months later, they are having solar panels installed on their rooftop. “The cost is about the same as paying our electric bills for three or four years based on the current rate,” Cantera said. “But in the fifth year, we’ll have recovered our investment, and electricity will essentially be free.” Cantera is one of a growing number of Filipino homeowners turning to solar power in a country that had Southeast Asia’s highest electricity costs even before the war. They were comparable only to Singapore, where the average income is more than 10 times higher. A report by the energy think tank Ember estimated that rooftop panels had nearly doubled in the Philippines since early 2025. And in the first months of the war from March to May, the rush for solar power led to $407m in panel imports, according to government trade data from China, where most panels are manufactured. The Philippines became the biggest single overseas market for that period. Only the Netherlands bought more, but it redistributes them to the rest of Europe.      Lexus Grepo, CEO of the solar power supplier Solarmaxx, can attest to the boom. “There is a 30-day wait because solar panel shipments can’t keep up,” Grepo said. “In March, we had 40 projects, which was almost triple our monthly clientele. Since then, we have been setting up 25 to 30 systems a month.” Grepo does not expect demand to slow down even if tensions in the Middle East ease and shipping routes for energy supplies reopen. “I think people now realise that the world is an unpredictable place, so they have to be ready for any eventuality. Filipinos now see that they don’t necessarily have to be at the mercy of the global energy market.” The Philippines, one of the few countries in the region where electricity is not subsidised, relies on imported coal and gas for more than 70 percent of its power mix. The value of its currency, the peso, which has slid to a record low of more than 63 to the US dollar, is making these imports even costlier. In late March, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr declared a national energy emergency in response to the war ⁠and what he described as the “imminent danger” posed to the national energy supply. Still, electricity rates have continued to increase.      The shift to solar is also partly driven by anger at electric companies that have come under scrutiny for charging customers for so-called system losses, which include illegal connections. Cantera said learning about having to pay for someone else’s electricity consumption was the last straw. “Who would agree to paying for something that you did not use? It’s not like the money we spend for electricity just fell from heaven,” he added. But while the soaring demand is real, the upfront cost of a solar power system is still too high for most Filipinos. The government in March launched a new initiative offering loans for residential rooftop installations, but these are available only to public sector workers. What officials hope can bring power rates down for the majority of people are the dozens of renewable energy projects in the pipeline, including a 3,500-hectare (8,650-acre) solar farm north of the capital, Manila, that is projected to be the largest in the world. When fully operational, the project is expected to generate 850 megawatts of electricity for 2.4 million households. But some consumers said such projects could take years to complete, leaving them with ballooning electricity bills unless they take action themselves. “It’s just so unpredictable nowadays. You have the impending El Nino weather pattern. There’s still war, the continuing fuel price hikes and so much more,” Cantera said. “So why not utilise a natural resource?”          Follow Al Jazeera English:

Paul Green (left) and Emma Hayes (right) built a formidable team at Chelsea When Paul Green left Chelsea after 13 years, he had achieved so much success that the majority of his medals were hidden away in a box under the bed. It was only when he had gone that he truly began to appreciate what he had done. The former Chelsea head of women's football formed a formidable partnership with ex-manager Emma Hayes and helped lead the Blues to 19 major trophies. He left suddenly in February amid reports of unrest in Chelsea's hierarchy.  Asked about his exit, Green told BBC Sport: "Look, football clubs move on and a lot of people have changed at that club in recent years.  "I think ultimately they chose to go in a different direction but I feel very proud of the job that I did there and I left the club in a lot better position than when I first went in there." Under Green's leadership, Chelsea won six successive Women's Super League titles, the last coming under current manager Sonia Bompastor in 2025. They became the most dominant force in the WSL and reached the Women's Champions League final in 2021. "It was an incredible time. There was a lot of potential that Emma Hayes sold to me and that came to fruition," said Green.  "What the [players] went on to achieve, in my eyes, will never be beaten and it will be difficult for any team to replicate that type of dominance.  "It was some of the best times of my life. It's probably not until you're out of it that you actually appreciate what the success was.  "I had so many medals that were just chucked under the bed in a box. I've had time to get them framed. Now I've got a new chapter here at Bay FC." Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed Are the European Women's World Cup play-offs working? Women's billion-dollar boom leaves players behind, says Fifpro Green had seven months out of football before he was appointed as chief football officer of San Francisco club Bay FC in September. He admitted the response to his Chelsea exit had been "overwhelming" and he needed time to adapt, spending time with his family in the meantime. "It was people just in the general women's football world who really appreciated the work and success that we had there," said Green. "Of course, that touched me and it took me forever to get back to everybody who had reached out because there was that many.  "I guess all things have to come to an end at some stage and I've gone in a different direction now. "In the early days, having a lack of structure was difficult because I had gone from 13 years of having certain routines. That part was difficult." It is clear that Green is excited by the future at Bay FC. He has taken over a project that is being led by former Football Association (FA) director Kay Cossington and comes under the multi-club ownership of Bay Collective. Green hopes to use his extensive knowledge in the transfer market to recruit some of the world's best players and to build an effective organisation.  "They sold me the vision for the club. It became too good an opportunity to turn down," said Green. "The potential there of building something really special is what I'm looking forward to. I think it's got some similarities to the early days at Chelsea." Bay FC are moving into new training facilities next year and Green has vowed to act in the transfer window to improve their league position. They are currently third bottom with three matches left in the National Women's Soccer League 2026 season. "The team hasn't done as well as everybody would like it to do. We are where we are in the league so we need to try and improve the roster immediately," said Green. "With the connections and network that I've built up over 20 years, I'm confident that I can bring in a few players to help the good nucleus of talent we've got. "You have to have the infrastructure right off the pitch in terms of staffing and facilities and that's something we are working on." Aggie Beever-Jones (left) went on to win Euro 2025 with England During Green's time at Chelsea, he oversaw the development of several English players including homegrown talents Aggie Beever-Jones and Lexi Potter. Potter made her debut in England's 5-0 win over Greece last week, while Beever-Jones was part of the squad who won Euro 2025. However, there is concern for the future of England's youngsters with gametime for homegrown players reducing in recent years. What does Green suggest the solution is? "Players still need exposure and the way we tried to do it at Chelsea was by having a good loan programme," said Green. "You need to find the right partner club to develop the player. But if you haven't got that resource, maybe young players have to go abroad to play. "There is the proposal of a 'B team' that a lot of other European leagues have that works very successfully in Germany and Spain.  "I do think if they came in at level three of the pyramid that would help because the academy isn't what it used to be. I know that's very controversial." The FA's director of women's football Sue Day said it was an area that needs addressing, while England manager Sarina Wiegman admitted her concern. "Not enough of our young players are playing enough football and I think we'd all agree with that," said Day. "I don't think you ever want to, even if you could, impose anything regulatory. We all need to work together in this system to make it work.  "The FA, the clubs and the league are all on the same side. Clubs are going to create value from investment they are putting into developing players." 'Alarming' - does WSL have a homegrown problem? + 413.66 + 148.80 + 285.00 + 414.00 + 626.00 + 413.66 + 148.80 + 148.80 + 285.00 + 285.00 + 414.00 A bl.portfolio analysis of liquidity stress data released by the mutual fund industry body AMFI shows that actively managed small-cap mutual funds have reduced their estimated liquidity risk over the past year, despite a sharp rise in valuations. The Nifty Smallcap 250’s price-to-earnings (PE) ratio rose to 34.45 as of September 30, 2026, from 29.96 a year earlier, indicating richer valuations. However, the category’s average time to liquidate 50 per cent of a portfolio fell to 11.9 days from 17.6 days. Our analysis suggests that the improvement was driven largely by higher market trading volumes and changes in portfolio composition, including greater exposure to relatively liquid stocks and an increase in the number of holdings. We analysed AMFI’s liquidity stress-test data for 31 smallcap schemes for September 2025 and September 2026, covering liquidation time for 25 per cent and 50 per cent of portfolios, market-cap allocation, cash holdings, AUM and instrument-wise portfolio composition. Here are the key findings: The category’s average time required to liquidate 50 per cent of a portfolio fell to 11.9 days in September 2026 from 17.6 days a year earlier. The time required to liquidate 25 per cent also declined to 6.2 days from nine days. Of the 31 schemes analysed, 19 recorded an improvement in their 50 per cent liquidation time. Most large schemes saw meaningful improvement. Tata Small Cap reduced its liquidation time from 63 days to 35 days, Quant Small Cap from 71 to 46 days, HDFC Small Cap from 69 to 52 days, SBI Small Cap from 61 to 51 days and Nippon India Small Cap from 43 to 27 days. Only five schemes saw their liquidation time increase, including Bandhan Small Cap, from 14 to 19 days, and Invesco India Smallcap, from eight to 13 days. Seven schemes reported no change, all of them relatively small schemes. The improvement was broad-based, particularly among larger schemes, indicating a reduction in estimated liquidity stress even as valuations rose. One key reason for the improvement was increased trading activity in smallcap stocks. The total traded value of Nifty Smallcap 250 stocks on the NSE rose 24 per cent to ₹31.8 lakh crore during April-September 2026, from ₹25.6 lakh crore during the preceding six months. This matters because the liquidity stress test estimates the time required to liquidate a portfolio partly on the basis of stocks’ trading volumes. Higher traded volumes mean a given position can theoretically be sold faster, lowering the estimated liquidation time. The share of Nifty 100 stocks in the overall smallcap fund portfolio increased to 22 per cent in September 2026 from 18 per cent a year earlier. These stocks generally have higher trading activity and deeper market liquidity than smaller, less-traded stocks, potentially improving portfolio liquidity. Seven of the 31 schemes also increased their allocation to midcap stocks. Among them, Quant Small Cap, DSP Small Cap, HDFC Small Cap and Bandhan Small Cap raised their midcap allocation by one to seven percentage points. However, the trend was not uniform. Axis Small Cap, SBI Small Cap and Nippon India Small Cap increased their smallcap allocation by three to eight percentage points while reducing midcap exposure. Eighteen of the 31 schemes increased their allocation to their top 10 holdings, while 13 reduced it. The trend was mixed across fund sizes. A higher allocation to the top holdings can support liquidity if these stocks are relatively large and actively traded, enabling fund managers to unwind positions more easily. Twenty-two of the 31 schemes increased the number of equity stocks in their portfolios. Bandhan Small Cap added 39 stocks, taking its total to 269 as of September 2026, the highest in the category. JM Small Cap added 27 stocks to reach 88, while Nippon India Small Cap added 21 to reach 256. A larger number of holdings can reduce dependence on individual stocks and allow funds to spread their positions across more securities. This can reduce the size of individual positions relative to trading volumes and, in turn, lower estimated liquidation times. The improvement in liquidity stress is a positive development for smallcap fund investors, particularly as valuations have risen. Higher trading volumes, greater exposure to relatively liquid stocks and broader portfolios have helped reduce the estimated time required to unwind positions. However, lower stress-test estimates do not guarantee that a fund can exit its holdings quickly during a market-wide sell-off. Liquidity can deteriorate sharply when markets turn volatile and trading volumes dry up. Investors should therefore view liquidity stress tests as an additional risk indicator, alongside valuations, portfolio concentration, fund size and investment strategy. The bl.portfolio MF Star Ratings can serve as another reference when evaluating funds, but should not be the sole basis for investment decisions. TL;DR: Binance says its bStocks tokenized-equity offering has surpassed $1 billion in assets under management, four months after launch. The milestone illustrates growing interest in trading blockchain-based representations of traditional shares. Binance says its bStocks platform has crossed $1 billion in assets under management, marking a significant milestone in its effort to make conventional financial assets tradable through cryptocurrency infrastructure. The company reported the figure on October 15, approximately four months after the product launched. Binance also cited more than $40 billion in cumulative trading volume and an expanded range of tokenized US shares and exchange-traded funds. The numbers suggest that traders are interested in moving between familiar Wall Street exposure and blockchain-based platforms. Eligible users can trade tokens designed to track exposure to underlying securities held through custody arrangements. Unlike holding ordinary shares directly, these instruments may not confer the same corporate voting or shareholder rights. Their attraction lies in features such as fractional access, transferability and integration with other digital asset products. Binance has already explored using tokenized equity holdings as collateral for derivatives positions, offering investors a reason to hold the instruments beyond simple price exposure. That integration is one potential advantage over conventional brokerages, although it also introduces counterparty, custody and market-structure risks. The products are not available to US persons and are subject to eligibility restrictions elsewhere. Tokenization does not remove the obligations surrounding securities trading. For the broader sector, the important question is whether these products can continue attracting demand when crypto market enthusiasm weakens. A $1 billion milestone is meaningful, but sustained growth will depend on transparent backing, dependable liquidity and the ability to offer advantages that conventional market infrastructure cannot easily reproduce. It was another crazy busy week for Apple, headlined by Tuesday seeing the company take the wraps off of several home-related products as part of a "Welcome home" launch wave. And as if that wasn't enough, Friday saw the start of iPhone Duo pre-orders with delivery estimates quickly slipping by months amid its popularity and apparent product shortages, while we're looking forward to even more products launches later this month, so read on below for all of the details!  Apple's long-rumored smart home hub is finally official, with Apple debuting the $299 HomeView as part of its "Welcome home" product launch this week. Apple HomeView features a 7-inch Liquid Retina display and Siri AI support, and it's available in both tabletop and wall mounted versions. The device is able to recognize multiple users and adjust its presentation of information depending on how far the user is from the screen, and it supports Photos faces, Apple Music playlists, FaceTime calls, and more. Pre-orders are underway now with a launch coming on November 13.  While the Apple HomeView was the headline attraction of this week's introductions, the Apple TV box also got its first update in four years with the unveiling of the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K. The new box gets a big upgrade to the A19 chip, which provides Siri AI support and improved performance. A new Siri Remote (also available separately for older boxes) includes Find My support with Precision Finding and a speaker to allow it to make itself heard when lost. And for times when you want to use Siri without the remote, the box itself also now includes microphones for hands-free Siri AI. The new box comes with a significant price hike to $299, and it's available for pre-order now ahead of a November 13 launch.  Apple's third home-related product announcement for the week was a new HomePod mini equipped with Siri AI, new colors, and improved audio experiences. The ‌HomePod‌ mini 2 has an S10 chip that supports advanced computational audio, and Apple says it optimizes dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance in real-time. A Sound Glow feature turns the ‌HomePod‌ mini's top into a "visual canvas" that glows and animates in sync with music, reacting to bass and treble. It uses colors generated from the song's album artwork for a unique experience for each song. The HomePod mini 2 is priced at $149 and is available for pre-order now ahead of an October 30 launch. Siri AI won't be available at launch, however, as it will come in a future software update.  Apple began accepting iPhone Duo pre-orders in a number of countries at 5 a.m. Pacific Time on Friday, with delivery estimates starting to slip within minutes if not seconds. Within half an hour, delivery estimates in the U.S. ultimately stabilized at late January 2027, a three-month delay. In remains to be seen how much, if any, stock Apple will have at its retail stores for walk-in purchases on the October 23 launch date, and scalpers are already selling off early pre-orders for as much as $5,000.  After previously reporting that Apple was planning a two-day product showcase in Los Angeles on October 27 and 28 for select content creators and members of the media to experience even more upcoming Apple products, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman now says Apple has begun explicitly inviting members of the media to the event for October 28. We're expecting to see several more products launch on either October 27 or 28, including new high-end 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook models with touchscreen OLED displays, new iMac and entry-level MacBook Pro models based around the M6 chip, and a new iPad mini with an OLED display. ArtsJournal: Arts, Culture, Ideas This Week’s Highlights: Getty Images, whose photographers cover most red carpets and owns a significant portion of the world’s historical photo archives, plans to go private through Chapter 11 with up to $533 million from Charles Koch’s investment firm; its iStock stock-image business is losing demand to AI tools, while its news-photo division is forecast to grow from $369 million to $400 million by 2029 (The Hollywood Reporter).  Netflix has used AI on roughly 300 titles (The Hollywood Reporter) and this week laid off about 1,000 employees while profitable (Variety). Staff at HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster and Hachette tell Wired their executives are directing them to use ChatGPT and Claude for publicity copy and cover art (Wired). The Public Media Bridge Fund has raised about $87 million and stabilized 186 public radio stations, and is starting a $38 million drive to make those stations sustainable without federal money (AP). After Pensacola State College dropped PBS on July 1, residents formed Emerald Coast PBS, which goes on the air November 1 and needs $1 million in its first year (NorthEscambia.com).  Hadestown, filmed at London’s Lyric Theatre, opened in North American cinemas to $10.2 million, a record opening weekend for a live-theatre film (ArtsHub). The Kennedy Center, mostly closed while a court weighs the closure, named Rick Canny, a talent manager and consultant there since April 2025, its artistic director (The Washington Post). Hospitals across the occupied West Bank have been hit by a funding shortage. Save Share Beit Jala, occupied West Bank – Khaldoun Atwan starts each day in the oncology ward at Beit Jala Government Hospital, not knowing what barriers will come his way. The Nabi Yunis checkpoint in Halhul seems to be “always closed”, so the head of the daytime oncology unit at the hospital leaves his car and finishes the commute from Hebron by taxi. “More than once, by God, I found the mirror broken. I found the wiper broken,” he said about his journey through an area where settlers are now active. Traversing a dizzying array of gates and checkpoints opening or closing at will, he does not know whether he will reach the hospital, whether his patients will, or whether the drugs they need will be on the shelf when they do. Beit Jala is the only government hospital in Bethlehem governorate, home to some 320,000 people. Inside his tiny, spartan office, Atwan is struggling to keep up with his cancer patients who have regressed because they missed crucial appointments or essential drugs needed for their chemotherapy treatment. Not even during the second Intifada, he recalls, was drug supply an issue. Now, it’s inescapable. “Everything’s short … whatever’s available we give,” he said. “It’s a disaster.” The Palestinian Authority (PA)’s finances have collapsed over the last three years due to a reduction in international aid and disruptions in Israel’s transfers of tax receipts. Israel’s actions in the occupied West Bank since October 2023, including widespread road closures, checkpoints and a series of settler pogroms against Palestinian communities, have also impacted the economy. As a result, the occupied West Bank’s healthcare system is rapidly deteriorating, with staff receiving just half their salaries, while the PA can’t pay for essential medications. Alongside others nervously pacing in the courtyard, an older cancer patient from a village in Bethlehem governorate stood at the entrance of the hospital, weighing with his son what to do. “Every month they do their best, the doctors and the cleaning staff, but they aren’t provided with anything,” he said. Ministry clinics are now operating part-time, with doctors seeing well more than 100 patients a day when they are. Now, even a doctor’s visit is rushed and unaffordable: “If we want to go to the doctor for a checkup, we need 200 shekels [$65],” said an older cancer patient. “It’s not a story of there being no staff,” said Iyad Dari, the attending physician at the dialysis unit at Beit Jala. Getting paid only half their salaries, “the government employee is working just two or three days a week, because he hasn’t got enough to come in for his full hours,” he added. As a result, the hospital ends up covering emergency cases only. “At first, [patients] were [angry]. But now everyone understands: Everyone’s suffering,” Dari said. The medical supplies crisis in Beit Jala and across the West Bank is the result of Israel’s withholding of tax revenues earmarked for the PA, an action spearheaded by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. “This crisis is very predictable, and we saw it coming 100 percent,” said Milena Ansari of Physicians for Human Rights Israel. Even before the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, Israel was periodically withholding tax revenues, endangering the Ministry of Health’s coffers, Milena said. According to Yosef Ojra, an internal medicine specialist at Beit Jala, the withheld revenues have depleted the Health Ministry’s funds to pay medical suppliers, who are now withholding their services. The ongoing borrowing of supplies between the public and private arms of healthcare has greatly strained private clinics, pharmacies and hospitals. Hisham Amle, an oncologist at the hospital, said shortages are “an old problem, not a new one”, but that about 90 percent of important items – for chemotherapy, above all – used to be there. Now, even immunotherapies and biologics are missing, and cancer treatment runs on an unbroken chain. “If the patient misses a session or two, he’s lost all the treatment before it,” he said. “When I first took over the department, the drugs were available,” said Atwan, the lead oncology nurse. He then began to list all the crucial drugs he was now missing for his patients. “There’s not one single complete protocol I’ve got.” Khuloud Dweib, the hospital’s director of pharmacy, said the ministry recently managed to obtain eight previously missing oncology drugs and four biologics. This should be enough for between a month and a half and two months. But many other drugs are still out of stock, she said. Unlike in Gaza, Israel is not blocking medicines from entering the West Bank, Ansari noted. The problem is “strictly” that the PA has no money to buy them. But “Israel has the primary legal obligation as an occupying power,” she notes, to ensure adequate medical care and access to occupied populations. For all of the southern West Bank, Beit Jala’s hospital is the only public option available for cancer and dialysis treatment, with patients coming from Bethlehem and Hebron governorates, parts of occupied East Jerusalem and sometimes Jericho. But as Israeli checkpoints and gates multiply, reaching the hospital has become a nightmare. Dari described a dialysis patient from Nahalin, with an appointment at seven or eight in the morning, whose village was sealed. “He sat about four, five hours at the checkpoint,” Dari said. Then he took the long way round, through Jaba, Surif, Halhul and Hebron, and reached the unit at four in the afternoon. A normal journey costs about 10 shekels. “A detour like this costs more than 100 shekels,” Dari said, and some patients need dialysis four times a week. The ministry’s central supply warehouse, meanwhile, is in Nablus, Dweib said – and an hour-and-a-half drive can now take six to 10 hours when closures hit. Often, Atwan’s patients require treatments split between his unit and the Augusta Victoria Hospital in occupied East Jerusalem. Before the war, cancer patients from the West Bank routinely received medical permits to enter Jerusalem. Some treatments are in Beit Jala, while others are only available in East Jerusalem. But there are no guarantees any more that patients can reach Jerusalem. “I’ve got a cancer patient … He waited on a referral, and there’s no treatment, and after all the running around it comes back he’s security-rejected, too,” Atwan said. “I mean, he doesn’t get a permit to go to [Augusta Victoria]? Where’s he supposed to go?” Atwan recalled patients who became neutropenic due to missed treatment sessions, and one was lucky not to end up with sepsis. “These are disasters.” He’s not sure exactly how many cancer patients he’s lost due to missed and incomplete treatments; many of the poorer patients, he said, simply go home and die there. As crowds swell at front desks and people wait at the hospital’s entrance, a nervous exhaustion percolates through the hospital’s aged halls. “People are really tense. Everyone’s scared,” Dari said. Atwan, who receives half his salary, struggles to cover his commute from Hebron and help support his daughters at university. “Let’s not talk about our state of mind – we’ll start crying, for God’s sake,” said Atwan. “Our morale is at rock bottom … We smile in spite of ourselves.” Amid mass unemployment with labour permits systematically revoked, more sick Palestinians are pushed towards public hospitals just as those hospitals have less to give. Hospitals “will prioritise someone who will actually pay them”, Ansari added. Ahmed, a Palestinian from Bethlehem with a medical degree, would check every couple of days with the pharmacist to see if they had Humira, an injection every two weeks that his sister with Crohn’s disease needs. For three months, the pharmacists were out of stock. Buying directly from the pharmaceutical company would cost about 2,000 shekels ($650) for one or two injections. “We couldn’t afford that,” he said. “So we just struggled until it became available again.” The elderly cancer patient from a village facing settler pogroms has cut back on his own medication. “It’s not supplied regularly,” he said. A course of it costs 20,000 shekels ($6,500). “I’ve started cutting back, not taking much,” he added. Amid supply and staffing shortages, surgery backlogs have piled up. Sayed Ayyad, 22, from al-Eizariya, fell during an accident, fracturing his ankle badly last month. With serious operations taking priority, he waited three weeks for a slot. “They told me there’s 60 people waiting for an operation,” he said. “One day we couldn’t do the surgery because there were no medicines, no painkillers, no anaesthetic, nothing.” Khuloud Dweib, who heads the pharmacy department at Beit Jala, has to manage the worsening crisis as patients struggle with their health and finances. “There’s no security. We don’t have political, or health, or even financial security,” she said. She’s left thinking of cases like a young man with multiple sclerosis studying medicine in Egypt. The Health Ministry used to provide his medicine through private purchase until the company stopped supplying without payment. His mother came to see her. “I want to sell my house so I can get the injection for my son,” the mother told her. “Because he’s in Egypt, away from home, studying, and … he’s stopped seeing, stopped walking.” “So, what can I tell you,” Dweib said, fighting back the tears. “God help people.” The medical staff fear that with their supplies being hollowed out, they could face a similar fate to their colleagues in Gaza who have been kidnapped or killed. “We know that at any moment we could be targeted as medical staff, just because we’re medical personnel providing services to people,” Dweib said. “We’re a father and a mother in this society.” Nobody in the ageing hospital wards sees an end in sight. “The longer we stay, the worse the situation gets,” said Dari. At three o’clock each afternoon, Atwan has to leave in the hope that he can reach Bab az-Zawiya in Hebron, where he waits for a shared taxi. “Maybe there’ll be a checkpoint for me, maybe there won’t be,” he said. It’s not so different from the conundrums his patients face. “When a patient gets sick, it’s his luck if the medicine’s there,” he said. “We’ve got no future. I swear: We’ve got no future.”          Follow Al Jazeera English:

Reminding me of those toys where you could swap around parts to make a brand-new toy, Anduril's new Steelfin interceptor missile family uses a two-stage design that allows the vehicle to be quickly reconfigured to counter emerging missile threats. Two major challenges in military circles are how to create new countermeasures against emerging missile threats that seem to develop like something out of a lunatic video game, and how to maintain a proper stock of interceptor missiles to prevent defenses from being overwhelmed by sheer force of numbers. There are many advanced interceptor missiles, such as the Lockheed Martin PAC-3 family, that can take on everything up to and including hypersonic missiles with a high probability of success, but even when their design puts a priority on keeping down per-unit costs, they are still on the pricey side. Worse, as hostile powers field new threats, entirely new missiles traditionally need to be developed to counter them, which takes valuable time and makes it more difficult to keep weapons stockpiles up to requirement. Steelfin tries to get around this by replacing the traditional fixed interceptor design with a modular, two-stage configuration. The second stage is common to all variants, consisting of a common airframe, avionics, software, flight control system, and swappable sensors for zeroing in on targets and destroying them. Meanwhile, the first stage can handle different solid rocket motors for pre-selected range, speed, and performance profiles, as well as different booster types and other modular components. The idea is that Steelfin can be manufactured cheaply in large quantities of several thousand units per year while being able to handle a wide variety of threats, from low-altitude aircraft and cruise missiles to high-altitude hypersonic and ballistic missiles. Crucially, the missiles are built to work with existing launch canisters, such as the Mk 41 VLS and Patriot M903A2, and standard battle management software like Aegis and IBCS. As new threats arise, new configurations can be quickly integrated without having to shut down and retool entire production lines, avoiding inventory gaps. It all sounds good, but while Anduril has completed ballistic testing with representative air vehicles, full flight testing is not slated to begin until next year, leaving key real-world performance questions still to be answered. In addition, questions remain as to whether Anduril's open-architecture and commercial component approach can reliably support the extreme hit-to-kill precision required for high-speed warhead intercepts. However, the biggest hurdle will be the broader industrial bottleneck facing both Steelfin and conventional interceptors: the tight supply chain for solid rocket motors and propellants. With ambitious plans to build several thousand units annually, the company will not only have to assemble the missiles themselves, but also find a way to navigate and scale up rocket motor supply lines to meet that demand. Markets in Southeast Asia, Latin America, Africa and the Middle East see increasing demand for stablecoins.  Stablecoin issuer Circle is seeking to enter about 40 developing markets, according to the company’s CEO and ​chairman, Jeremy Allaire. “We’re kind of going through an inflection point...a transition right now, ‌and that transition is essentially moving from the early adopter phase of blockchain technology into the mainstream scaling phase,” Allaire told Reuters, speaking Friday on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank meetings ​in Bangkok. Markets in Southeast Asia, Latin America, Africa and the Middle East are experiencing increasing demand for stablecoins as businesses and individuals seek to enter the internet-based economic system, Allaire reportedly said.  Cointelegraph reported on Aug. 24 that analysts at Bernstein were bullish on Circle, foreseeing a new growth cycle for its USDC stablecoin may provide a significant boost for the company over the next 12 months. Bernstein said the next phase of stablecoin growth could be driven by several factors, including renewed momentum in crypto markets, greater US regulatory clarity, tokenized capital markets and growing adoption of stablecoins for payments. The analysts also pointed to early signs of stablecoin use in payments made by AI agents. Although USDC remains the second-largest dollar-backed stablecoin by market capitalization, well behind Tether’s USDt (USDT), it has gained significant ground in transaction activity. Bernstein said USDC’s share of adjusted stablecoin transaction volume rose from about 40% in 2025 to more than 60% so far in 2026, overtaking USDt by that measure. On Sept. 8, Cointelegraph reported that Circle had agreed to acquire Singapore-based cross-border payments platform Tazapay in a $400 million all-stock deal expected to close in 2027. BMWBLOG » News  News BMW is ramping up its China offensive with a major Neue Klasse rollout and a growing focus on local production.    Adrian Padeanu    October 17, 2026 BMW is preparing a major product offensive in China, with 20 new and updated models planned by the end of next year. The announcement came during the company’s 2026 China Innovation Day, where it also confirmed that production of sixth-generation high-voltage batteries had officially started at its Shenyang plant. The timing is hardly coincidental. BMW faces mounting pressure from domestic automakers that have become increasingly competitive in the electric-vehicle market. The German luxury brand is responding by accelerating its product rollout and bringing more of its latest technology to China, its largest single market. The Neue Klasse is at the center of this strategy, but BMW isn’t simply betting on a handful of electric vehicles to turn things around. The company wants to apply its next-generation technologies across a broader range of products, many of them developed specifically for Chinese customers.  Introducing 20 new and updated models in roughly 14 months is an ambitious target, even for a company with BMW’s resources. However, the figure shouldn’t be interpreted as 20 completely new nameplates. The rollout includes updated vehicles alongside new models incorporating Neue Klasse technologies. In other words, both facelifts and next-generation cars are on the way. BMW has already given us a few clues about what’s coming. A product roadmap revealed earlier this month points to many upcoming vehicles. The camouflaged models could include the next-generation iX1 Long Wheelbase, the next 3 Series Long Wheelbase, and facelifted versions of the 5 Series and i5 in their stretched configurations. These identifications remain educated guesses rather than confirmed additions to the lineup. The new BMW iX3 and i3 will also play important roles in the company’s plans, with long-wheelbase versions tailored to local preferences. China remains a market where rear-seat space matters most, making extended-wheelbase derivatives a natural fit for BMW’s strategy. The same applies to the larger SUV featured here: the stretched X5 and its electric iX5 counterpart. The upcoming models will need to offer more than familiar styling and a premium badge, though. Chinese buyers have become accustomed to rapid advances in infotainment, driver-assistance systems, and electric powertrains. BMW’s challenge is to deliver those features without losing the driving characteristics that have traditionally set its cars apart.  During the same event, BMW also highlighted the capabilities of its long-wheelbase electric i3. As we reported this week, the prototype completed a 1,213-kilometer (754-mile) trip without recharging. That’s even farther than the stretched iX3, which covered 1,030 kilometers (640 miles) on a single charge a few months ago. These tests underscore the potential benefits of combining a more energy-dense battery with efficiency improvements and better vehicle integration. The battery alone doesn’t tell the whole story; the electric drivetrain, aerodynamics, thermal management, and software all contribute to how far an EV can travel. BMW’s ambitions extend beyond flooding the Chinese market with new models. The company wants to manufacture more than 95% of the vehicles it sells in China locally by the end of the decade. It’s also exploring exporting China-built vehicles to other Southeast Asian markets. The strategy makes sense in a market where local brands have gained ground with products designed around Chinese customers’ expectations. Developing vehicles closer to those customers can help BMW respond faster to changing tastes while making greater use of the country’s established supplier network.  However, a bigger lineup and more local manufacturing won’t automatically guarantee success. BMW still needs to convince buyers that its vehicles offer something worth paying a premium for, particularly as domestic competitors continue to improve their technology and expand their model ranges. The next wave of launches will therefore be crucial. With 20 new and updated models planned by the end of 2027, BMW is committing substantial resources to its Chinese business. It needs every success it can get after years of falling sales, with 2026 shaping up to be one of its worst years in about a decade. See more of our coverage in your search results. On September 26, 2024, the Sensex closed at an all-time high of 85,836.12 points. Multibaggers were everywhere, compounders were fashionable, and valuations were an inconvenience best left to old-fashioned investors. Two years later, benchmark indices are down about 13 per cent, with individual stocks suffering far greater damage, including corrections of 50-60 per cent.  Six out of 10  BSE 500 stocks have delivered no positive returns since September 2024, while nearly 7  out of 10  have failed to beat bank fixed deposits. Evidently, the much-celebrated power of compounding has been taking a rather extended holiday. But a new explanation for this disappointment is gaining currency. The problem, apparently, is taxation.  Ahead of the Union Budget consultation process, sections of the market intensified demands for relief from Securities Transaction Tax (STT) and Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) tax. The clamour peaked on October 13 when Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman expressed her willingness to hear the debate, even though she didn’t promise any change. Markets nevertheless found reason to celebrate, gaining 3.5 per cent in the next few sessions.  Even an invitation to debate taxation is apparently worth a rally.  Benjamin Graham, the father of value investing, warned nearly a century ago against believing that good stocks remained sound investments regardless of price, calling it a rationalisation of speculative excess.  Had Graham visited Dalal Street in September 2024, he would have found material for another ‘Security Analysis’. The Nifty 50 traded at about 24 times earnings (NSE), while its constituents averaged a staggering 44 times, as per Capitaline.   Consider the stock-specific valuations investors enthusiastically accepted. Trent commanded around 221 times earnings, Tata Consumer Products 90 times, Nestlé India 82 times, Britannia 68 times and Asian Paints 62 times, according to Capitaline. What extraordinary wealth have these extraordinary valuations created since? Trent is down 43 per cent, Britannia 24 per cent, Asian Paints 29 per cent, Tata Consumer 19 per cent and Nestle India 8 per cent. The businesses did not suddenly become worthless. Investors had paid prices leaving little room for slower growth.  The celebrated IT industry offered another example. IT giants TCS, Infosys and Wipro traded at 25-33 times earnings, growth valuations difficult to reconcile with their maturity and emerging AI disruption. Their sharply negative 32-43 per cent returns underline the danger of assigning growth multiples to mature businesses. Excessive valuations can also reduce pressure on managements to innovate. When investors reward the status quo with premium multiples, dividends and buybacks become easier responses than difficult investments in innovation.   The problem extended beyond large-caps. In September 2024, the Nifty 500 traded at 28 times earnings, Nifty Smallcap 250 at 32 times and Nifty Midcap 150 at an extraordinary 45 times. Two years later, the latter two indices are down 4 and 3 per cent, respectively.  The relationship between starting valuations and subsequent returns is revealing. The set of stocks trading above 28 times earnings in September 2024 have delivered an average return of just 3 per cent in the ensuing period. Those below that threshold have gained 13 per cent on average.  The biggest casualties include PB Fintech, Sobha, Inox Wind, Adani Green, Kaynes, Jubilant FoodWorks, Voltas, D-Mart, Thermax, Whirlpool India, Havells, Varun Beverages and Godrej Properties. Their P/Es ranged from 80 to 741 times in September 2024, preceding declines of 31-72 per cent.  Of course, valuations alone cannot explain every subsequent decline. Earnings disappointments, business conditions and shifting investor expectations also matter. But paying extravagant prices leaves precious little room for any of these to go wrong.   Until recently, India was apparently losing out because it lacked a compelling artificial intelligence (AI) story. Now, taxation has emerged as the explanation for foreign selling. Between September 26, 2024 and October 15, 2026, FIIs sold a net ₹5.7 lakh crore ($63 billion) across 496 sessions, averaging ₹1,150 crore daily. Mind you this coincided with shifting US yields, a firmer dollar and global rotation trades.  But were these foreign investors always so allergic to Indian taxes? FIIs invested ₹1.77 lakh crore in equities in calendar 2023 and ₹2.08 lakh crore in FY24, when global interest rates were still cheap and liquidity in flow. Even after the LTCG rate rose from 10 to 12.5 per cent in July 2024, they invested another ₹61,471 crore in equities during August and September. Apparently, the same taxes that were perfectly tolerable during a bull market became unbearable when valuations stopped making sense.   India’s 12.5 per cent headline LTCG rate on qualifying listed equities is also hardly extraordinary internationally. In the US, combined federal, state and local capital gains taxation can exceed 35 per cent for wealthy investors in high-tax jurisdictions.  Even as foreign capital went elsewhere, relentless domestic SIP inflows have somewhat absorbed the deluge, effectively funding the exit of offshore funds at elevated multiples while retail investors have indirectly funded the ‘Atmanirbhar market’ dream.  None of this means equity taxes are irrelevant. STT raises transaction costs and LTCG tax reduces returns. But the 2019 corporate tax cuts, intended partly to encourage investment, did not immediately unleash the much-awaited private capex boom. Yes, tax concessions can improve profitability and investment incentives, but they cannot create demand or attractive business opportunities. So, there is little reason to assume that reducing stock market taxes will somehow produce better corporate earnings or justify excessive valuations.  Published on  October 17, 2026   					Copyright© 2026, THG PUBLISHING PVT LTD. or its affiliated companies. A simple Jev-like decision maker. Without the hype. Hand it one whole message — an email, a ticket, a review, a doc, whatever you pasted out of the support queue — and tell it what you want done with it. It hands back one decision, as JSON: That's the whole thing. No agents. No orchestration. No prompt engineering. No five-hundred-token preamble to memorise. One message in, one decision out, in a file you can just read. One line, copy-pasteable: Then type shev. The installer uses a user bin directory already on PATH where possible. Otherwise it adds a small, removable PATH block to your shell profile; open a new terminal and type shev—no manual shell edits needed. Prefer npm? This installs the package @noorslvt/shev, with the terminal commands shev and shev-cli. The unscoped npm registry name shev belongs to an unrelated project; do not use npm install -g shev for this tool. You can also install straight from the repo without the registry: Both installers prefer a matching prebuilt release and otherwise build with Rust (installing the minimal Rust toolchain if necessary). npm runs a postinstall step that fetches the right binary or builds it; macOS/Linux are supported by the npm launcher, and Windows users can use WSL. Recent npm releases gate install scripts. If your install is skipped, shev tells you what to run; you can also fix it up front: Got Rust already? Same thing, just as short: For full cleanup, whether installed with curl or npm, close other running shev sessions first: This removes registered shev binaries, its saved keys/config, local model data, tracked chat records, unchanged tracked shev MCP registrations, and the exact PATH blocks added by its installer. A full npm-backed uninstall also runs npm's package removal. Modified binaries/profile blocks, externally managed weights, host recovery backups, unrelated host settings, non-chat metadata in export files, source checkouts, and shared tools/caches (Rust, Node, uv, Codex, OpenCode) are not deleted. You can also remove the npm package directly: This removes the npm package and its binaries. Modern npm does not execute uninstall hooks, so it cannot also remove persistent settings/models/history or external MCP registrations. Use shev --uninstall for full cleanup; it handles the npm package removal too. Persistent npm data deliberately lives outside the package so a normal npm upgrade does not erase private keys, history, or model downloads. No background uninstall watchers or npm overrides are installed. Only the local model cares about the Mac. It runs on MLX, and MLX is Apple Silicon only, so "run it on your machine" means "run it on a Mac". Point shev at a DeepSeek key instead and the work goes over the network — then it builds and runs on any platform Rust does. After the first run it's just: run shev, type, done. The home/start screen has a white ASCII wordmark directly over the wallpaper, without a background box or JSON pane. Once a chat starts, two windows appear: Text panels use #0F0E08 over the dimmed photo wallpaper. Type / for commands: Panels are inset from the terminal edges. Skills/tools menus show names only; long menus scroll around the selected row instead of clipping it off-screen.   Handy keys: /clear starts a fresh chat view; /history can reopen retained records. /reset and history deletion default to cancel in their confirmation menus. Confirmed changes update the responses file, so MCP clients see them too. /model switches between two backends and manages each one. DeepSeek — the secondary, explicitly selected remote option; needs an API key. Options: enter a new key, remove the stored key, or cancel. Bonsai (default) — prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-2B-mlx-2bit, a small ternary model that runs on Apple Silicon through MLX. Options: install it from the internet (about 1.2 GB, into ~/.local/share/shev/models) or uninstall it. The Bonsai pack ships its own loader, because its weights can't be loaded by stock mlx-lm/mlx-vlm (they report Unsupported model type: prism_hadamard_qwen35). So shev runs the pack's bundled runtime in a resident worker, using uv with the pack's pinned requirements. Repeated requests in the same session reuse the loaded model; a one-shot loader remains as fallback. Nothing listens on a port. The first local request installs the MLX stack into a uv environment, which can take a few minutes. This pack ties its output to language_model.model.embed_tokens.as_linear; there is no separate language_model.lm_head. Its native 2-bit operation requires the pack's Hadamard transform. Changing a bits parameter alone is not a valid conversion. tools/bench-bonsai-head.py compares native 2-bit with a correctly repacked 4-bit output head in memory, leaving input embeddings and installed files untouched. Run with the pack's runtime/requirements.txt, after a local shev request has created ~/.local/share/shev/models/shev_bonsai_worker.py: With the current deterministic prompt, one local run measured 1.55 ms/head and 669 ms/decision for native 2-bit, versus 2.29 ms/head and 734 ms/decision for repacked 4-bit. Both scored 6/6 action labels on a tiny smoke test; an earlier prompt/sampled baseline scored 3/6. This is not evidence of general accuracy, and the improvement is from the prompt/sampling changes, not from repacking. Repacking cannot recover precision already lost in the 2-bit checkpoint. Native 2-bit therefore remains the default. Hardware, prompts and output length affect these timings; existing explicit provider selections are preserved. Shev's MCP server lets another assistant read your saved decisions. It does not run Bonsai/DeepSeek or edit your files. No API key, OAuth login, terminal, network port, or separately started TUI is required: the MCP host starts shev as a subprocess and talks JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout. Save at least one decision using an explicit file path, for example: Inside that TUI run /mcp install (or /mcp → install). This writes a descriptor under ~/.config/shev/mcp/ and registers the executable and absolute history path in an existing global OpenCode config, with a private backup. /mcp status reports the registration; /mcp uninstall removes shev's own unchanged registration. It does not delete your decisions. For OpenCode, reconnect shev from /mcps or restart the client after installation. Alternatively, register it explicitly from a shell (replace the executable path if you built from source): The equivalent OpenCode V2 configuration is: For Codex, add this to ~/.codex/config.toml (or your CODEX_HOME config), replacing the paths, then restart Codex and check codex mcp list: Both shev --mcp and shev-cli --mcp work. Example prompts in OpenCode/Codex: Resources are shev://decisions (all records) and shev://decisions/latest (latest record). Reads use the file afresh, so decisions saved by an open TUI become available without restarting the MCP process. Troubleshooting: unknown option --mcp means the host is launching an old TUI binary. Update/rebuild the exact executable in the MCP command and reconnect shev. Current releases dispatch --mcp before terminal setup. If connection succeeds but no decisions appear, check that the host and TUI use the same absolute history path. Starting shev --mcp manually will wait quietly for protocol input; this is normal, not a frozen chat window. /skills reads existing SKILL.md files from Codex, Claude, shared ~/.agents/skills, ~/skills, OpenCode's XDG config directory, and ancestor project .opencode, .agents, and .codex skill folders, plus local skill directories configured in OpenCode. It loads guidance into memory; it does not install, edit, or execute skill scripts. /tools reads MCP registrations from Codex's config.toml and OpenCode's global/project JSON or JSONC, including V2 mcp.servers. CODEX_HOME and XDG_CONFIG_HOME are respected. Selecting a server connects and lists tools; selecting a tool shows its argument schema and prepares /tool server/tool {}. Edit the arguments, then enter to call it. Successful results become reference context for the next decision; /skills off unloads them. Supporting context does not replace the user's original intent in history. Only tools with readOnlyHint: true and without destructiveHint: true can be called. Unknown/mutating tools are blocked, not silently approved. MCP annotations are declarations from your trusted server, not a security sandbox; only use servers you trust. Starting a configured server can run its startup code. Calls have time/output limits and cannot request sampling or approvals. Stdio and streamable HTTP (JSON/SSE) are supported. Configured headers and environment-based tokens are reused without logging them; host-managed OAuth credentials are not copied. An OAuth-only server reports an authentication requirement rather than claiming success. The top of the right pane names the loaded skill or successfully called tool and its source. Integration identity is also stored with its decision. Merely discovering/selecting a server is not reported as a successful tool call. OpenCode's configured JavaScript plugins are listed with compatibility notices. Host-specific plugins cannot run natively in shev; they require their host runtime. Their MCP interfaces, where registered, can be used through /tools. shev never rewrites host configuration during discovery or tool use. Explicit /mcp install is separate and backs up configuration before registration. The TUI is the friendly front door. The line CLI is shev-cli and it's meant for pipes: Useful environment variables: The footer shows token usage and the last decision's elapsed milliseconds. The resident worker reports real local token counts; the cold fallback has no usage metadata and reports zero rather than guessing. The concise summary and generated response remain alongside the JSON. A measured warm run took about 750 ms versus 2500 ms including initial model loading—not a claim of Jev's sub-100-ms latency. Malformed local decisions receive at most two format-correction retries; usage includes those attempts. Retries can add latency and still fail rather than silently recording invalid JSON. Token Terminal data shows synthetic wrappers still dominate a tokenized equity market worth approximately $3.7–3.8 billion             Share Tokenized stocks have a sizable market now. Most of it, though, is not actually stock. According to Token Terminal data from October 17, 2026, about 10.7% of tokenized stock market value comes from issuer-sponsored shares. The other 89.3% is synthetic: wrappers and Special Purpose Vehicles that track a stock’s price without being the stock itself. Token Terminal puts the total tokenized stock market at approximately $3.7–3.8 billion. That figure covers both camps: shares companies tokenize themselves and products built by third parties. Two very different products share the same label. A synthetic token gives you price exposure. An issuer-sponsored token aims to give you the equity itself, with standard shareholder rights like voting and dividends attached. The synthetic side has its own heavyweights. Ondo Global Markets and Binance’s bStocks are among the major players credited with driving the sector’s rapid growth. Custody is also heavily concentrated. Alpaca serves as custodian for about 83.5% of the tokenized stock market, including synthetics issued offshore. Securitize has been the most active name on the issuer-sponsored side. Unsubscribe anytime.  On October 8, 2026, Securitize launched its Convertible Entitlement Token program. The CETs are backed 1:1 and run on the Solana blockchain. The initial lineup targets familiar names: Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT) and Nvidia (NVDA). It also includes crypto-related stocks such as Circle (CRCL). Securitize is pairing the launch with fireside chats featuring public company executives. The program also leans on traditional plumbing. Partnerships with infrastructure providers like Computershare, a transfer agent that maintains shareholder records, are part of what could move the model toward fully issuer-sponsored structures. Superstate continues to build direct-issuance programs that let public companies raise capital by selling tokenized shares. The 89.3% synthetic share reflects a simple reality. Wrapping a stock is faster than convincing a public company to tokenize its own shares. A synthetic issuer can buy shares, park them with a custodian and mint tokens against them. No boardroom approval is needed from Apple or Nvidia. Issuer-sponsored tokens require the company to participate. That means legal work, transfer agent coordination and a willingness to run part of the cap table on a blockchain. Synthetic buyers often get the price exposure without the voting rights or direct claim on dividends that come with owning the stock. For investors, the 10.7% figure is a reminder to read the label. A token named after Nvidia is not necessarily Nvidia stock, and the rights attached can vary widely between products. With Alpaca custodying about 83.5% of the market, much of the sector’s backing depends on one firm’s operations, including for offshore products. Ondo Global Markets and Binance’s bStocks have helped scale the synthetic market, while Securitize and Superstate are betting that real ownership becomes the selling point. Securitize’s pace suggests demand exists: over $250M in added market cap within about a month in a sector valued at approximately $3.7–3.8 billion. It's been a theory for quite some time now that Nvidia is — what's the polite way to put this? — let's say deprioritizing PC gamers, perhaps, or more specifically, its gaming graphics cards. But this week has added more evidence to the collective weight that GeForce GPUs are increasingly at risk of being sidelined further by Team Green. I'm talking first about the story that emerged a few days ago, where a leaker claimed Nvidia is diverting all GB202 (Blackwell) chips to make AI (RTX Pro) graphics cards. That's the graphics processor used in the RTX 5090, but apparently not anymore; it's for AI boards only now, we're told. That makes some sense as the RTX 5090 is already disappearing from shelves, certainly in the US, where you can't buy one for less than the best part of 10 grand (from gouging third-party sellers, with no major retailers actually having stock anymore). So arguably this effective discontinuation of the RTX 5090 is already happening. On top of that, the latest developments are that Micro Center is reportedly listing the Blackwell flagship as 'not carried', and Nvidia itself has removed all mention of the RTX 5090 from its own GPU marketplace (though it is still mentioned elsewhere on the site). Search for the RTX 5090 on that marketplace, and you won't find it any longer — the highest-end graphics card listed is now the RTX 5080 (hat tip to Wccftech for spotting this being flagged up on Reddit). Aside from an actual announcement from Nvidia (which probably wouldn't ever happen anyway), that seems like about as clear an indication you can get that the RTX 5090 has been shoved out of the exit door, never to return, because Nvidia needs those GB202 chips where they are most profitable. RTX Pro GPUs offer a much heftier premium that Team Green can heap on top.      So, what does this mean? For starters, if it is true that the RTX 5090 has been scrapped, the RTX 5080 becomes the flagship Nvidia GeForce GPU. Once the existing stock of RTX 5090s has been depleted, this could mean the price of the RTX 5080 is inflated. When I say inflated, I mean jacked up even more, because it has already seen some nasty price hikes. Currently, the RTX 5080 is at around $1,800 in the US on Newegg, or £1,450 on Overclockers in the UK – and those are the lowest prices; it goes up from there. It's a very similar story in many other regions. This is clearly a concern for gamers as you can see from the Reddit thread I pointed out above, with comments such as: "If you want a 5080 better buy one while you can still afford one." Really, it's debatable if the card is anything like 'affordable' relative to its graphical frame rate muscle even now. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. Here's where another rumor comes into play. Elsewhere on the grapevine, there's talk that Nvidia may actually release the RTX 5080 Super variant which has long been speculated about. This would be a 24GB graphics card, and it'd essentially replace the discontinued RTX 5090 – with the theory being that Nvidia would also ditch the vanilla RTX 5080 (16GB). This would leave the rumored RTX 5080 Super as the sole high-end GeForce graphics card, quite some distance above the RTX 5070 Ti. If that happens, imagine the pricing concerns here – what MSRP would Nvidia attach to the RTX 5080 Super? And then consider the cost inflation that will be added when you take into account that this card will also be sought after for AI usage (as seen with the RTX 5090). If an RTX 5080 Super is indeed inbound for early 2027, that would also suggest that the next-gen RTX 6000 family is further away than some rumors believe – as this Super version would be a stopgap GPU to keep the Blackwell range ticking over. The RAM crisis may have a fair bit to do with this strategy also, given that most predictions foresee it getting worse next year (and the misery continuing into 2028, and maybe beyond). Of course, launching a new GeForce range into such memory headwinds wouldn't be easy.      All in all, it feels to me like there's a stream of subtle – and not so subtle – hints and rumors that Nvidia is very much slowing down the development of gaming GPUs (while not wanting to give that impression, naturally). The other part of the equation here is the increased focus on the software side, of course, rather than the hardware. DLSS 5 is out and Nvidia is already pushing hard with honing and refining that neural rendering tech, and something else that happened earlier this week was that Team Green highlighted some big leaps in performance here. Pretty huge strides forward, in fact. Of course, you could argue that all the development resources being ploughed into DLSS – including frame generation, which got a hefty boost alongside DLSS 5 – shows Nvidia isn't abandoning gaming GPUs for PC gamers. And I concede that's true to an extent, but there is very much a vibe of a major slowdown leading towards the feared deprioritization of GeForce GPUs – and there's another angle to consider here too: cloud gaming. Don't forget that GeForce Now also benefits from DLSS. Just this week, Nvidia added DLSS 4.5 override controls to the streaming service to help push up frame rates – those on the RTX 5080 (Ultimate) plan can use Dynamic Multi Frame Generation of up to 4x now. Ray Reconstruction for bolstering ray-traced visuals is available, too, among other options. Would Nvidia rather have you subscribed to its cloud gaming service, making monthly payments, than buying a GeForce GPU for a one-off sum? It seems an obvious direction for the company to be heading in, and with increasing warning signs around Team Green's gaming GPUs, I'm becoming more convinced that this is where Nvidia's priorities are shifting for the future of PC gaming. This isn't to say GeForce graphics cards are definitely on their way out, or that an RTX 6000 line-up won't happen – it's already well underway after all – but beyond the next generation, I'm increasingly dubious about where GeForce GPUs might fit into the big PC gaming picture. Between AI demand and cloud gaming (plus increasingly faster internet connections), there's a squeeze underway that could prove painful for the GeForce line-up – and the ongoing RAM crisis is hardly helping, either. Sign in to your designboom account.  co-founder martin pošta reflects on the origins of the digital art festival that transforms prague’s streets, landmarks, and historic buildings with light, sound, and performance.   annalise kamegawa October 17, 2026 7 min           Signal Festival reemerges for a weekend of immersive digital art installations that light up the corners and monuments of Prague. Founded by Martin Pošta, alongside producer and curator Jan Rolník and artist Amar Mulabegovič from the art group The Macula, nearly fourteen years ago, the event has grown from a yearly festival to also include a permanent space, open year-round in the Czech capital. Following the opening night of the event’s fourteenth edition, Dream On!, Pošta catches up with designboom in the recently opened Signal Space in Prague’s city center to chat about the event’s history.       From the beginning of his career, even before Signal Festival, Pošta was interested in creating things people would love to watch. He started out producing films and documentaries, eventually attending film school in Prague and going on to organize a film festival in the Czech Republic. After leaving the television industry, he was asking himself what he would do next when he met up with some friends in a bar. As they were chatting, they got the idea to transform a local church with projection mapping. This was 2010, the nascent days of the technology, which had even Pošta himself asking, ‘what is video-mapping?’   After discussing the project with the deputy mayor at the time, he suggested that they instead work with the Prague Astronomical Clock (Orloj), which at the time was about to celebrate its 600th anniversary. ‘I went to roam around and to check out what’s the vibe amongst the people,’ remembers Pošta of the crowds that gathered for this first project. He recounts seeing an older gentleman looking up at the clock tower in awe, telling his wife that she ‘must come and see the installation.’ ‘And I literally got tears in my eyes,’ Pošta admits. ‘I was touched… it was the moment when I kind of knew that I found my next calling.’ It was from this first project that he’d go on to champion new media projects.       After that event in 2010, Pošta and his team at The Macula created and produced these types of installations around the world. Seeing all the emerging talents in the sector spread across the world, he began to work on an event that would bring them all to one place. ‘I was lucky enough that the guy who was deputy mayor for culture, was still there. He knew what we were doing, so it was easier to explain to where we were heading towards,’ Pošta reflects on the early days of organizing what would become Signal Festival. ‘And then I was lucky to get introduced to the Ministry of Regional Development. And I got the first funding for the festival… honestly, we hardly knew what we were doing, but that’s how it happened. We had the list of the artists that we really wanted. There was no curation back then – we were just like, OK, we love this guy, this guy, that guy.’       ‘It’s a huge matrix of the stuff that you have to combine,’ says Pošta of bringing the festival to fruition each year. Not only do they invite artists from around the world, but they also commission new, site-specific works. ‘Some of them are super ephemeral, like with the video mapping projections, there are four nights and that’s gone,’ he says of the installations. Nevertheless, with the newly opened Signal Space, a permanent mainstay in the heart of Prague, some of the works can be seen year-round under Old Town Market Hall. Inside the space, the ceilings open up to reveal some of the turquoise metal supports that hold up the historic building.   Over fourteen years, Pošta has built up a team of what he affectionately calls ‘like-minded lunatics,’ who have come together to create ‘a lot of things that would be deemed impossible.’ These are the coordinators, administrative staff, and tech teams that pull together the festival. They also include the artists who realize the installations, some of whom return for subsequent editions. keep up with our daily& weekly stories   One group that reappears in the dark evenings of Signal is Laterna Magika. Pošta shares a bit about the group’s history in the Czech Republic, saying that ‘they are a faction of the Czech National Theater.’ He describes their technique as one where, ‘They play with the fact that you cannot see people dressed in black against a black stage. You can just see what is lit up, so they created first illusions,’ with this particular technique and projected light and video. He goes on to say, ‘about six years ago, we introduced performative aspect to the festival, and it’s always super interesting to explore with [Laterna Magika] the possibilities of performance, dance, body and visuals.’ This year, they create a live, site-specific performance at the Old Wastewater Treatment Plant in Bubeneč, working from a poem by the Czech author František Vinant. Banks may be able to slow the growth of stablecoins like USDT and USDC by paying savers more, according to a working paper published by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS). Researchers Rashad Ahmed and Iñaki Aldasoro studied weekly data from January 2019 to June 2025, accounting for bitcoin prices, Treasury yields and broader financial conditions. They found that a one-week, one basis point rise in average bank deposit rates predicted slower stablecoin growth. That small figure, just 0.01 percentage points, cut average ten-week growth in stablecoin market capitalization from about 15% to about 12%, the paper found. Under the authors’ preferred estimate, which adjusts for banks raising rates in response to stablecoin growth, the effect was roughly three times larger, slowing growth to about 6%, though the authors flagged some weakness in that method. In both cases, growth slowed but did not reverse. The relationship was stronger for Circle’s USDC than Tether’s USDT, a pattern the authors said was consistent with USDC’s closer ties to U.S. users. The findings add evidence to a debate that has drawn warnings from bank executives. Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan warned in January that as much as $6 trillion in deposits could move into stablecoins and related products offering returns, potentially reducing lending capacity and raising borrowing costs. The effect is partly based on where issuers put their reserves. A December Federal Reserve staff analysis explained that money placed in stablecoins can return to banks as issuer deposits, changing who supplies banks’ funding even when total deposits remain unchanged. Larger, uninsured balances could require banks to keep more liquid assets and leave less room for long-term loans that financial institutions issue. Paying more to retain customers also raises banks’ funding costs. The Fed analysis suggested banks could target better rates at customers most likely to switch, while keeping lower rates for less mobile depositors. The BIS paper does not establish losses of bank deposits or lending. Its sample covers one high-rate episode, and the findings may change as yield-bearing stablecoins and tokenized money market funds gain ground. Banks “retain some influence over the pace of that adoption through deposit pricing,” the authors wrote. A hardline religious ruling justifying the theft of Palestinian olive harvests escalates violence and political tensions before Israeli elections. Save Share Prominent Israeli Rabbi Dov Lior issued a Jewish religious ruling on Friday permitting settlers to steal olives from Palestinian orchards in the occupied West Bank. Lior’s ruling claims that Palestinian landowners who could not access their olives during the harvest season due to Israeli restrictions have been sufficiently compensated in the years they had access to the fruit. According to the ruling, Jews are permitted to pick these olives to claim ownership of the Palestinian land. Lior, born in Poland in 1933, went as far as classifying the theft of olives from Palestinian farms as an “additional virtue”, as settler pogroms and Israeli occupation continue in the West Bank. He added that settlers should “conquer the land” far from Jewish communities in order to publicly “demonstrate our ownership” and follow biblical commandment. “The Jewish people have never given up on the Land of Israel, as we express in our prayers every single day,” the ruling continues. “The Arabs never purchased the land from the Jewish people or from any individual Jew, and therefore it is stolen land in their hands… They never bought it in any way and it remained under the ownership of the Jewish people.” The ruling coincides with another wave of settler pogroms against Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest season. On Friday. at least 19 people were injured in 34 attacks by the Israeli military and settlers on Palestinians harvesting their crops across the West Bank. An American photojournalist working for The Washington Post was assaulted by settlers while covering the daily violence, and five vehicles were torched. Many Palestinian farmers have been unable to access their crops due to Israeli restrictions and the dangers from the settlers. While settler pogroms are not exceptional, they come weeks before Israeli elections, with a push by far-right parties to gain the support of settlers and their supporters. But not all Jewish religious leaders backed the call to steal Palestinian olives.      Rabbis from the religious council of the Gush Etzion settlements published a letter calling the illegal harvesting of Palestinian crops theft, blasphemy, and a moral defect. Tzohar, an organisation of 800 orthodox rabbis, said in a statement that only the state has the authority to confiscate property. As long as the state recognises Arab ownership of the olives, they belong to them, it added. Mamoun Abu Amer, an analyst on Israeli politics, told Al Jazeera that there could be political reasons behind the religious groups’ rejection of Rabbi Dov Lior’s comments. “The position of the other rabbis who rejected this call might be a move driven by political motive and pressure from entities within the government to give the impression that these are anomalous voices that do not represent the general opinion of the settlers. “The Israeli government is trying to portray that those who carry out these riots are a limited-number group that does not represent public opinion in the settlements, and that the settlers are peaceful, good, and law-abiding, and that the issue is confined to the ‘Hilltop Youth‘ boys who commit these crimes,” he explained. Rabbi Dov Lior holds immense influence among hardline settler groups, such as the Hilltop Youth, who fiercely back his hardline religious decrees that oppose any territorial compromise with Palestinians. He is also a prominent figure within Israel’s Religious Zionist movement and serves as the spiritual guide for the far-right Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. “Ben-Gvir relies on the religious rulings of Rabbi Dov Lior, which rely on biblical texts and the Book of Deuteronomy,” Abu Amer noted. He claimed that Rabbi Lior adopts the most extreme interpretations in the Jewish religion. “There is an important matter, which is that Ben-Gvir competes via the TikTok platform, propaganda, and populist rhetoric, and this is a rhetoric that serves him and brings him votes, given the environment and general atmosphere in Israel after the events of October 7, as there is a ‘market for extremism’ in the Israeli society,” Abu Amer added. Knesset member Gilad Kariv of the left-wing Democrats Party criticised Lior, accusing him and his followers of dragging Israel into a flood of moral vice. “Whoever stands on the sidelines in this issue joins the camp of Rabbi Dov Lior and his criminals,” Kariv said.
