Share Article Comments Share Article An analysis released Friday by Democrats on the congressional Joint Economic Committee details how US President Donald Trump loaded up on shares of major pharmaceutical companies last year as his administration and Republican allies enacted policies that benefited the industry—at the expense seniors and other patients. The JEC analysis estimates that Trump increased his stock holdings in the pharmaceutical sector from $1.7 million in 2024 to as much as $56.2 million last year. The committee notes that Trump, who has repeatedly promised to cut drug prices while implementing policies that raised them, “held as much as $39.1 million in stock in the same Big Pharma companies that directly benefited” from a budget package that the president signed into law last summer. “Trump and congressional Republicans intentionally force seniors to pay more for cancer treatment so that Big Pharma can rake in more money that Trump can personally profit from,” said Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-NH), the JEC’s ranking member. “It’s outrageous and yet typical from this president, who makes the American people foot the bill again and again for his own gains.” Tucked in the Trump-GOP budget law was a provision exempting some widely used, high-priced prescription drugs from Medicare price negotiations. Merck’s cancer medication Keytruda was one of the drugs temporarily shielded by the provision; Merck appears more than 60 times in the president’s 2025 financial disclosure. The JEC analysis notes that “in 2025, Merck reported $18.8 billion in US revenues for Keytruda, which helped the company net $22.5 billion in profits that year, a 16% increase compared to 2024.” The president also made big purchases of stock in Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie, Pfizer, and Amgen last year. The JEC found that each of those companies “had at least one drug that benefited from the carveouts” in the Trump-GOP budget law. Additionally, the Trump administration has entered friendly agreements with pharmaceutical companies in which the president is invested, including Pfizer and Eli Lilly. “Trump’s drug pricing deals are a mirage, designed to convince Americans that he’s taken significant action on drug pricing while creating minimal if any downside for Big Pharma,” Peter Maybarduk, access to medicines director for the consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, said last month after his organization obtained heavily redacted texts of the agreements. “The texts show Trump handing out favors to Big Pharma, undercutting his own models to lower prices, and throwing the support of the US government behind corporate decisions to deny medicines entirely to other countries,” said Maybarduk. Δ A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.  Δ In January 1966, a South African ship caught fire at sea. In port in Bristol, England, after firefighters pried open the smoking container, the conflagration spread and burned for five days. A little over a month later, a Liberian steamship caught fire near Rotterdam, ignited a storage area with barrels of petrol and sank. The month after that, a Danish ship caught fire off Long Beach, California, injuring three firefighters, killing a longshoreman and causing over a million dollars in estimated damages. The culprit in each fire was fishmeal, a dark yellow powder made by drying and pulverizing fish that, if left untreated, is known for spontaneously combusting as it decays and oxidizes.  Tied to at least 90 ship and plant fires from the 1950s through the 1970s, fishmeal’s combustibility was a serious worry for seafarers, insurers and dock workers, according to a sweep of historical news coverage by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, D.C. In 1967, American feed producer Cargill announced a solution: ethoxyquin.  Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one. Here's How A crew abandons ship as the SS South America burns in Rotterdam in 1966.​ Sepia Times, NY Daily News, Evers, Joost / Anefo​ A fire retardant previously used to keep rubber tires from drying out and applied as a preservative on fruits and alfalfa, production of the antioxidant was soon ramped up.  “Antioxidant treatment has made bulk handling an easy matter,” the director of the Canadian Department of Fisheries told an industry publication in 1966, arguing it should be required for fishmeal shipments.  The chemical was highly effective. By the 1970s, press-reported fires dropped sharply—from a typical 16 ship fires a year, according to the Liverpool Underwriters Association, to five.  Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one. To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How By 1976, the U.S. Coast Guard imposed mandatory ethoxyquin treatment on fishmeal shipments, and three years later, the United Nations body that oversees maritime activity recommended fishmeal be treated with it “to prevent spontaneous combustion.”  But there was a problem: Ethoxyquin is a carcinogen.  “Toxic effects had been observed in laboratory animals fed high concentrations of ethoxyquin,” said a 1969 paper by U.N. food and agriculture authorities. As its use in animal feeds and aquaculture grew, a 1987 study by British researchers found the chemical “caused severe damage” and had a potentially “carcinogenic effect” in rats. In 2015, the European Food Safety Authority said an impurity within ethoxyquin, known as p-phenetidine, was capable of causing mutations in genetic material.  There is a lack of scientific consensus on whether it is safe to eat farmed seafood raised on feed treated with ethoxyquin, but some countries have considered the risk to be high enough to justify banning or limiting the use of the chemical. In 2017, the European Commission suspended authorization for its use in animal feed across the European Union. Today, ethoxyquin has been banned in the U.K. and by members of the European Economic Area, including Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein. But ethoxyquin, within limits, is still permitted in animal feed in Australia, Japan, South Korea, and the U.S. With more than half of the seafood eaten worldwide now coming from fish farms, and with the majority of such species fed fishmeal and fish oil, studying the chemicals added to feed is critical for understanding the possible contamination of our global food supply. Although ethoxyquin is not banned in the U.S., it has been at the center of a half-dozen lawsuits, typically involving claims of false advertising. Some lawsuits targeted seafood companies for marketing their products as “sustainable” even though they contained ethoxyquin, while others highlighted the potential risks that the additive poses to the environment.  In 2022, a New York resident brought a class-action lawsuit against Aldi Inc., a German supermarket chain with stores in the U.S., alleging its Atlantic salmon products were falsely labeled as “sustainable” due to “environmentally destructive” practices. The complaint cited the EU’s ban on the chemical and a study linking ethoxyquin to mortality and deformations in fish and crustaceans, noting the chemical “poses a risk for aquatic life.” The case was settled out of court.  The same year, a New York and a California resident jointly sued Gorton’s Inc., a seafood company, for labeling its frozen tilapia as “sustainably sourced” despite containing ethoxyquin. This lawsuit also cited the “risk for aquatic life” and the European Union’s ban, and was settled out of court. In Canada, the country’s Food Inspection Agency requires feeds containing ethoxyquin to carry a label declaring that it meets the legal limits, but the agency does not specify how it tests for the chemical in feeds. Inspectors also do not check whether ethoxyquin ends up in the seafood itself, according to the agency’s latest food inspection report from 2022.  And a 2024 audit of the Canadian agency by the EU found it completed only about 40 percent of its planned inspections, citing “systematic and significant under-delivery” in terms of testing seafood products. Cargill said in a statement that it has assessed alternative antioxidants since 2005 and no longer uses ethoxyquin in its global salmon feed business or in any market where ethoxyquin is not authorized for use in aquafeed. The company also noted that it did not develop ethoxyquin. Globally, producers and feed makers have also increasingly shifted to alternatives, including natural additives such as rosemary extract and vitamin E compounds. “More and more destinations are not accepting ethoxyquin, starting with our local Peruvian market,” said James Frank, managing director of the Peruvian fishmeal company MSICeres, during a 2022 webinar. He added that 100 percent of Peru’s fishmeal exports to Europe, Canada, the U.S. and Australia are now ethoxyquin-free, a shift also seen among companies in the U.K. and Norway.  The most popular alternative to ethoxyquin is now butylated hydroxyanisole, or BHA, favored for its lower costs and strong antioxidant properties compared with fully natural additives. But like the chemical it aims to supplant, BHA has its own significant health risks, according to researchers.  The U.S. National Toxicology Program identified BHA as “reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen” as early as 1991, and Japanese researchers found it caused malignant tumors in laboratory rats in 2008. In February, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced it was reassessing the safety of the substance as a food additive.  To address the world’s insatiable hunger for seafood, the aquaculture industry will continue to expand. Perhaps there’ll be a shift away from carnivorous fish, or a replacement will be found for fishmeal. But for now, the aquaculture and fishmeal industries find themselves in a perilous loop: pivoting from deadly ship fires to a carcinogenic fire retardant, and then to yet another one. Getty Adam Maguire Business Journalist The origins of the Paris Motor Show date back to the late 19th century - long before most of the car brands we know today even existed. And while the biennial event is open to car-makers from around the globe, it's traditionally served as a chance for Europe’s car industry to flex its motoring muscle on the world’s stage. This year, though, the Europeans had to make room for a major rival. A lot of room. Because, of the 64 manufacturers that were exhibiting this week, nearly one third were Chinese-owned. That has underlined the stark challenge now facing Europe’s car industry, as its major players struggle to keep up with what is often more advanced – as well as cheaper - competition. That has sparked an industry-wide reckoning, with deep cost-cutting programmes underway. But China staking a claim for Europe’s car market has also created political concern, at a time when the EU-China trading relationship is under intense scrutiny. Accelerating sales  In a lot of ways, China is still a relatively small player in the European car market. In Ireland, for example, the biggest Chinese brand here is currently BYD. It had just over 4,400 car registrations in the first nine months of the year, according to the Society of the Irish Motor Industry. The next biggest is MG (which many may think of as English, but has actually been Chinese-owned for more than 20 years). It had a little over 2,800 new cars registered in Ireland in the first nine months of this year. After that you have Volvo – again, now Chinese-owned. It had a bit over 2,000 registrations between January and September. And then you have smaller brands like Xpeng, Leapmotor* and Polestar, which have registered a few hundred cars each so far this year. (*Leapmotor’s European business is actually a joint venture between China’s Leapmotor and Europe’s Stellantis – which owns a range of brands like Fiat, Peugeot and Opel.) It means that, all in all, a little over 10,000 cars registered in Ireland so far this year were made by Chinese-owned companies. That’s out of around 128,000 registrations total in the nine months – giving Chinese brands 8.3% of the new car market here. So - a decent share, but not exactly dominant. Meanwhile data from the ACEA - or the European Automobile Manufacturers Association – can then tell us how these brands are doing across the EU, European Free Trade Area and UK. According to its figures, Chinese-owned brands sold around 725,000 vehicles across the region in the first eight months of the year; out of a total of 7.5 million sales. So that’s a 9.6% share. Again, decent but not dominant. What is notable, though, is how quickly China’s share has been growing. For example, while Chinese-owned brands only have an 8.3% share in Ireland so far this year, that’s well up on the 5% share they had in the same period of 2025. In the first nine months of 2024, those brands held less than 4% of the market. Bear in mind, too, that BYD – the biggest-selling Chinese brand in the country - only launched in Ireland in 2023. In Europe, meanwhile, while Chinese brands have a near 10% share of the market so far this year – it was just over 6% in 2025. Cornering EVs  The numbers are even more stark when you isolate out full electric vehicles. It has been the main – but by no means exclusive - focus of Chinese manufacturers’ expansion into Europe. When you look at the SIMI stats for EVs only, you can see that Chinese producers are very big players. Like with car sales in general, they’re not dominant - established brands like Kia, Volkswagen and Hyundai currently sit in the top three of EV makers here so far this year. But, when you add all of the China-owned brands together, you can see that they make up around 17.8% of all EV sales here in 2026 so far. That compares to a 13.6% share of EV sales in the same period of last year – so they’re taking a bigger piece of what is a rapidly growing market. The European figures are a bit harder to break down – the ACEA don’t give EV sales by car-maker. But, if we were to use the Irish figures as an indication, it would suggest that Chinese company’s account for around a quarter of all EV sales in Europe – possibly even more. Hitting the brakes  This is of particular concern to European car-makers because they’ve tended to do well in their home market. EVs are also where the industry is moving. They are now the best-selling engine type in Ireland, and they’re in joint second across Europe. (The most popular are hybrids – where Chinese car-makers are also very competitive). It means that, just at the time when European firms need to invest heavily in new types of vehicle, new platforms and new technologies, they’re finding themselves being undercut by cheaper, more advanced and more nimble competition from China. And it’s taking away sales they may previously have relied upon. Those sales - which could have justified all their investment plans, and all of the existing costs they have relating to factories, brands, and marketing – are now in doubt. And that – along with US tariffs on the other side - is forcing many of these companies to undertake significant restructurings. Germany’s Volkswagen is perhaps the best example – it recently struck a deal with unions that would see it cut 50,000 jobs across its operation. That’s on top of a 50,000 job cut previously announced. That’s more than 15% of its total workforce. The move is part of a plan that will see it cut its costs by 20% in the coming years – because that’s the cost disadvantage it reckons it has with its Chinese rivals. Some of those savings will come from administration – but key to the restructuring is also a simplification of the group’s business. After all, Volkswagen Group is not just Volkswagen – it also owns Audi, Skoda, Seat and Porsche. Each of these brands have countless makes and models and variations, but head office now Plans is to slash that dramatically to simplify its structure. It’s also looking at potentially shutting down or repurposing some of the factories it has – though that’s something that has been kicked down the road, and could cause political headaches in Germany. But it’s not just Volkswagen – French-Italian group Stellantis is aiming to cut €6 billion in costs by the end of 2028. That includes trying to make the factories it runs more efficient, while also potentially selling some of the less productive ones off. It’s also looking at cutting thousands of engineering jobs globally. Jaguar Land Rover is cutting thousands of jobs in the UK, as part of a £1.7 billion cost-cutting programme. Meanwhile BMW is also trying to cut costs, though it’s focused on slashing middle-management while also investing in its production as part of its turnaround plan. All-in-all it’s estimated that European car-makers are shaping up to cut 30-40% from their cost base just to stay competitive. European Drive  But it’s not just the car-makers themselves that are repositioning themselves in the face of Chinese competition. EU politicians are trying to respond, too. That’s because there’s a distinct memory in Europe of both the steel and solar panel industries being decimated by Chinese competition in the recent past. Both markets were flooded with cheap product from China, regional producers couldn’t compete, and they were ultimately pushed out of business. And given how important car-making is to the European economy – and particularly big European economies like Germany, France and Italy – the prospect of them becoming bit players in the market, or even out of business altogether, would have huge ramifications for the region’s economy. But it also poses a broader challenge – as it would further erode Europe’s manufacturing base while also increasing its reliance on China. This is at a time when the EU is trying desperately to boost European manufacturing in order to make it less reliant on others. In particular China. Central to Europe’s concern too is the belief that Chinese car companies are not playing fair – and are only able to put up such stiff competition because they received substantial subsidies from the state. The view is that, many years ago, China decided to build a domestic car industry, so it pumped lots of money into multiple producers. They then ramped up production to the point that they were making more cars than Chinese consumers could buy, so then they turned all of that extra output towards other markets, like Europe. And given the state’s effective backstop, they don’t have to worry about running the business in a sustainable or profitable way – so they can sell for much cheaper than would otherwise be possible. For what it’s worth, China and its car-makers have consistently denied that they’ve benefitted from unfair advantages. They say that they can make cheaper cars because they’ve been more focused on EVs for longer – unlike European producers, who have been slow to move towards EVs and hybrids, because they wanted to protect their share of the combustion engine market. They also say they benefit from more efficient manufacturing. BYD, for example, is vertically integrated, so it makes most of what’s in its cars rather than relying on third party suppliers. It was actually a battery company that eventually started to build a car around that key component. Today it even owns its own cargo ship so it doesn’t have to pay third parties to bring its cars from one part of the world to the other. So, China’s argument is that European car-makers are just too bloated and slow – and Chinese producers shouldn’t be punished for that. To a certain degree, European car-makers seem to be accepting that argument. They wouldn’t be undertaking such hefty cost-cutting programmes if they felt they were already running as lean an operation as they could. Interestingly, though, they’ve also been slow to back moves to punish Chinese car-makers for other reasons. Because most major European car-makers also have joint-ventures in China. They know that, if Europe makes it too hard for Chinese companies to sell here, their lucrative partnerships could be targeted by any retaliation from China. Safety first  As important as the economics of China’s rise may be, another thing concerning European officials is the security risk it may pose. Because modern cars – and especially EVs – are absolutely laden in sensors. They have GPS, telemetry monitors, they’re covered in cameras, they have microphones inside. They can also connect to smartphones and potentially tap into all those sensors too. And, if all that information from the right person got into the wrong hands, it poses a significant security risk. Chinese companies routinely deny that there’s any security risk coming from their vehicles. Some say the data they gather never leaves Europe, while others deny claims that Chinese security services have backdoor access to their systems. But there have been numerous tests and experiments to show that some cars sent data back to Chinese data centres. That includes a recent case in Norway, where researchers drove a Chinese-made SUV deep into an underground tunnel that would block any signal. Despite that, it kept trying to ping Chinese servers. The concern in Europe is that having lots of Chinese cars on European roads could give the country lots of valuable information. It could also represent a significant lever that could be pulled in any hostile situation – with the functionality of millions of cars on European roads open to exploitation. Trading in  To try to tackle this, two years ago the EU imposed some fairly hefty tariffs on Chinese-made cars. These differed from company to company – and were calculated based on the extent to which the EU felt each firm had benefitted from unfair assistance. But at the top of the list was SAIC Group (MG’s owner), which was hit with a 35.3% tariff. That was on top of the 10% base tariff that applied between the EU and China. That added to a growing trade dispute between the two sides – with China hitting back with tariffs on some European goods. But there have also been talks between the two sides in the months since – with those negotiations leading to a prospective deal this week which would see the number of hybrids China ships to Europe being capped at 350,000 a year. The tariffs remain on pure EVs for now, though. But how much they’ve impacted Chinese car-makers in debatable. After all, the data shows that Chinese car firms have continued to grow rapidly despite the supposed rebalancing of the fairness scale. Another complicating fact is that, while the companies themselves may be headquartered in China, that doesn’t automatically mean the cars they produce are Chinese-made. Because many of these car companies have been preparing for exactly this trade situation for years. Some already have manufacturing facilities in Europe, some are planning to build some in the near future. BYD, for example, is just about to start full-scale production at a plant in Hungary. It’s also reportedly looking at setting up production operations in France. It’s estimated that around 90,000 "Chinese" cars will be made in Europe this year – with that number rising to one million by 2030 and 1.5 million by 2035. And those cars will technically be European – and so not subject to tariffs. It means that Europe is now facing a new challenge of potentially having lots of factories that are really little more than assembly plans. Plants similar to the ones we used to have in Ireland, where parts were imported and put together locally (in order to avoid Irish tariffs). These kinds of facilities provide very little local economic benefit – especially now that car assembly is so heavily robot and automation-based. That means they wouldn’t do much to help the European car industry, its workers, or the surrounding economy. As a result Europe is now moving to try and get ahead of that new threat – with proposals moving forward that would require a certain percentage of each car is made from European-sourced parts. This 1968 BMW R60 is one of 728 US-market examples built for the model year and it was restored by its previous owner between 2015 and when it was acquired by the seller on BaT in February 2020. The bike is finished in black with white pinstripes and is powered by a 594cc opposed-twin paired with a four-speed transmission. Features include a low-rise handlebar, 18″ alloy rims, a driveshaft, a Denfeld saddle, bar-end mirrors, a locking storage compartment, a center stand, and dual Bing carburetors. This R60US is now offered with a Clymer service manual and a clean Arizona title in the seller’s name.  Manufactured from 1967 until 1969, the R60US was delivered from BMW with a conventional fork and without sidecar lugs, unlike its R60/2 counterpart. This example was stripped down to its frame during the restoration, and the 4.5-gallon fuel tank and fenders were refinished in black with hand-applied double-row white pinstriping. The frame and swingarm received a powder-coat finish, and the hardware was re-plated in chrome or zinc. A luggage rack was added under current ownership.  Polished aluminum rims are laced to drum-brake hubs with a set of stainless-steel spokes. Suspension is provided by a conventional leading-axle fork fork as well as preload-adjustable shocks mounted to the swingarm on the left and the final-drive housing on the right. Braking is handled by front and rear drums.  The chrome low-rise handlebar fronts a refurbished 120-mph speedometer and a pair of indicator lights. The five-digit odometer shows 946 miles, 650 of which were ridden under current ownership. Total mileage is unknown.  The 594cc opposed-twin was disassembled, including the crankshaft, before the aluminum castings for the case and covers were cleaned. The engine was reassembled with new first-oversize pistons, as well as new bearings for the crankshaft and camshaft. The heads received new valves and guides. Induction is through a pair of Bing carburetors wearing part numbers 1/24/149 and 1/24/150, as pictured in the gallery below. A break-in service was performed at 200 miles, which included re-torquing the heads, adjusting the valves, and changing the oil.  Power is sent to the rear wheel through a four-speed transmission as well as a driveshaft enclosed within the right leg of the swingarm.  The headstock plate indicates that this bike is a R60US with serial number 1815824, and photos showing the numbers stamped on the frame and engine case can be viewed in the gallery. While the iPhone is a popular brand, despite what you might think, it isn't the best-selling mobile phone of all time; that honor goes to the Nokia 1100. While Nokia isn't in the phone business anymore, it played a huge part in shaping the industry, partially because it questioned what it meant to be a cellphone. When most people think about Nokia phones, their mind goes to the Nokia 3310, a popular retro device with a numeric keypad (the number buttons doubled as an alphabet keyboard) that was touted as virtually indestructible. But Nokia frequently experimented with designs. Just look at the Nokia 3650: a phone that was nothing but rounded edges and a keypad that resembled a rotary phone. Sure, the 3650 was one of the first smartphones in the US to include an integrated camera, but users found the key layout so ungainly that its successor, the Nokia 3660, utilized a more traditional (and comfortable) grid-style key layout. And this was just the tip of the iceberg, as several designs were so unusual, many people erased them from their collective memories. In this article, we'll go over some of the strangest phones Nokia ever sold that you might have forgotten, ordered in weirdness. We'll not be discussing the Nokia N-Gage because Nokia's failed gaming platform is widely remembered for its poor implementation (and taco shell design). Also, the Nokia 7700 is out because it was canceled before release. Back when Nokia made phones, text messaging was in its infancy. If you wanted to type out "Hello" on the Nokia 3310, you needed to press the buttons "43555555666" on the keypad. Nokia experimented with alternate methods. These included the 5510, which crammed an entire QWERTY keyboard onto the front, and the Nokia 6800 line. At first glance, the Nokia 6800, 6810, and 6820 looked like standard cellphones of the time. They had a large screen up top, a numerical pad at the bottom, and squeezed between them were several buttons and a thumbstick for menu navigation. But then you notice the bottom could hinge, and you discover the 6800's secret sauce: the phones could unfold into a full QWERTY keyboard. Unlike modern smartphones with physical keyboards, a large screen split this device's keyboard down the middle. The result looked like an art piece designed to resemble a wristwatch. The Nokia 6800 line was known as the "messaging phone" or "messaging devices" and supported services based around their typing capabilities. These included email and BlackBerry support. The 6800 line only lasted from 2002 until 2006, when Nokia replaced it with the E70. However, that phone carried on the flip-out keyboard design and spirit. When the Nokia 6800 line flips open, the phones reveal a new set of keys, but they still use the same screen, albeit flipped on its side. But what if the phones opened to not only a keyboard but also a new screen? That's precisely what Nokia released a few years later. Like the Nokia 6800, Nokia 9300 initially appeared to be your standard cell phone with an equally standard keypad, but once you opened the device lengthwise, it turned into a completely different device. Sandwiched between the 9300's two halves, Nokia hid a larger screen and a full, albeit miniature, keyboard, complete with space bar and thumbstick. While in this secondary mode, the Nokia 9300 was basically a miniature laptop, squashed and stretched to a shape that could fit into most pockets. The device could even run programs like Microsoft Excel. Confusingly, the Nokia 9300 was remarkably similar to the Nokia 9500 Communicator — both could flip open to reveal a new screen and keypad. Yet the two phones were part of very different lines. Eventually the E90 Communicator (another phone with the same flip function conversion scheme) replaced both the 9300 and 9500. Smartphones are no longer just about phone calls and instant messages. Many people consider which smartphones have the best cameras when they shop for a new one. Even though many people carry the best cameras designed for tourists, some would rather just reach into their pocket and use their phone, inferior resolution be damned. But before smartphone cameras could fly, Nokia made phone cameras that walked. The Nokia N90 was arguably one of the most novel entries in Nokia's Nseries, sporting a unique design that revolved (figuratively and literally) around numerous swiveling parts. You could flip the phone up like normal, but if you tilted the screen 90 degrees, you could then swivel it perpendicularly another 90 degrees and turn the N90 into a makeshift camcorder.The camera portion could swivel as well, just in case you wanted to take a selfie video. Nokia followed up the N90 with the N93, which continued aping camcorders but with different arrangements of swivels. Instead of letting the camera twist around, Nokia installed a different joint that let the top section swivel even when closed, making it one of the only phones that could flip open on two different axes. However, that was it for the camcorder design. The next in the N90 series, the Nokia N95, was just a high-end phone that could slide open in two directions — one for phone calls, one for multimedia. So far, we've mostly gone over phones that flip and fold every which way but the ones you'd expect. But Nokia is as famous for a phone design so plain it's downright iconic — the Nokia 3310 — as it is infamous for the taco-shaped Nokia N-Gage. While the company was usually more restrained in its strange designs, sometimes it built devices that made you ask, "That's a phone?" The Nokia 7600 was basically a Rorschach test you can touch. Was it shaped like a leaf, or did it resemble an artisanal bar of soap? Whatever it was, one side featured a central screen, number buttons arranged on each side of said screen, and a d-pad underneath. And on the other side rested a camera lens. And we can't forget about the Nokia 7600's voice memo button and optional leather wrist strap. In the spirit of fairness, owners could swap out plates to customize the Nokia 7600, but they did nothing to mitigate the unorthodox silhouette and painfully unergonomic keypad layout. And how did you make calls on this device? Much like how you needed to hold the Nokia N-Gage on its side, you had to tilt the 7600 at a slight angle, which put one of the sharper corners right in your ear canal. Even if the person you called didn't talk your ear off, using the Nokia 7600 for long enough would certainly make it feel like your ear was ready to fall off. Design quirks aside, every phone in this article has one thing in common: They have plenty of buttons. Some have more than others, but you can still quickly type out the number of the person you want to call. Even smartphones and their touchscreens display simple grid button layouts so you can swiftly enter a phone number. But once upon a time Nokia got rid of all that and called it fashion. The Nokia 7280 is arguably the company's most unorthodox phone, if not the most unorthodox phone period. The device was introduced as part of Nokia's "fashion line" and was purportedly "inspired by the glamour and elegance of the lavish 1920s." In other words, the Nokia 7280 looked less like a phone and more like a lipstick holder. Or a very fancy MP3 player. The only telltale signs of the device's cellphone nature were its screen and dial. Yes, the Nokia 7280 was a completely keyless phone. Owners could only navigate its menus — and input numbers for calls – by using the dial and buttons on its "front," which was glacially slow and tedious. To make matters more confusing, the screen was stuck in landscape mode. And the icing on the cake? In order to snap pictures or talk, owners had to pop the top up, turning the Nokia into an art deco "Men in Black" neuralyzer. Little fun fact: You might have seen a Nokia 7280 without realizing what it was, as the phone appeared in music videos for Jennifer Lopez' "Get Right" and The Pussycat Dolls' "Beep."

It is essential to emphasize that Spanish anarchism was not merely a program embedded in a dense theoretical matrix. It was a way of life: partly the life of the Spanish people as it was lived in the closely knit villages of the countryside and the intense neighborhood life of the working class barrios; partly, too, the theoretical articulation of that life as projected by Bakunin’s concepts of decentralization, mutual aid, and popular organs of self-management. That Spain had a long tradition of agrarian collectivism is discussed in this book and examined in some detail in Joaquin Costa’s Colectivismo Agrario en Espagna. Inasmuch as this tradition was distinctly precapitalist, Spanish Marxism regarded it as anachronistic, in fact as “historically reactionary.” Spanish socialism built its agrarian program around the Marxist tenet that the peasantry and its social forms could have no lasting revolutionary value until they were “proletarianized” and “industrialized.” Indeed, the sooner the village decayed the better, and the more rapidly the peasantry became a hereditary proletariat, “disciplined, united, organized by the very mechanism of the process of capitalist production itself” (Marx) — a distinctly hierarchical and authoritarian “mechanism” — the more rapidly Spain would advance to the tasks of socialism. Spanish anarchism, by contrast, followed a decisively different approach. It sought out the precapitalist collectivist traditions of the village, nourished what was living and vital in them, evoked their revolutionary potentialities as liberatory modes of mutual aid and self-management, and deployed them to vitiate the obedience, hierarchical mentality, and authoritarian outlook fostered by the factory system. US President Donald Trump has suspended sweeping new sanctions against Russia that he signed into law just a month ago, invoking a national-interest exemption to waive penalties targeting Moscow’s economy and countries purchasing Russian energy. In an executive order issued on Friday, Trump waived sanctions and tariffs mandated by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, including proposed 500% tariffs on imports from Russia and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification,” Trump wrote. China and India, the two largest buyers of Russian crude oil, were expected to be among the countries hardest hit by the legislation. The bill, championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, has been described by supporters as a “bone-crushing” measure aimed at driving Russian energy exports out of the global market. Hawkish US lawmakers argued that existing restrictions had allowed Moscow to circumvent economic pressure. Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports earlier this month in an effort to curb rising energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections. The move sparked outrage in Ukraine and among America’s European allies, prompting a bipartisan group of US senators to accuse Trump of betraying Kiev. According to US media reports, Trump decided to ease sanctions after Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky refused to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities, which Trump blamed for high energy prices. On Friday, US Representative Gregory Meeks introduced a bill in Congress seeking to block the diesel agreement with Russia. The Democrat accused Trump of “cozying up to [Russian President Vladimir] Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine.” Trump has defended the agreement as beneficial to American consumers and consistent with his “America First” agenda. In response to the backlash, he attacked Zelensky as “not a good guy for us to deal with” and suggested that Ukraine needed “a new president.” Russia has maintained that it has adapted to mounting Western economic pressure, while describing the Graham bill as a hostile move that would undermine Trump’s efforts to broker peace between Moscow and Kiev. “[Russian] diesel has begun reaching global markets, and it will have a certain positive effect on stabilizing oil markets,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Thursday. Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s investment envoy and a negotiator on Ukraine, hailed the waiver as “an important and historic moment.” Economic cooperation serves the interests of both countries, “contributes to global economic stability, and lays the foundation for building trust and achieving lasting peace,” he wrote on X.
